#2837. Eagles continue reshaping roster by reportedly releasing veteran wide receiver

Eagles continue reshaping roster by reportedly releasing veteran wide receiver originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Hollywood Brown's brief and odd Eagles career is over after four games and five catches.

The Eagles are releasing Brown by mutual consent of the player and the team, Jordan Schultz of the Scultz Report posted on social media Thursday night.

The Eagles signed Brown to a one-year, $5 million contract in March with the expectation that he'd be a significant part of the Eagles' passing game following the departure of A.J. Brown. But even with Brown gone and DeVonta Smith and Dontayvion Wicks both hurt much of the season, Brown has been an afterthought.

He's only played in four of the Eagles' nine games, getting nine targets and catching five passes for 63 yards along with two rushing attempts for 12 yards. His longest catch was a 19-yarder from Tanner McKee in the loss to the Cowboys. He had a season-high 30 yards in that game.

Brown expressed frustration with his limited role in a recent conversation with NBC Sports Philadelphia:

"Of course, you want to be somewhere where you play, but at the ultimate end of the day, it's not my plan. So I might want to play, I might want to contribute, but if that's not the plan for me, I can't dwell on it too much or you'll be unhappy. And then you're taking that back home. I can't take that back home to the wife and kids. So I gotta try to stay as positive as I can."

Asked how that was going, he laughed and said, "Some days better than others."

He added: "We're all dealing with something and we're dealing with something as a team. So I don't wanna add that extra stress."

Brown said he expected to play more but was dealing with it because he didn't want to put personal issues ahead of team needs.

"I did (expect a bigger role), but I do understand stuff happens," he said. "I mean, you can't take anything personal in this business, so you kind of just got to go about your process and when that time happens, whatever happens, you've just got to be ready for it."

Brown, a 1st-round pick in 2019, had a 1,000-yard season for the Ravens in 2021 and over 700 yards in both 2020 and 2022. He was 49-for-587 with five touchdowns last year. In his career, he has 378 catches for 4,385 yards and 33 touchdowns.

The Eagles, 2-7, have lost seven straight game. Their offense is ranked 32nd in the NFL in yards per game, 30th in points per game and 29th in passing yards per game.

With Brown no longer on the roster, the Eagles have rookie 1st-round pick Makai Lemon, 2nd-year undrafted free agent Darius Cooper and Elijah Moore as healthy wide receivers. Smith and Wicks have both missed the last two games but could be back after the bye week.

Lemon is the Eagles' leading receiver with 37-for-312 and a touchdown and Smith (26-310-2), Wicks (19-284-1) and Cooper (13-200-4) are next.

The Eagles have two WRs on the practice squad – Erik Ezukanma and Xavier Gipson.

Because it's after the trade deadline, Brown is subject to the waiver claim process despite being a vested veteran with seven years of pension credit.

#2836. Cunningham’s 52 points help the Pistons outlast the Wizards 144-140 in double overtime

Cade Cunningham scored a career-high 52 points and had 11 assists, and the Detroit Pistons outlasted Washington 144-140 in double overtime Thursday night after the Wizards twice extended the game with last-second shots.

Trae Young's 3-pointer at the buzzer forced the first overtime, and then rookie AJ Dybantsa's midrange effort with less than a second left sent the teams to another OT. But Cunningham quickly made a 3-pointer, and then Anthony Davis fouled out to give Detroit the upper hand.

It was still a two-point game in the final minute, but Cunningham scored from the baseline to make it 142-138 with 25.3 seconds left. Washington has lost six straight.

Detroit's Ausar Thompson had 17 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists for his first career triple-double.

Young had 37 points for the Wizards but shot just 8 of 23. Davis and Alex Sarr scored 30 each as the franchise had its first trio of 30-point scorers since Mike Davis, Earl Monroe and Gus Johnson for the Baltimore Bullets on Nov. 18, 1969.

Young had 14 assists, two more than Washington's whole team managed in a loss at Indiana the previous night.

Cunningham's previous career high was 46 points, just over a year ago — and also against Washington. He became the first NBA player with 50 points, 10 assists and no turnovers since the league began tracking turnovers in 1977-78, according to OptaSTATS.

Detroit beat the Wizards for the second time in four games. The Pistons overcame Davis' 44 points to win Monday, and Washington looked ready to end its skid when it scored the first seven points of the first overtime Thursday to lead 128-121. Then Cunningham rallied Detroit.

He finished 16 of 25 from the field and 17 of 18 on free throws. Daniss Jenkins scored 21 points for the Pistons before fouling out. Kyshawn George fouled out for the Wizards after scoring 14.

Sarr was 10 of 10 from the field in regulation and finished 12 of 14.

Pistons: At Miami on Saturday night.Wizards: Host Houston on Sunday night.

#2834. Dame Time is back in Portland — and the Blazers look dangerous

A new head coach will roam the sidelines. A franchise icon will make his long-awaited return. An All-Star will begin his redemption tour.

And a new ownership group will watch its first season opener from Paul Allen's former seats along the Moda Center baseline.

The Blazers open the 2026-27 NBA season Wednesday night against the Phoenix Suns — a team they upset in April in the play-in tournament — and if you're just now tuning in for the start of the regular season, well, there's a lot you missed.

RELATED: Suns vs. Blazers predictions, odds and best bets: Dame is home, and the model likes Portland on opening night

The Blazers are expected to unveil a new starting lineup that features a pair of notable All-Star additions: Damian Lillard and Ja Morant. The backcourt duo is joining a fivesome that includes returning starters Deni Avdija, Toumani Camara and Donovan Clingan. It's a versatile, star-studded lineup that features three All-Stars, a former All-Defensive Second Team selection, one of the best young centers in the NBA and loads of scoring potential.

Micah Nori, the Blazers' first-year head coach, said he plans on using a 10-man rotation to start the season, which will allow the Blazers to capitalize on their depth and versatility. In addition to the starters, Jrue Holiday, Scoot Henderson, Sidy Cissoko, Robert Williams III and Vit Krejci are expected to open the season in the rotation. The group could change depending on matchups and Williams' availability — he did not play in back-to-backs last season — and it's likely that Micah Potter, Branden Carlson and Yang Hansen will occasionally see spot duty, as well.

The Blazers stabilized their turbulent coaching situation in June, hiring longtime NBA assistant Nori to replace interim coach Tiago Splitter. Nori, who interviewed for head coaching jobs seven times before finally landing his first chance, is entering his 29th season in the league and is universally revered in NBA circles for his positive approach, ability to connect with players and sharp basketball mind. Early indications have been encouraging, as the Blazers players seem to love him and the front office works well with him. The Blazers' coaching position had been embroiled in controversy, of course, as former coach Chauncey Billups — who was placed on indefinite leave by the NBA — is facing federal felony charges related to money laundering and wire fraud conspiracy for his alleged involvement in a rigged underground poker game.

In a stark contrast to recent seasons, the Blazers are constructed around their offense rather than their defense. The roster is unbalanced, featuring five dynamic ball-handlers and playmakers (Lillard, Morant, Avdija, Holiday and Henderson), a solid center combination (Clingan and Williams) and little wing depth. As a result, the team is expected to play fast and free under Nori, bringing lots of speed, passing, cutting and flow. Nori said he hopes to rotate his players liberally in shorter shifts during games — perhaps as short as three minutes — which will enable them to play with maximum effort before giving way to teammates. The interior defense is strong with Clingan and Williams patrolling the middle, Camara remains one of the NBA's best and most versatile defenders and Cissoko will be asked to guard one-through-five. Holiday is still capable of locking down opposing guards and Avdija has pledged to be more of a two-way threat now that he doesn't have to serve as the team's primary ball-handler. But the backcourt combination of Morant and Lillard, while lethal on offense, is not imposing on defense and relatively small (both stand 6-foot-2).

Portland defied pundits last season, winning 10 of its last 14 regular season games to secure a spot in the play-in tournament, where it beat the Suns in Phoenix to earn the seventh seed in the Western Conference. The San Antonio Spurs dismissed the Blazers with a gentleman's sweep in the playoffs, but the strong run — combined with the additions of Lillard and Morant — has raised expectations in Portland. How much? Camara said in training camp that the Blazers' goal is to win 50 or more games and secure home-court advantage in the postseason. It won't be easy. The league is as deep and talented as ever, and new rules surrounding the lottery should discourage teams from tanking, meaning most of the league will be chasing wins instead of lottery ping-pong balls late into the season. It seemed like a third of the league had given up last year by the All-Star break.

Hopes for a Blazers, Moda Center deal by December deadline appear all but dashed

Joe Freeman's 3 takeaways from the Trail Blazers' back-to-back sweep vs. Thunder

Trail Blazers lose rotation player for 2 months

Joe Freeman's 3 takeaways from Trail Blazers' rout over the Thunder

Thunder vs. Blazers predictions: Portland looks to snap two-game skid in the first of back-to-back meetings

As the Blazers' new-look lineup works to build chemistry and a first-year coach settles into a new role, the schedule will be challenging. Six of the first eight games — and 12 of the first 17 — will come on the road and include a slew of playoff contenders, including the Spurs, Oklahoma City Thunder (twice), Minnesota Timberwolves (twice), New York Knicks, Philadelphia 76ers, Denver Nuggets and Los Angeles Lakers (twice).

The most uplifting part of opening night figures to be the return of Lillard, the franchise icon who is back after spending two seasons in Milwaukee and one season on the injured list. The nine-time All-Star and franchise leader has not played in an NBA regular-season or playoff game since April 27, 2025, when he suffered a torn left Achilles tendon. And he has not played with Portland since March 22, 2023, six months before it traded him to the Bucks. Lillard showed no ill effects from his injury during the exhibition season, when he played in three of the Blazers' four games and averaged 17.3 points, 2.7 assists and 22.7 minutes. If anything, he looked like the same old Dame, swishing three-pointers, creating off the dribble, initiating offense and drawing defensive attention. Lillard joked earlier this week that he's "not an old man," but also acknowledged that he isn't likely to play upward of 38 minutes a game like he used to and may even take a night off here and there for rest, most likely on a random back-to-back. His addition not only should help cover up two of the Blazers' biggest weaknesses last season — three-point shooting and shooting in the clutch — but also inspire a thirsty fan base, which has rarely loved a player more. All the while, Lillard says he intends to play with more "joy" than ever.

#2832. Stats Rundown: 3 numbers to know from the Mavericks’ 133-94 embarrassment at Minnesota

The Dallas Mavericks (7-5) had no stomach for the fight on Thursday, dropping an embarrassing 133-94 loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves (9-3) at Target Center. Bones Hyland led all scorers with 24 points off the Minnesota bench, while LaMelo Ball dropped 22 for the Wolves in just 25 minutes in the win.

Zaccharie Risacher led the Mavericks with 22 points off the bench in the loss.

Let's not belabor the point. This was a straightforward ass-whipping. Here are some stats from the Mavericks' no good, very bad day at the office.

If you blinked late in the first quarter, you may have missed the moment the Mavericks went from firmly in control to flailing. PJ Washington drove for a contested layup, and Naji Marshall followed that, the next time down, with a pair of free throws to extend the Mavs' early lead to 24-19 as Flagg took his normal rest stretch on the bench.

From there, Bones Hyland and Ayo Dosunmu keyed a 15-2 run over the last 2:48 of the first. Dosunmu hit his first bucket of the game, a 3-pointer from the right wing with 1:38 left in the opening frame, to swing the Wolves back in front, 26-24. Then, after Marshall stopped the bleeding with another 2-for-2 trip to the line, Jaylen Clark banged in a last-second 3-ball of his own to extend Minnesota's lead to 34-26.

The Mavs did not connect on a field goal in the final 3:34 of the quarter after Flagg went to the bench a minute before that. Dallas finished the first 9-0f-25 (36%) from the floor, while the Timberwolves shot a much healthier 12-of-22 (54.5%) to open the game.

The Mavericks scored 22 of their first 42 points off Minnesota turnovers on Thursday. That's a full 52.8% of the points the Mavs scored over the first 19 minutes of the game that came off the Timberwolves' nine turnovers.

Dallas got out and ran early in the second to battle back from what eventually bloomed into a 10-point hole. Flagg got into a passing lane for his first steal of the contest with seven minutes left in the half, which led to a ferocious dunk from Zaccharie Risacher that cut the Timberwolves' lead to 43-42.

But Minnesota embarked on another 12-3 run from that point, and guess what they didn't do during that run? If you guessed "turn the ball over," you would be correct. The Mavs weren't able to manufacture a whole lot of offense in the halfcourt throughout the first half. Dallas' defense was the only thing fueling the team's offense. Meanwhile, on the other end, The Wolves were pouring it on.

Minny shot 27-of-44 (61.4%) from the field in the first half, while the Mavs shot just 20-of-48 (41.7%). That disparity led to the Timberwolves' swolen 67-52 lead at the break.

A vibrant, colorful and above all, ridiculous rapid-fire discussion erupted in the MavsMoneyball Slack channel in the third quarter on Thursday, partially debating whether it was the Mavericks' offense that failed the defense or the defense that called it a night early and left the offense on an island. Whichever way you lean, neither of these things can happen when you're facing a bona fide early-season juggernaut like the Anthony Edwards-less Timberwolves. The Wolves came into the game with the NBA's best defensive rating (105.1).

Flagg did nothing on the defensive end. Marshall one-upped him by beating his head against a wall on both ends of the floor. Someone tried to make the argument that Martin was the best player on the floor for Dallas for long stretches of the first half. Risacher's stat line ended up looking good in the loss, but that was influenced loudly by the fact that garbage time against the Wolves stretched into most of the second half. For the record, Risacher led the Mavs with 22 points on 9-of-14 shooting (4-of-8 from 3-point range), to go along with six rebounds, two steals and a blocked shot in the loss.

After coming into the second half leading by 15, the Timberwolves outscored the Mavs 36-17 in the third to put Dallas to bed early. Just a piss poor effort on all fronts against a foe that will embarrass you if effort and execution elude you for 48 minutes. Which it did. So they did.

#2831. Russian crude production rebounds after Trump diesel deal, IEA says as oil markets return to surplus

Russia's crude oil production rose to 8.73 million barrels a day in October, a 210,000-barrel-a-day surge, as a rebound in Gulf shipments pushes oil markets into a surplus for the first time since the Middle East conflict began, the International Energy Agency said Friday.

Global supply and stocks have both swelled, though Middle East disruptions and attacks on Russian energy infrastructure tightened diesel supply, according to the agency's latest monthly oil market report.

"Persistent attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continue to choke off the country's diesel supplies to international markets, adding to losses from the Middle East," the IEA noted.

U.S. President Donald Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to supply diesel to global markets on Oct. 9. The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a general license authorizing certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027.

Crude supply can rise even as diesel remains tight, with refinery capacity and refined product exports still constrained.

Global oil supply reached 105.4 million barrels a day in October, up 2.3 million barrels a day from September, the IEA said, adding that supply rose by an "extraordinary" 5.3 million barrels a day since August, despite ongoing attacks on energy infrastructure and tankers.

Inventories also rose for the first time since June, with observed global stocks increasing by 52 million barrels in October, or 1.7 million barrels a day.

"The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," IEA analysts observed.

Higher export flows have strengthened supply expectations for the fourth quarter, with Middle East and Russia losses partly offset by growth from the U.S., Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana, which together are set to boost output by 1.6 million barrels a day this year.

The IEA has raised its fourth-quarter supply estimate by 3.3 million barrels a day, and now forecasts a 6.6 million barrels per day increase in 2027.

#2830. Oregon QB Dante Moore ruled out for rest of 2026 season

Oregon Ducks quarterback Dante Moore will miss the rest of the season, coach Dan Lanning announced Monday night.

"I'm not anticipating him being back this season," Lanning said.

"Really got clarity for us this past week, for him," Lanning added. "And I think if it were up to Dante in any shape, way, he would want to be out there playing for the guys. But, unfortunately, it's not really up to Dante. It's not really up to me. We can control the setting and practice where he's able to do things for us, but that's not always the case in the game."

Lanning said he expects Moore, who has run scout-team offense in practice, to fully recover.

"That hasn't changed," Lanning said. "Definitely feel that way, but for him to be out there on the field for us right now, that's not gonna happen."

Lanning added that Moore would remain involved with the team.

"He's still going to be a big part of this team and helping us move forward and find opportunities for us to be better," Lanning said.

The announcement comes days after the reeling Ducks lost 21-10 at Illinois on Saturday in the third straight game Moore missed while in concussion protocol.

Before the Illinois game, Moore told The Oregonian/OregonLive that he felt good but didn't know if he'd return this season and was taking it "one day at a time."

He then began throwing passes on the field in shorts and a sweatshirt.

Saturday's loss all but knocked Oregon (4-3, 2-2 Big Ten) out of the national playoff picture and led Lanning to fire offensive coordinator Drew Mehringer on Sunday.

Without Moore, Oregon scored 42 points over three games and lost twice while rotating between backup quarterbacks Dylan Raiola and Brock Thomas.

Moore was injured on Sept. 26 at USC while sliding to end a 10-yard run to the USC 13-yard line. As Moore began to slide, Trojans linebacker Desman Stephens II hit him in the head with his shoulder.

Oregon quarterback Dante Moore, center bottom, takes a hard tackle by lSouthern California inebacker Desman Stephens II, center top, during the first half of an NCAA college football game, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026, in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill)AP Photo/Mark J. Terrill

Moore was taken off the field in a cart and loaded into an ambulance.

Following Moore's injury, Raiola entered the game and led the Ducks to a 41-27 win.

Moore entered the concussion protocol but returned to practice the following bye week.

Speculation was that Moore would return once he cleared the protocols. But each subsequent availability report listed Moore as out.

On Oct. 10, Oregon lost 17-15 to UCLA, with Raiola struggling through three quarters before being replaced in the fourth quarter by Thomas.

Thomas started the following week against Nebraska, but he played poorly before Raiola entered the game in the fourth quarter and led the Ducks to a 17-14 comeback win.

Oregon's realistic national playoff hopes remained alive at 4-2 — until the loss to Illinois.

At 4-3, the Ducks must win their final five games to reach 9-3 and hope enough playoff contenders finish with three losses so the Ducks can receive a berth.

If Moore enters the 2027 NFL Draft, his announcement will end his brief Ducks career, during which he led the program to one of its best seasons.

Oregon quarterback Dante Moore walks off the field after the No. 5 Ducks fall to the No. 1 Indiana Hoosiers, 56-22, in the Peach Bowl at the College Football Playoff semifinals from Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta on Friday, Jan. 9, 2025. Sean Meagher/The OregonianSean Meagher/The Oregonian

Lanning said he wasn't sure what Moore's plans were after this season.

"That's not fair for me to say or speculate," Lanning said. "Obviously, he'll have a decision again at the end of the season and what that looks like. I think we all can acknowledge that Dante is a great player and he will get an opportunity to get drafted. But what that looks like in the future, I think that's a decision for a later date. I don't know where his mind is at on that. We haven't had a conversation. That's not where my focus is at. I don't think that's where his focus is at right now. There's a reason you get time to make that decision later on."

Moore committed to Oregon in the summer of 2022. Later, he flipped to UCLA in December of 2022 rather than back up Ducks quarterback Bo Nix in 2023.

That summer, Moore learned that his mother had been diagnosed with cancer, adding to the pressure he was feeling while trying to perform as a highly touted freshman.

Moore had a rough freshman season at UCLA. His midseason struggles led Chip Kelly to bench Moore.

Following the season, Moore entered the transfer portal and committed to the Ducks in December 2023.

Moore transferred to Oregon to develop while backing up the team's new starter, Oklahoma transfer Dillon Gabriel.

That plan paid off in 2025. Moore passed for 3,565 yards, 30 touchdowns and 10 interceptions while leading the Ducks to a 13-2 record and the playoff semifinals, where they lost to eventual national champion Indiana.

Moore, a projected first-round pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, returned to Oregon for his senior season to keep improving with a team that returned eight defensive starters and was expected to contend for a national championship.

Oregon quarterback Dante Moore (#5) celebrates with running back Tradarian Ball (#4) after Ball's touchdown as the No. 21 Ducks face the Portland State Vikings in a non-conference college football game at Autzen Stadium in Eugene on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. Sean Meagher/The Oregonian

Oregon entered the season ranked No. 2 — the highest preseason ranking in program history — and defeated Boise State, 34-27, in the opener.

Moore passed for a career-high 378 yards with three touchdown passes.

The season began to unravel the following week when the heavily favored Ducks lost 39-31 at Oklahoma State.

The following week, Oregon won 84-0 over Portland State. Next came the USC game.

The Ducks, who host No. 20 Northwestern (6-1, 3-1), could continue to start Raiola or turn to former four-star recruit Akili Smith Jr.

Chances are, Lanning will go with whichever quarterback he believes can win games.

In the offseason, Oregon is expected to seek a quarterback in the transfer portal. With high expectations at Oregon, Lanning likely won't bank on Raiola or Smith as the starter in 2027.

#2829. Nvidia scandal draws in Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who reportedly agrees to testify about China chip sales

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies.

Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security.

Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."

"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment.

The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns."

Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday.

There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough

Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military."

In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved.

Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities.

Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick.

Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June.

Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.

#2827. NHL’s next media deal will test the league’s strength

One of the biggest developing stories in entertainment and sports is how the world's biggest media companies judge the value of non-NFL rights — and the NHL is giving us our first window into this new era in media values.

My colleague Mike Ozanian is out with his new NHL valuations this morning. See the full list here.

The NHL can begin formally negotiating a new media rights deal with its incumbent partners — Disney/ESPN and Skydance, the new owner of TNT Sports — on Jan. 1. Sources tell me the league wants an increase in overall rights fees between 50% and 100% over its current deal. The NHL inked a 7-year, $4.5 billion deal with ESPN and TNT Sports in 2021.

Whether the league actually gets that type of increase is still unclear — and that will be one of the most watched data points in the world of sports business next year.

National media rights for the NHL currently make up about 13% of its annual revenue, which is around $8 billion, according to CNBC estimates.

I'm told both Disney/ESPN and Skydance want to renew a deal with the league. Both companies have engaged in preliminary conversations with the league in the past few weeks, and while there's still work to do in terms of price, there's mutual interest in getting something done.

In its current deal, ESPN has access to 100 exclusive games for the 2026-27 season. Fifty-three of them air on ESPN or ABC, and the other 47 exclusive stream on ESPN. Under current terms, the league's playoffs are split between Disney and TNT Sports.

I'm told Disney is particularly interested in acquiring the rights to more playoff games. The NHL had its most-watched playoffs on record last season, averaging 1.8 million viewers per game. The Stanley Cup averaged 5.2 million viewers — the largest audience since 2019. It was played between the Carolina Hurricanes and the Vegas Golden Knights — not exactly marquee NHL franchises.

Last year's regular season averaged 546,000 viewers across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports, up 25% from a year ago — the highest average in more than a decade.

The sport is also having a moment culturally. Earlier this year, HBO Max said its hockey-romance series "Heated Rivalry" averaged a whopping 10.6 million viewers per episode.

International hockey competitions, such as the league's annual "4 Nations Face-Off" midseason tournament and the 2026 Winter Olympics, have drawn huge ratings. The last "4 Nations Face-Off" game — 2025's U.S. vs. Canada final — drew 9.3 million viewers.

This year's Gold Medal men's hockey game between the U.S. and Canada averaged a stunning 26 million viewers on NBC and Peacock in the U.S., according to Nielsen data. That made it the most-watched sporting event in U.S. history with a start time before 9 a.m. ET.

"We think we've got the best content," NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman said on CNBC last month. "Our ratings have continued to increase. We were up dramatically into the double digits last year. So we view ourselves coming into the marketplace in a very strong position. Having said that, the marketplace is extremely competitive and extremely fragmented. But, I believe that with fierce competition that's going on between traditional television and the newer media platforms that there'll be a great opportunity for us to both expand our reach and get paid what we think is an appropriate reflection of our value."

Recent history suggests the NHL will get the rights increase it wants. The NBA nearly tripled its national media rights revenue, signing an 11-year, $77 billion contract with Disney, Amazon and NBCUniversal in a deal that started last season.

The NHL also renewed its TV rights deal in Canada just last year with Rogers Communications, scoring an increase of more than 100% annually when adjusting for currency fluctuations.

But recent history may not match up to present reality.

While I've been told Skydance is interested in getting a deal done, sources also tell me Skydance's top two priorities are paying down debt and saving money to pay for what's going to be a huge NFL rights increase — potentially $1 billion per season or more.

Skydance is dead set on renewing the NFL, I'm told. Those talks will likely occur in 2028, as the league has an opt-out clause at the end of the 2029-30 season.

Now that Paramount and WBD have been pushed together, the NHL isn't as important to Skydance for distribution leverage, which already has premier sports media rights such as the NFL, The Masters, college football, March Madness, UFC and UEFA Champions League.

That's not to say the NHL isn't a priority for Skydance. Sources both from Skydance and the NHL tell me they'd like to get a new deal done. Skydance still needs programming for the cable networks it owns to keep that business chugging along. But relative to WBD, it's not as much of a must-have.

"As it relates to future rights, we'll be disciplined," Skydance CEO David Ellison said during an earnings conference call this week — perhaps hinting at his company dropping not only NHL but also other rights from the WBD portfolio in the coming months and years. "Every right has to earn its place."

Perhaps Skydance remains a partner but buys fewer NHL games. This potentially opens the door to new bidders. I'm told CNBC's own parent company Versant would be interested in a slice of NHL games. Amazon sniffs around just about every national sports property that comes to market.

Netflix? Regular season NHL games are certainly not events. Fox? NBCUniversal? Both companies need to worry about how much it's going to cost to renew the NFL. A big package of NHL games may not fit the strategy.

How much the NHL can extract from its media partners will likely set the bar for other media rights set to come to market, including MLB, which could be delayed by labor negotiations. New York Yankees President Randy Levine told Ozanian this week that "I don't know whether they'll reach an agreement or not."

Disclosure: Versant Media is the parent company of CNBC.

#2825. Luke McCaffrey knew the rules and made a heads-up play, causing a kickoff out of bounds

Commanders kickoff returner Luke McCaffrey made the smartest play of the game by not returning a kick in Thursday night's win over the Giants.

With McCaffrey back to field a Giants kickoff, the ball landed near the sideline at the 5-yard line. The kick stayed in bounds, and some returners would have grabbed the ball and started running. But McCaffrey let the ball bounce, then stepped out of bounds, and then grabbed the ball with his feet down on the sideline.

By rule, the ball is out of bounds if it touches a player who is out of bounds, even if the ball actually stays in bounds. By touching the ball while his feet were out of bounds, McCaffrey forced a kickoff out of bounds penalty on the Giants, putting the ball on the 40-yard line for the Commanders.

"I thought Luke McCaffrey made a really smart play that won't show up on the stat sheet," Commanders head coach Dan Quinn said. "That's a difficult play. Is it out of bounds? Is it not? I was nervous about it, that's one of the ones where you hold your breath."

Every kickoff returner needs to know that rule, but knowing the rule is easier than having the quick-thinking ability to do what McCaffrey did, in the fourth quarter with the game on the line. It was among the smartest football plays you'll see.

#2824. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2823. Did Giants beat Commanders? Final score of NFL 'Thursday Night Football' game last night

If you did, well, you missed quite the finish on "Thursday Night Football" between the Washington Commanders and New York Giants. A first-half snooze fest quickly picked up in the second half as the teams traded blows in another tightly contested NFC East battle.

With the Commanders fighting for their playoff lives, it came down to the wire once again. It wasn't an unfamiliar spot for the visitors, who've faced that situation more than enough this season. Except this time, they were trying to flip the script.

That was never going to be easy against the Giants, who have been able to win the close games since John Harbaugh took over as head coach.

So did J.J. McCarthy or Jayden Daniels get the last laugh under the bright lights of "Thursday Night Football" at MetLife Stadium?

The Washington Commanders won the Week 10 "Thursday Night Football" game against the New York Giants.

In a back and forth affair, it was the road team that left with a 24-21 victory in a game they had to win. Stefon Diggs scored the game-winning touchdown with under a minute to go and McCarthy tossed an interception to Rasul Douglas on the ensuing Giants' drive.

The Commanders' season would've been on life support with a loss, putting them four games back of the Giants without owning the tiebreaker.

Instead the Commanders now own the tiebreaker and are just two games behind the NFC East-leading Giants.

The NFC East is now wide open: The Giants came into the night with a chance to essentially eliminate the Commanders from postseason contention. New York would've owned the tiebreaker with a win and held a four-game lead over Washington. Instead, it's Washington that now has the tiebreaker. And Dan Quinn's team is only two games back. With the Cowboys still lurking, the Giants can no longer feel comfortable atop the NFC East. In some ways, this race is just getting started.

The Giants' special teams are far from special: It's easy to point to J.J. McCarthy's interception at the end or how the loss of Jaxson Dart is being felt. Special teams was the difference in this one though. Dominic Zvada, the rookie kicker, missed a 33-yard field goal and had a kickoff out of bounds. Jordan Stout's 12-yard punt gave the Commanders good field position on the go-ahead touchdown drive. It was Zvada that missed multiple kicks in Washington that helped lead to a tie. The Commanders now own the tiebreaker instead of splitting the series. That could loom large as the season heads down the stretch.

Jayden Daniels reminded everyone of who he is: He tossed two uncharacteristic interceptions, but Daniels appeared to be in control all night long. He was active with his legs and efficient through the air, while showing plenty of poise on the go-ahead touchdown drive. Daniels has been the subject of jokes all season long for his late-game failures. On this night, it was Daniels that got the lost laugh.

#2822. CFTC Chair Selig tells CNBC crypto industry is embracing agency rules as legislation hopes fade

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is already seeing demand from crypto exchanges planning to opt in to its newly proposed rules governing digital assets, according to Chairman Michael Selig.

The commodities regulator in October proposed rules aimed at preventing abuse in crypto markets and codifying crypto transaction rules under a federal rulebook. In the announcement, Selig said the move was a "critical step" in ensuring the United States remains the crypto capital of the world.

Speaking this week at Cantor Convergence, an annual FinTech conference held in Miami Beach, Selig told CNBC in an exclusive interview that many of the major crypto exchanges are already registered with the CFTC because they offer financial derivatives, including perpetual futures, on their platforms and would now be able to add spot trading.

"We're also getting interest from new entrants who say, 'Look, signing up with 50 different state regimes is tough. We'd rather come to one regulator and get a license at the CFTC' so those new entrants are lining up to come register with us as well," he added.

After the Clarity Act, a comprehensive market structure bill that established a regulatory framework for digital assets, stalled in the Senate in September, the CFTC and the SEC moved to establish federal frameworks using their existing statutory authorities.

"We need to protect our markets and protect our customers using those markets so we'll continue to do exactly that in the wake of the Clarity Act failing to get the votes it needed to get to the president's desk during the current Congress," Selig said.

"Our statute does provide for authority of the agencies to register exchanges that want to offer margined, leveraged, or financed crypto assets or other types of commodity trading so we're utilizing that authority to allow our existing exchanges to begin offering these products under a regulated framework," he said.

Selig added that the oversight is opt-in for exchanges that are not currently offering margin leveraged financing, which is not permitted under existing state regimes.

But the CFTC's new rules could face new scrutiny and oversight in 2027, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate after the midterms. Selig told CNBC he hopes the U.S. won't see a wave of software developers moving offshore, as many crypto businesses threatened to do under the Biden administration.

"I really hope that we learned lessons from the last several years in this space," he said.

Crypto firms were at odds with Washington during the Biden administration, asking for clear operating rules, while also facing lawsuits brought by the SEC under former chair Gary Gensler's leadership. That shifted after President Donald Trump's 2024 victory.

"I do hope that we can work together with both sides of the aisle to protect software developers who want to do the right thing," Selig said, adding that those looking to commit crimes and engage in fraud should be held accountable.

When asked whether he's prepared for increased scrutiny from Congress in 2027, Selig said, "Congress will do its job investigating where it needs to investigate."

"I'm happy to answer any questions that Congress has for me just as I would answer Congress' questions today as I've done before hearing committees several times already," he said.

Selig has also faced heat from Democrats for his handling of prediction markets. In February, 23 Democratic senators sent a letter to Chairman Selig urging him to reverse the agency's greenlighting of prediction markets.

Selig has argued that prediction platforms are federally regulated as more states try to rein them in. The CFTC has sued several states to defend what the agency views as its exclusive jurisdiction to regulate event contracts, which it classifies as swaps.

"We're going to fight this up to the Supreme Court if that's where it's going," Selig said. "Our view on the statute is that we have exclusive jurisdiction over these markets, and I will not allow for states to go bring lawsuits against our exchanges, claiming that they're unlicensed gambling."

CNBC's Tanaya Macheel contributed to this report.

#2821. Apple, Alphabet and Uber survived major founder transitions. Nvidia will be a harder test

Jensen Huang is not the first CEO to leave a company he helped build.

But experts told CNBC that his sudden resignation from Nvidia at a critical juncture is unique and leaves his eventual successor with challenges in leading the company that's powering the artificial intelligence boom.

In 33 years, Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a spy for China, made the company he co-founded the world's most valuable.

Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein wrote on X that he was "indispensable" but "the graveyards are filled with indispensable men," referencing a quote attributed to French leader Charles de Gaulle.

While the board looks for a new CEO and CFO Colette Kress does the job temporarily; analysts say Huang's charisma and bullish drive will be hard to replicate.

"I'm not sure we've seen a situation quite like this, where the founder and CEO of one of the world's largest companies faces such a sudden departure amid scandal," Michael Withers, professor of management at the University of Notre Dame's Mendoza College of Business, told CNBC.

Whoever follows will "face challenges that go well beyond those of a typical CEO replacing a founder," he added.

Apple's image was inseparable from Steve Jobs when he resigned in 2011. But unlike Nvidia, the company had had other CEOs — and an internal successor.

Tim Cook invested in Apple's chip strategy and services business and became a key corporate diplomat in dealings with the U.S. and Chinese governments. He was known as an operator who controlled Apple's supply chain.

Cook had "considerable preparation" for becoming CEO, Withers said. Apple's market cap went from about $350 billion to $4 trillion in his 15-year tenure.

Larry Page and Sergey Brin left their executive roles at Alphabet in 2019, 21 years after founding Google.

Page and Brin's departures were expected. Page said at the time that it was the "natural time" to simplify the company's management structure. Alphabet shares are up more than 300% since then under Sunder Pichai.

Travis Kalanick left Uber in 2017 after mounting pressure over a series of scandals and governance concerns.

But his departure "unfolded over several months, and while it certainly attracted attention, it pales in comparison to what Nvidia is currently facing," Withers added.

Former Expedia CEO Dara Khosrowshahi repaired the organization and found a path to profitability.

Withers said successor CEOs often struggle "under normal circumstances" to juggle maintaining what made a company successful while establishing their own leadership.

"It becomes considerably more difficult when the transition follows such a high-profile scandal involving the company's founder," he added.

Huang had an extraordinary 60 direct reports, as part of a flat structure that favored fast communication over layered hierarchies.

Withers told CNBC Nvidia did not appear to have a succession plan for Huang, who is also often described as inextricably linked to the company.

"We're talking about a company that was, until recently, the largest in the world by market capitalization. That's a pretty remarkable situation," he added.

As well as having to "step out of his shadow," the new CEO will have to deal with the "scandal" arising from Huang's conduct and "the extent to which it sticks with Nvidia," Withers said.

Huang's successor will also have to tackle the longer-term business strategy, while picking up the relationships he managed.

Huang cultivated a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump and accompanied him to China in May. Huang consistently pushed for the U.S. to relax export restrictions that prevent Nvidia from selling its chips to the world's second-largest economy.

He also managed close relationships with the bosses of the company's key suppliers, from SK Hynix to Samsung.

Storm Uru, co-head of the Global Innovation team at Nvidia investor Liontrust Asset Management, said two key priorities were changing company culture and managing the supply chain.

The supply chain was "where Jensen was able to provide a vision for the future and able to bring people to the table and to expand capacity to enable the build-out of this technology," Uru told CNBC, adding it mattered especially "when supply chains are already so tight."

Nvidia continues to face rising competition from rivals such as AMD and hyperscalers, which are ramping up efforts to develop their own chips.

Investors noted that the new CEO will have a roadmap of products for the next few years, unaffected by Huang's removal.

"We have to look beyond Jensen ... there are thousands upon thousands of engineers," Joanne Feeney, partner and portfolio manager, Advisors Capital Management, told CNBC on Thursday, as pressure was mounting on Huang to go.

#2820. Jensen Huang scandal casts doubt on Nvidia’s AI dominance — how we got here

Nvidia is facing one the biggest crises in its 33 year history, with founder Jensen Huang resigning as CEO Thursday after multiple reported affairs, including one with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Now CFO Colette Kress has taken the helm as Nvidia's interim CEO.

The implications of Huang's affair with Alice Huang run far deeper than infidelity. That's because her ties to Nvidia customer Megaspeed put her in the middle of a sprawling effort to accumulate AI chips across Southeast Asia. And Megaspeed is under investigation for possibly diverting restricted Nvidia chips into the hands of Chinese companies.

The relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang dates back to 2023, according to The New York Times. That was a "turbulent" period for Nvidia, Jensen Huang told CNBC during an interview at the time. Nvidia was in the midst of redesigning some chips to comply with the first in a series of strict export controls imposed by the U.S. government that restricted sales to China.

"The regulation is going to be just fine. We're going to be able to work through it," Huang told CNBC from Nvidia's headquarters in February 2023. The interview was for a documentary about how Huang created Nvidia and built it into the backbone of the AI boom.

That same day, CNBC also interviewed Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair.

It's not the first time Nvidia has faced an uncertain future. The company nearly went bankrupt in the early years after it was founded in 1993.

"Every company makes mistakes and I make a lot of them," Huang said in the 2023 interview. "And some of them put the company in peril."

In the early months of the AI boom, after OpenAI launched ChatGPT in November 2022, Nvidia was on the precipice of historic growth. Jensen Huang told CNBC he'd like to keep running the company for "three or four decades," as long as "I feel that I'm making a real contribution to the company."

Less than four years later, Jensen Huang is out, and we're taking a look back at our interviews with the Nvidia co-founder and other company executives as the chipmaker enters this next critical chapter. Watch the video for the full story.

#2819. Game Preview: Knicks at Pacers, November 13, 2026

There are sports movies, there are even some good sports movies. And then there is Hoosiers.

As a basketball romantic you are definitely not flipping the channel when old ball coach Norman Dale a.k.a. Gene Hackman drives his 1951 Chevy Styleline Deluxe through the backwoods of Indiana all the way to the little town of Hickory, where he hopes to find a new life, new love and redemption. You let yourself be mesmerized by Angelo Pizzo's and David Anspaugh's timeless fairytale, by the very essence of "Hoosier Hysteria," the beautiful yet tragic tribulations of high school sports, the rough, simple charm of small town America. And you enjoy every second of it, despite a rather predictable underdog story unfolding in front of your eyes that Hollywood has repeated many times over.

The current Indiana Pacers would kill for some of that predictability, the kind they expected going into this season. After a surprising Finals berth in 2025, their following year was doomed by Tyrese Haliburton's ruptured Achilles. They punted on the next campaign and thought, with their point guard's return, everything would return normal; that the half-court offense would run smooth as a "picket fence;" and that the jumpers would automatically fall like the ones by Jimmy Chitwood. But Haliburton (unfortunately) isn't as quiet nor as down to earth as Mr. Chitwood, nor is an NBA season comparable to a Hollywood movie. It's a lot more complicated than that.

The Pacers are finding that out the hard way. It only took testy Tyrese a handful of games until he got injured again (it's a hamstring now) and his team sorely misses the All Star as their 4-8 record puts them in the lower region of the Eastern Conference. On Friday against the New York Knicks, Haliburton will also be reduced to trolling from the sidelines, and he won't be able to right the wrongs that have plagued his squad so far this season. It's a huge advantage for Mike Brown's men as Haliburton is the straw that stirs the Apple Cider for Indiana. Most of their strategy revolves around his talent, his scoring and his distribution.

But it's not like the Pacers are just struggling out of the gate because Hali has only played four games. Even with him they lost to Milwaukee, barely got by New Orleans and were annihilated by Dallas. Indiana can't shoot threes (just over 33 percent), despite a traditionally fast pace their offense isn't even close to functioning well (20th in offensive rating), and their D is nothing to write home about either (15th in the league). The Pacers are an atrocious rebounding team (29th in rebounding percentage) and they struggle mightily to hit their free throws.

Do they do anything well? They do, in fact, take good care of the ball and have a one of the best assist-to-turnover-ratios in the entire Association. Individually Pascal Siakam is enjoying a strong start to the season (22.7 points) and Andrew Nembhard has come firing out of the gates as well (17.1 points, 42.9 percent from downtown). A lot of guys are still left from that Finals team two years ago, so in theory they should know what it takes. And Rick Carlisle is still a tremendously respected coach, at least when he isn't whining like a five year old who didn't get his wish at Toys-R-Us.

The skipper really has his work cut out for him early in the year. New center Ivica Zubac, a classic, plodding back-to-basket big man with considerable post skills, hasn't really found his place in an adjusted Pacers system that once was predicated on playing five-out at all costs. Continuity has also been a big issue as Carlisle has already started 11 different players, at times making it seem like the Pacers are still on their tanking ways from last year. They obviously aren't and it should be noted that slow starts are nothing new for Indiana under Carlisle. Consider yourself warned.

With Friday's game being another Cup contest you can bet that the Pacers will be highly motivated and our beloved Knicks better be ready for a hostile environment. Keep calm if Haliburton tries some stupid sideline voodoo as he certainly will when he senses a camera being on him. Feed Karl-Anthony Towns in a favorable matchup for him, let Brunson do his thing against Indiana's supposed Brunson stoppers who always seem to just limit him to 35. Make use of your more talented depth, outshoot the struggling shooting team and control the tempo. Just show that you are the better team – which the Knicks, even with their current ups and downs, are at this point in the season.

And please leave the Indiana underdog stories where they belong and where they are actually fun. Leave them to Hoosiers.

Who: New York Knicks (6-5) at Indiana Pacers (4-8)Date: Friday, November 13, 2026Time: 7:00 PM ETPlace: Gainbridge Fieldhouse, Indianapolis, INTV: Prime VideoFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

#2817. Huang's downfall may undo cozy ties between business and government: analysis

The resignation of Jensen Huang, together with the results of the recent congressional election, could make this a watershed moment in the relationship of American business to government, one that sees the pendulum swing back toward greater regulation and greater separation of finance from politics.

Corruption topped the list among issues that motivated voters in the overwhelming and nationwide midterm election victory for Democrats, according to the CNBC Voter Poll. It showed 90% identified corruption as a crucial or major issue in their voting decision, a percentage point higher than the cost of living.

When voters were asked which party was best able to deal with the corruption issue, Democrats led Republicans 37% to 30% — though, significantly, 32% said neither party.

It's impossible to know exactly what voters mean when they say corruption, but there are hints it involves the relationship of business to government. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey, taken two weeks before the election, asked respondents if elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, should personally own or trade stocks in companies that have contracts with the federal government. An overwhelming 93% said it should not be allowed. A similarly bipartisan 89% objected to the president's family members receiving government contracts.

The upshot: The very close relationship between business and the government, which has existed under both political parties but has come plainly and brazenly to the fore in President Trump's second administration, is now a major issue for voters.

The Huang affair encompasses all of that. Nvidia, along with several other large corporations, made large donations to the president's ballroom. Meanwhile, there are allegations that the administration did not act when informed of potentially illegal sales of Nvidia chips to China. It may be that the president ignored warnings from inside his own administration that Huang was involved with a woman who was reportedly a potential Chinese spy, instead bringing Huang on a state visit to China and giving him say in U.S. export policies for chips.

The Trump era has seen the virtual creation of the CEO Statesman: Huang and other tech execs draped around the president during foreign trips, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff negotiating with Russia, Elon Musk deciding who the federal government fires.

Could the Huang affair be the end of that phenomenon?

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., wasted no time in signaling the new Congress was ready to get tough on tech execs.

"It's clear that the American people cannot rely on Big Tech billionaire CEOs to put our national security above their bottom line – which is why Congress must pass the AI Overwatch Act and other bipartisan bills to keep advanced American AI technology out of China's hands."

The enormity of Huang's fall cannot be overstated. Imagine J.P. Morgan resigning — or Jack Welch or Steve Jobs or Tim Cook. Few have stood astride the pinnacle of political and corporate power during their era like Huang during the AI boom.

This comes at a time of massive wealth increases for the elite that have helped undermine faith in capitalism. The CNBC Voter Poll showed 56% with a strong or somewhat favorable opinion of capitalism, with 32% reporting an unfavorable opinion and 12% saying they don't know.

But those numbers are overwhelmingly driven by older Americans. Younger Americans, ages 18 to 34, have a deeply negative opinion. Those aged 35 to 49 are favorable toward capitalism by only a 46%-41% margin.

For starters, it could result in a return to more traditional separation of business and politics, where business has less of a direct say in policy. But this could be the start of a more significant change.

In the wake of the Great Financial Crisis, the banking system was put under such strict regulations, many of which exist to this day, that one commentator remarked it was "in receivership in everything but name only." One can go back even further to more extreme measures taken when the public was deeply dissatisfied with business — to the fallout from the robber baron era when the trusts were busted up, or the wake of the Great Depression when the government put stricter regulations on banks and Wall Street and gave unions more power.

Democrats will be limited, even with large gains in both houses, in their ability to overturn presidential decisions with veto-proof majorities. But executives themselves may decide that it's not a good look any longer to be seen being too cozy with the White House. And some Republicans, especially those from swing states, may read the change in the electoral winds and side with Democrats on some of the most populist issues, like the data centers, the environment and even regulation.

The irony is that Trump ran, among other things, on a strong deregulatory agenda, one that business welcomed as unshackling overregulation during the Biden administration. With potential support from the public, and an overwhelmingly Democratic Congress, the pendulum may be about to swing the other way.

#2816. Nvidia stock inches higher as investors continue to weigh Jensen Huang’s departure

Nvidia shares were slightly higher in premarket trading on Friday as investors navigate the fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation after reports of at least two affairs.

It follows a wild day for the stock on Thursday, which dropped sharply before recovering to close just over 4% lower.

Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday after The New York Times reported that Huang had a romantic relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia.

Huang was already under scrutiny following an investigation by the board into his relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.

Reuters reported on Thursday the existence of another affair with an Nvidia employee, which the news agency did not name. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Shares of Nvidia were 1.7% higher as of 8:13 a.m. ET.

Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that his departure could cost Nvidia as much as 20% of its market value, given how critical he has been to the company's success. Nvidia's stock is already down more than 20% over the last month.

A lot of the company's success has been built around Huang, said Stephane Houri, head of equity research at ODDO BHF.

It's about more than just Nvidia, but also about the "architecture of the AI industry that really depended on the vision" and expertise of Huang, Houri told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday.

#2815. Devin Booker’s 30 points lift Suns past Hornets, 101-96

The Phoenix Suns led 48-31 halfway through the second quarter, and it looked like they were on their way to another stress-free win against a depleted Charlotte Hornets team. Without the franchise cornerstone players Kon Knueppel and Brandon Miller, and with a superb stretch from the Suns bench, the Hornets looked dead in the water, but ultimately fought back and made this game a slog for the final two and a half quarters for the Suns, who won 101-96.

Two things were apparent in this game: the Phoenix Suns could not rebound, and the Charlotte Hornets could not stop turning the basketball over. The Hornets outrebounded the Suns 64-to-43 and outscored the Suns 16-7 in second-chance points. The Suns forced 27 Hornets turnovers (each Hornets starter had at least four turnovers) while the Suns committed eight turnovers. So the rebounding numbers are skewed in favor of the Hornets because they had 13 fewer shots on goal than the Suns did. However, 22 Suns defensive rebounds compared to 15 Hornets offensive rebounds is not getting the job done at all for a Suns team that can be much better than they have been this season at rebounding.

Because the Suns could not rebound the ball and play as fast as they needed to get the offense going, the game became a half-court slog in the second half. The Suns shot 13-for-42 from the 3-point line, and a lot of the looks that went in on Tuesday did not fall for the Suns against the Hornets. Overall, the Suns were 41% from the field, and only one player had a field goal percentage higher than 50%. Devin Armani Booker scored 30 points on 12-of-20 shooting, 4-for-8 from the 3-point line, and had seven assists with just two turnovers. He made every big shot for Phoenix in clutch time, including a deep dagger 3 with 23 seconds left to give the Suns a decisive six-point lead.

All eyes were on Miles Bridges, Grayson Allen, and Royce O'Neale in this game because of the Bridges trade that happened this offseason. Bridges scored 11 points, grabbed six rebounds, and had three assists, and was effective playing with the bench units, but continued to struggle to make an impact with the starting group. Allen scored 14 points, while O'Neale scored 7 points, all coming in the fourth quarter. The Hornets were led by Coby White, who scored 21 points but did not play in the fourth quarter due to what appeared to be a minutes restriction. That certainly helped the Suns win this game, because White was getting wherever he wanted against the Suns' defense.

A win is a win, but the Suns' starting unit continued to not find any type of consistency in this game. The best stretches of basketball continue to come from this team at the beginning of the second and fourth quarters when there are at least four bench players in. The Suns closed the game with a Booker-Luke Kennard-Jordan Goodwin-Dillon Brooks-Oso Ighodaro lineup, while Jalen Green played just 21 minutes and none in the final quarter.

Green's continuing to show growth in the areas the Suns need him to grow in, but the fit with everyone else on the roster continues to be a problem, and the trust in him is obviously dwindling as he continues to not see minutes in fourth quarters. The Suns' record is now 5-6, and sometime in the near future they are going to have to change the starting lineup if it continues to look this disconnected.

All eyes were on Miles Bridges, Grayson Allen, and Royce O'Neale to start this game, and it was Grayson Allen who got things going for the Hornets early, connecting on a pair of triples. The Suns' defense lacked focus and gave up multiple wide-open layups and threes early, with Coby White hitting a wide-open 3 in semi-transition to go up 15-10. Jordan Ott called a timeout and subbed out Bridges for Ryan Dunn. The Suns' energy immediately changed on that end of the floor, as they quickly jumped on the Hornets defensively, leading to a 7-0 run engineered by Jalen Green knocking down two free throws and a corner 3 off of Suns stops.

There were two big takeaways from the Suns' first quarter: defense forced 10 turnovers and Devin Booker's pull-up 3-point shooting. Booker was dialed in, scoring 13 points on 3-of-4 shooting from 3. His comfort level shooting from long range continues to grow, and it is opening up everything for the rest of his game. The Suns led by six to end the first quarter because the Hornets did just enough on the offensive glass to stay in it, down 28-22 after one.

The Suns bench took over in the second quarter because of their hustle and tenacity on both ends of the floor. Jordan Goodwin forced multiple turnovers, leading to a wide-open dunk for Bridges and free throws off of an excellent out-of-bounds play. Collin Gillespie got free for multiple long-range bombs that went in as the Suns pushed their six-point lead out to 15 four minutes into the second quarter, 46-31.

The Suns led by as much as 17 before putting the starters back in, but there was some slippage. The Hornets went on a 14-2 run to cut the Suns' lead to 50-43. A couple of defensive breakdowns and Bridges fouling Grant Williams on a 3-point shot, leading to a 4-point play, were the catalysts for the Hornets getting back into the game. Williams scored 9 points in the second period, and another Allen 3 got the Hornets' deficit down to five at halftime, 55-50.

Even though the Suns were out-rebounded 28-to-15, the Suns still won the possession battle because the Hornets had 15 turnovers compared to the Suns' three total turnovers in the first half. The two worst stretches of the game came when the majority of the Suns' starters were on the floor, as they continued to get in their own way of being a good team.

The Suns' sloppiness from the starters continued to start the second half. As the Hornets jumped out to a 12-to-4 run to start the third quarter, the Suns' poor offensive flow led to easy shots and even more offensive rebounds for the Hornets, who led 62-59 with 8:22 left to play in the third. Since the Suns' 17-point second-quarter lead, the Suns were outscored 31-to-11 across both halves, and Coby Whites 19 points up to that point were a big reason why.

For the rest of the quarter, the Suns started to play better once Dunn, Gillespie and Maluach checked in for Ighodaro, Bridges and Green. But the Hornets responded immediately after two tough Booker midrange buckets. Both teams finished the quarter cold from the field, but Christian Anderson's solid play off the bench for the Hornets put the Hornets up 76-72 after three quarters. The Suns continued to look allergic to rebounding and playing consistent, mistake-free defense, and now a game that was once in cruise control completely slipped away from them. At no point should Jalen Green ever lead the Suns in rebounding with four total rebounds after three quarters.

It wasn't the prettiest 11-3 run ever to start the fourth quarter, but the Suns bench just never relents on their pressure. It started with the Suns grabbing a defensive rebound and a Bridges dunk in transition. The Suns attacked the rim and glass early in the quarter, capped off by a Gillespie midrange pull-up after a travel from Reid. Next play, the Suns force a turnover, Gillespie misses another midrange shot, but Goodwin chases down the rebound and lobs it up to Ighodaro to give the Suns an 83-79 lead.

The Suns continued to string together good possessions for the most part but could not create much separation. Luke Kennard scored multiple midrange shots, and a Gillespie drive-and-dump off to Maluach should have ended in a dunk, but he mishandled it, and O'Neale sprayed in a triple on the other end.

Booker, Brooks, and Ighodaro checked and left Goodwin and Kennard in. After Williams got open for a layup, Booker found Goodwin for an open 3 that just rimmed out. Booker connected on a midrange jump shot to give the Suns a three-point lead. The Suns continued to get multiple stops, and finally a Brooks 3-point shot gave the Suns a 92-86 lead.

The Suns and Hornets traded multiple empty possessions until Reid broke the seal with a 3 of his own, but Booker responded with a tough floater in the lane to get the Suns back up five with one minute to play. A cutting Diabate layup on the other end got it right back to a one-possession game with the Suns up 94-91. Then it was Devin Booker time as he hit a deep, deep 3-point pull with 23 seconds left to give Phoenix a decisive six-point lead. That is, until Brooks fouled O'Neale on a 3-point shot, which, of course, went in for the four-point play.

The Suns inbounded the basketball to Booker. He quickly passed it back to Bridges, who was fouled by Allen, and he made both free throws. Then Booker poetically stole an Allen pass for the Hornets' 27th turnover of the night, and sank both free throws as the Suns went on to win 101-96.

The Phoenix Suns finish up their homestand with the Los Angeles Lakers on Sunday afternoon.

#2813. ‘We will sue them’: Canada threatens Stellantis as Trump trade war reshapes Jeep production plans

Canada has threatened to sue auto giant Stellantis over the planned sale of an idled assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario, alleging breaches of a federal funding agreement after the carmaker announced plans to shift production to the U.S. amid President Donald Trump's trade war.

Speaking at a news conference on Thursday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the government had served Stellantis with a formal notice of default, giving the company 30 days to address its concerns or face legal action.

"We sent a notice of default and, basically, they have 30 days — or else, of course, we will sue them," Joly told reporters in Toronto.

Joly said Stellantis had violated its contractual commitments to the Canadian government and the workers at Brampton by announcing an agreement to sell the plant to armored vehicle manufacturer Roshel earlier in the week. She added that the company was now "on the hook" for hundreds of millions of dollars over the move.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described the situation at the Brampton plant as "unacceptable" and a "betrayal" of its workers.

The standoff comes as the U.S. and Canada remain locked in a bitter trade dispute, with Trump repeatedly putting pressure on automakers to move vehicle production south of the border.

Stellantis, which owns auto brands including Dodge, Fiat, Chrysler and Peugeot, had scrapped plans to build its Jeep Compass at the Brampton plant and shifted future production to a factory in Illinois amid U.S. auto tariffs and other market pressures.

Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley said in a statement shared with CNBC that the company would return $24 million it received in government support for the Brampton Assembly's original retooling plan. This amount, however, falls significantly short of the Canadian government's own estimate of what the company owes.

"We recognize the disappointment and uncertainty surrounding the future of the facility. While our decision to sell the plant represents a change from the original plans for Brampton, the agreement we have advanced with a Canadian manufacturer provides a path to return the facility to productive industrial use," Longley said.

"As Canada's largest automotive employer, this decision also allows Stellantis to focus its resources on sustaining competitive manufacturing operations in Canada in the face of challenging market realities," he added.

Stellantis said Monday that it had agreed to sell the Brampton assembly plant to Roshel for an undisclosed amount.

It also acknowledged its obligations to employees at the facility and said it remains prepared to work with Unifor, Canada's largest private sector union, to negotiate a settlement to assist union-represented employees.

Stellantis stock has fallen sharply since the start of the year, with its Milan-listed shares down more than 60% for 2026 so far.

— CNBC's Michael Wayland contributed to this report.

#2812. Broncos eager to use bye week to prepare for the stretch run

The Denver Broncos head into their bye week in a really good spot.

After a great road win in Charlotte against the Carolina Panthers, the Broncos sit at 7-2. The bye comes after a gauntlet of a start to the season, in which Denver played some of the best teams in the NFL.

For now, the Broncos lead the AFC West standings, are near the top of the AFC playoff seedings for home-field advantage, and are clearly one of the best teams in the league.

Now, with some injuries and guys dinged up, the bye comes at a great time.

We're in a really good spot, obviously where you want to be," Broncos quarterback Bo Nix said to the media after the win over the Panthers. "You want to be first in your division. You want to be winning football games. We've played a really tough part of our schedule. At 7-2, we feel really confident, but at the same time, there's a lot of things that we could get better at. We've said this every week, and some weeks we've gotten better at other things; some things we still got to clean up.

"But overall, we're finding explosive plays, doing better on third down today, stayed out of the third-and-long situations like we've been wanting to do. At the end of the day, we scored enough to win the game, and that's what's important going into the bye."

"You get stuck in Groundhog Day over time doing the same thing over and over every week. I can tell you exactly what I'm doing every day of the week, so this will be a good break, good rest for us. We all feel really good about it, feel like we need it, our coaches. We'll get some rest. Players will get some rest, and then we'll start right back up next week with our next opponent. It's just going to be a good time to relax and also debrief and look back at a few things and just have a great breakdown and sort of digest where we've been and what we're doing and where we want to go."

Since coming to Denver, Sean Payton knows how to handle the bye week and has the post-bye week figured out. The Broncos are 3-0 coming out of the bye under Payton. A big reason why is the time off he gives the players.

What waits for Denver after the bye is the Las Vegas Raiders on Nov. 22 at home.

"I think I told you guys this. I went two or three years practicing on Wednesdays and Thursdays, and we were OK. I can't recall the year, but I called (Kansas City Chiefs head coach) Andy (Reid) one year in Philly. He was 9-0 after the bye … and he just said I get them out of here, and I see them the next Monday. And ever since we've done that, we've been pretty good after the bye as well. So, they'll rest. The guys getting treatment will be in, and everyone else will. At some point, we'll get a jump start on Vegas."

Given how close the Broncos like to play and win their games, the bye comes at a great time for the fans, too.
