#2811. Oregon has 3 quarterbacks who could start Saturday. Illinois has a freshman who's never started before

The Oregon Ducks will face a team on Saturday with an even less desirable quarterback situation.

Illinois (3-3, 1-2 Big Ten) quarterback Katin Houser suffered a broken hand that will sideline him for four to six weeks during a 38-37 overtime win over Michigan State on Oct. 10.

Oregon has played its last two games without starting quarterback Dante Moore, who suffered a concussion in the second quarter of the Ducks' 41-27 win at USC on Sept. 26.

However, while Oregon can turn to junior Dylan Raiola — a Nebraska transfer with 23 career starts — and senior Brock Thomas, Illinois is relying on freshman quarterback Michael Clayton II, who will make his first start against the Ducks.

A positive for Illinois is that Houser was injured before the team's bye week, giving coach Bret Bielema two weeks to prepare Clayton.

"It was just good timing," Bielema told reporters during his Monday media session.

Illinois is off to a disappointing start after going 9-4 in 2025 and 10-3 in 2024. The defense is below average, while the passing combination of Houser and wide receiver Collin Dixon is one of the nation's best. Dixon is tied for third nationally with nine touchdown receptions.

Illinois head coach Bret Bielema celebrates their overtime win over Michigan State as he walks off the field after an NCAA college football game, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026, in East Lansing, Mich. (AP Photo/Lon Horwedel) AP Photo/Lon HorwedelAP Photo/Lon Horwedel

Now Illinois heads into Saturday's game against a resurgent Oregon defense, trying to get Clayton up to speed.

His performance against MSU elevated expectations.

Houser left the game late in the third quarter with Illinois leading 23-10. Clayton completed 6 of 8 passes for 88 yards and two touchdowns. The final touchdown came in overtime on a 25-yard pass that put Illinois up 38-31.

Sophomore quarterback Carson Boyd also played. He rushed once for seven yards but did not attempt a pass.

Bielema and offensive coordinator Barry Lunney Jr. both said Boyd could play against Oregon (4-2, 2-1), but Clayton is the starter.

Usually, Bielema said, his starting quarterback gets a lot of rest during the bye week while the staff works on player development. Given Clayton and Boyd's inexperience, both got valuable reps in practice last week.

"I think those two guys in particular took advantage of every rep," Bielema said.

Bielema has leaned heavily on transfer quarterbacks during his six years at Illinois, including Houser. But that could change if Clayton, a former three-star recruit, earns the job.

"I've said several times that hopefully the next starter comes from within our program," Bielema said.

Lunney said Clayton will be more prepared than he has in the past given the circumstances.

Michigan State Spartans defensive back Charles Brantley (4) tackles Illinois Fighting Illini wide receiver Collin Dixon (17) in a Big 10 football game at Spartan Stadium in East Lansing, Mich. on Saturday, October 10, 2026.Isaac Ritchey | iritchey@mlive.com

"He knows he's going to play now," Lunney told reporters.

"We feel like we have another guy on campus in that room that can help us win and we're very confident in that," Bielema said.

Oregon coach Dan Lanning said it's difficult to scout Clayton given his limited body of work. Oregon has watched some of his high school game film. But mostly, Oregon will focus on Illinois' system.

"There might be wrinkles, but very rarely do people change the identity of their offense based on a change of the position," Lanning said. "So you prepare and then you make sure you have answers for what you think that skill set is."

If Moore doesn't return this week, Raiola and Thomas will compete for the starting job against Illinois.

Raiola replaced Moore at USC and thrived in the win, but following a bye, struggled for three quarters during a 17-15 loss to UCLA on Oct. 10. Thomas performed better in the fourth quarter and almost pulled out the victory.

Thomas started Saturday's 17-14 home win over Nebraska, but struggled for three quarters before Lanning turned to Raiola. He led the Ducks from a 14-6 deficit to a win with a four-yard touchdown pass to tight end Jamari Johnson with 28 seconds remaining.

Lanning said he's confident in all four quarterbacks, including sophomore Akili Smith Jr., who had a play package ready for Nebraska if needed.

Illinois is most familiar with Raiola, who, as a Nebraska freshman in 2024, passed for 297 yards, three touchdowns and one interception in a 31-24 overtime loss to Illinois.

"Raiola is obviously a very accomplished player," Bielema said. "Kind of almost unusual. You got to almost prepare for possibly three quarterbacks on Saturday. But we'll kind of handle that during the course of the week and see where that goes."

Oregon (4-2, 2-1 Big Ten) at Illinois (3-3, 1-2)

Where: Gies Memorial Stadium, Champaign, Ill.

#2810. CNBC's Official NHL Team Valuations 2026: How the 32 franchises stack up

For the first time, hockey team valuations have crossed the $4 billion threshold, with CNBC's NHL valuations led by the Toronto Maple Leafs, at $5.4 billion, the New York Rangers, at $4.7 billion, and the Montreal Canadiens, at $4.1 billion. The average NHL team is now worth $2.71 billion, 23% more than a year ago.

Don't be fooled by the lone NHL control sale to close over the past 12 months: the $1.8 billion sale of the Pittsburgh Penguins to the Hoffmann family. Although the transaction was approved by the league in June, the price was negotiated about 18 months ago.

Look instead at the latest minority stake transactions. In March the NHL approved the sale of a 12.5% stake in the Carolina Hurricanes by Tom Dundon in a transaction that valued the team at $2.66 billion. Scott Malkin and other shareholders are close to selling a 15% stake in the New York Islanders at a $3 billion valuation. Sports bankers tell CNBC these deals are representative of what control stakes in the two teams would sell for given the hot market for sports teams.

"Like the other major sports leagues there is a strong demand to own hockey teams because their media content values are high and there is a scarcity of teams," said Sal Galatioto, whose firm, Galatioto Sports Partners, advises clients on both the buy and sell sides of sports team transactions. "Capitalism and technology are creating more wealth and the NHL, like the NFL, NBA and MLB, is an industry with a very long product life cycle, a hedge against risk in AI."

The NHL's current national media rights deals with Walt Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery are worth a combined annual average of close to $650 million through the 2027-28 season, but given the league's strong television ratings last season, a big increase could be in the offing.

"The 2025-26 NHL regular season averaged 546,000 viewers across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports, up 25% from last year and the highest average in more than a decade," Sports Media Watch wrote. "The 25% increase is on the high end of a general rise in sports viewership that includes gains of 35% for the NBA, 19% for men's college basketball and 10% for the NFL."

Sports Media Watch also wrote that the 2026 NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs averaged 1.8 million viewers in the U.S. across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports. That's up 68% from 2025, and it's the highest average on record for the playoffs on American television, going back to 1994, it said.

The NHL is pondering adding teams in cities such as Houston and Atlanta, and another factor fueling NHL valuations is the belief that the expansion fees paid by the new teams would surpass $2 billion. The Seattle Kraken, the NHL's most recent expansion team, paid a $650 million fee to join the league for the 2021-22 season.

According to CNBC's figures, revenue for the league's 32 teams averaged $257 million for the 2025-26 season, 6% more than the previous year, while EBITDA — earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization — averaged $48 million per team, a decline of 11% due to arena expenses. The league's profitability should rebound as money spent on hospitality, concessions and merchandise stores boosts revenue.

In April 2025 the NHL and Rogers Communications agreed to a 12-year national Canadian media rights deal worth $7.79 billion, based on exchange rates as of Nov. 24, that will begin with the 2026-27 season. That's more than twice the amount the league is getting from its existing 12-year deal with Rogers. This will help push up the league's hockey-related revenue — which includes media rights, sponsorships, premium seating, tickets, concessions and parking — to around $7.25 billion for the 2026-27 season, 7% more than last season.

CNBC's Official NHL Team Valuations are current enterprise values — equity plus net debt — calculated using revenue multiples, and include the economics of the team's arena, including non-NHL revenue that accrues to the team's owner. The valuations are meant to represent what a control stake valuation would go for in an arm's-length transaction and do not include the value of the arena or the real estate it sits on.

Revenue figures are net of revenue sharing and the 35% of home playoff non-premium gate revenue that goes toward the league's revenue-sharing pool. Revenue multiples are based on historical transaction prices, as well as what investors, league executives and bankers say about the current market.

CNBC values exclude other businesses related to the teams with separate financial statements, such as the Edmonton Oilers' mixed-use real estate project. For teams that sell their own merchandise, such as the Oilers, CNBC deducts the cost of goods sold from merchandise sales. Likewise, CNBC excludes the market value of affiliates/equity method investments to ensure consistent enterprise value-to-revenue and enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiples. Debt figures are the latest available and include both team debt and stadium debt.

CNBC incorporates the value of a pending new arena in our valuations if construction has begun and financing has been secured. For example, the $2.25 billion valuation for the Calgary Flames incorporates their new arena, which is scheduled to open in time for the 2027-28 season. Likewise, CNBC valuations anticipate a substantial increase in the NHL's next U.S. national broadcasting deal, which would begin with the 2028-29 season.

Revenue and EBITDA figures are for the 2025-26 season and net of revenue sharing and player escrow. CNBC presents revenue and operating income figures on a cash basis, rather than an accrual basis. CNBC figures are different from the league's official hockey-related revenue because we include non-NHL arena revenue that goes to the teams. When the owner of the arena also owns both the NHL team and NBA team that play in the same building — as is the case for several teams, including Toronto's Maple Leafs and Raptors, who are both owned by Rogers Communications and play in Scotiabank Arena — we divide revenue from non-sports events held at the arena evenly between the two teams.

All valuation figures are in U.S. dollars. The exchange rate for revenue and EBITDA is based on a one-year average, from June 2025 to June 2026, of CA$1 = US$0.72, and the exchange rate for team values and debt, as of Sept. 21, is CA$1 = US$0.71.

Sources for CNBC's Official NHL Team Valuations include team owners, investors and executives, as well as sports bankers and league consultants; public documents such as stadium lease agreements, stadium authority budget audits and credit rating reports; and sponsorship and broadcasting industry executives. Certain figures were provided by league executives who spoke to CNBC on the condition of anonymity because agreements are private and they do not have permission to speak about them publicly. Figures that could not be confirmed with sources are CNBC estimates.

— CNBC's Jungwoo Ethan Kim contributed to this report.

#2807. ‘Elite pocket passer’ Jared Goff not being underestimated by Patriots

No matter where you go on Al Gore's internet, whenever there is a list of the NFL's best quarterbacks you find familiar faces near the top. Mahomes, Allen, Burrow, sometimes — when he has his turnover tendencies under control — Maye.

Jared Goff, on the other hand, typically resides further down the list. It can't be due to a lack of production, at least this year: Goff has been one of the most efficient quarterbacks in football while leading the Detroit Lions to a 6-2 record.

But while fans and analysts might be underestimating the 32-year-old, his next opponent sure is not. The New England Patriots are well aware of the damage he has done, and is capable of doing this Sunday in Munich.

"I think Jared's playing at a high level," said head coach Mike Vrabel. "Continued the last three years, he's been at a high level."

"He's an elite pocket passer," linebacker Robert Spillane added. "He loves to step up in the middle of the pocket and deliver the ball downfield. Really can do it all. First overall pick for a reason, who just continued throughout his career to show why he was a first overall pick. Somebody who's going to get the ball to all of his guys."

Distributing the ball to the weapons mentioned by Spillane, as well as to NFL scrimmage yards leader Jahmyr Gibbs, Goff has played some of the best football of his career so far in 2026. The numbers show it, too.

In eight games thus far, he has completed over two thirds of his passes (185 of 273) for 2,134 yards, 15 touchdowns and just two interceptions. Whether you use traditional metrics or advanced ones such as EPA or CPOE Goff typically finds himself in the top 10 if not close to the league lead.

He might not be the same big-play hunter as the quarterback the Patriots faced last week, Green Bay's Jordan Love, but Goff has been steady and operating well within Detroit's offensive system.

"The quarterback runs the show very well," said defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr. "He gets them into plays for the whole unit, and he kind of has the freedom to do that."

There might not be one particular part about Goff's game or his physical abilities that stands out relative to other quarterbacks, which might contribute to his perception. However, that does not mean he cannot put intense pressure on any defense.

A large part of that is his willingness to disperse the football, and the chemistry and experience he has built with the players surrounding him.

"He's a great quarterback," said safety Kevin Byard. "He does a great job when he's able to stand in the middle of the pocket, he can fire across the middle of the field, deep, with obviously the weapons that they have with Jameson Williams, a guy who can stretch the field, and obviously Amon-Ra St. Brown, who's a guy who can work the middle of the field, work the intermediates and things like that. And Sam LaPorta's a really good tight end."

"He loves [Jameson Williams] down the field. He loves Amon-Ra underneath, LaPorta all over the field," added Spillane. "We know we have a huge challenge for us ahead."

#2806. Reeling Oregon Ducks remain positive, committed to the grind

EUGENE — The 2026 season is on the verge of completely unraveling for the Oregon Ducks. One more loss, and any shred of postseason hopes would be extinguished.

Yet even after two upset losses and falling out of the rankings — despite starting the season at No. 2 — the Ducks (3-2, 1-1 Big Ten) remain focused, together and committed to salvaging the season.

"One thing I really love is the way the people in the locker room have been responding to this adversity," sophomore cornerback Brandon Finney Jr. said.

After his team's 17-15 loss to No. 12 UCLA on Saturday, Oregon coach Dan Lanning said the team would be measured by how it responds moving forward.

On Wednesday, he said the team has elevated its work ethic and embraced accountability.

"I've been proud of the way that they've worked," Lanning said. "I don't see a lot of hanging heads, right? I think that's challenging, too, especially when you're young, to not lose a little bit of gusto and not lose a little bit of belief."

Oregon linebacker Devon Jackson (#9) drops UCLA running back Wayne Knight (#3) for no gain as the No. 13 Ducks face the No. 21 Bruins in a Big Ten college football game at Autzen Stadium in Eugene on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Sean Meagher/The Oregonian

The Ducks, who host Nebraska (5-1, 2-1) at 8 p.m. Saturday, responded well to adversity following a 39-31 loss at Oklahoma State on Sept. 12. Oregon won its next two games, including a 41-27 win at USC on Sept. 26.

That victory seemed to give the Ducks a fresh start. But two weeks later, they lost to the Bruins and dropped out of the rankings.

Now, Oregon must run the table to have a legitimate shot at the College Football Playoff, which seemed like a given for a team that returned most of its starters from last year's semifinal squad.

RELATED: Can the Ducks bounce back from UCLA loss? Experts release new Oregon vs. Nebraska predictions

It's not uncommon for teams with grand expectations to unravel in tough times. So far, that hasn't happened.

"The team is very connected and maintains its composure whether we're winning or losing," punter Bailey Ettridge said. "We haven't let the losses last week and against Oklahoma State bring us down. I think we've handled them well."

Wide receiver Dakorien Moore said the team is filled with players who came to Oregon to win and be great. He added that the team's goals remain attainable, and team leaders have worked to encourage togetherness and mutual trust.

"If you can't trust your teammate, then everything ain't going to form in the way that it's supposed to," he said.

This also means trusting the process, the plan and the team's goal to get better instead of blaming one another.

Oregon head coach Dan Lanning talks to the defense during a timeout as the No. 13 Oregon Ducks face the No. 21 UCLA Bruins in a Big Ten college football game at Autzen Stadium in Eugene on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Sean Meagher/The Oregonian

"Everybody knows what we want to attack this next week, being that Nebraska is a good team," he said.

The outside noise has been deafening. To say that many Oregon fans have melted down on social media would be an understatement.

Virtually all of the players have social media accounts. Moore said he is active on social media but ignores negativity.

Finney said he isn't very active on social media and doesn't care what people say outside the program.

"Why would I let your opinion inflict me or my thoughts on my performance or my thoughts on our performance," he said. "Because people are going to be there when you're doing good, when you're bad; when you're doing bad, they're going to leave you."

For that reason, the team lives by the motto F.E.B.U., which stands for "Forget Everyone But Us".

"F.E.B.U. is a true statement that we all follow," Finney said. "… Just back to work. We got to figure out what we did wrong, go to the doctor, and just get back to work."

Fifth-year linebacker Devon Jackson said before the season that his main goal was team-driven — winning the national title.

"At the end of the year, what happens, happens, but I promise if we focus on the day and focus on one game at a time, we will be okay," Jackson said.

On Saturday, the Ducks' defense played one of its best games of the season, while the offense played its worst without starting quarterback Dante Moore, who remains in concussion protocol.

On teams that lack closeness, such a contrast can cause issues. But that is not the case with Oregon.

"I mean, we're all in this together," Jackson said. "It's not like, the defense won the game and offense lost, or special teams won or lost. We all lost together and we all win together. So, we got each other's back no matter what."

Oregon offensive players celebrate a touchdown run by running back Jordon Davison (#0) as the No. 13 Ducks face the No. 21 UCLA Bruins in a Big Ten college football game at Autzen Stadium in Eugene on Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Sean Meagher/The OregonianSean Meagher/The Oregonian

Jackson said that after Saturday's loss, he and senior center Iapani Laloulu talked for 20 minutes about the team. He told Laloulu that he didn't care what was going on with the offense; the defense had its back.

"I wouldn't trade that group with anybody else in the country despite what other people may think," Jackson said. "And we're going to continue to lean on each other because it's we all we got and we all we need."

Realistically, Oregon can't expect much sympathy from outsiders. The Ducks have top-notch facilities, infinite uniform options, a roster with an estimated payroll of $50 million, and a coach who isn't afraid to speak his mind, as Lanning did after beating the Trojans.

Many in the football world certainly wouldn't mind seeing Oregon fall.

"Ain't nobody going to feel sorry for us," linebacker Matayo Uiagalelei said. "So just came back in the next day with the mindset ready to work."

#2805. U.S. seizes $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance

U.S. authorities have seized around $1.2 billion in virtual assets stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last month, the Department of Justice said Thursday, as it vowed action to tackle cyberscams originating from North Korea.

Over $6 billion was stolen from industry giant Binance on Oct. 29, which the DOJ attributed to actors linked to the North Korean military.

Collective efforts between the U.S. government and private sector have resulted in more than $2.7 billion of that amount being frozen.

The FBI blames the attack, which shook confidence in crypto market security, on members of the North Korean military it refers to as "TraderTraitor."

The DOJ said it was taking coordinated action against what it called the North Korean government's "schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency."

That includes "the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance," it said.

DOJ units, law enforcement partners and virtual asset service providers have been working to intercept the stolen assets.

But efforts to track and freeze the assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder them through various cryptocurrency channels.

Authorities have also seized cloud-based infrastructure used in a massive identity impersonation scam known as "FaceStealer," which has seen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen over 18 months, the DOJ said.

The scheme sees hackers set up fake video meetings using stolen accounts and recordings of people known to the target by using AI-generated deepfakes. The hackers then say a technical problem requires a fix, install malware on a computer and take over the victim's communications, steal their cryptocurrency and target their contacts — sometimes months or more than a year after the initial compromise.

Individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries are prime targets.

Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy, of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office, called FaceStealer "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user."

"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough," Grandy added.

"North Korea's government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft," Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor said in a statement.

"America will fight back against that corrupt regime's effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea's ill-gotten gains."

#2804. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2803. Wolves 133, Mavericks 94: You Like That?

Do you remember the last time the Minnesota Timberwolves played basketball?

Since the Wolves last played, the Minnesota football team got flat-out embarrassed on national television, then went through all five stages of grief before building a time machine that sent them back to the days of Kirk Cousins, and now, in one fell swoop, has gone from pumpkins to the NFL's new belle of the ball.

And somewhere in the midst of all of this, Joan Beringer is officially no longer a teenager and is starting to go gray.

I'm not saying having no Wolves games is responsible for any of this, or that if we had played sooner, maybe Beringer wouldn't have had to have a birthday (is that how that works?). I'm not saying that! But man, does it feel good to finally have this team back on the court and on our screens again.

In their first game back in eons, the Wolves laced up and faced off against a team in the Dallas Mavericks that seems to be fast-tracking a soft rebuild. On paper, both teams are pretty evenly matched in several categories, namely FG% (DAL #4, MIN #5), turnovers (DAL #10, MIN #11), and steals (DAL #14, MIN #15), so the Wolves needed to win the possession battle.

Certainly, the Mavericks would be up for the challenge, so it would stand to reason that this would be a challenging game for the Wolves. Right?

To start the game, Jonathan Kuminga was on a torrid pace, muscling to the basket for a lay-up and cutting to the rim for a dunk off a beautiful find by LaMelo Ball, who proceeded to find Jaden McDaniels on a similar play a few possessions later.

The Mavericks settled in and muddied the game as the quarter went on. At the 5:16 mark, TJ Shannon subbed in, and PJ Washington proceeded to bully him to the rim for an and-one. This was a great quarter for Washington, as he finished with 10 points in the quarter.

Perhaps an accurate distillation of the rest of the game, though, is that those 10 points would be it for Washington, and the Mavs 24-19 lead would soon be relinquished and gone for good.

Ayo Dosunmu and the bench mob of Bones Hyland, Jaylen Clark, Trey Lyles, and Joan Beringer burst the Wolves out of the mud like the Snoats brothers in "Raising Arizona", spurring an 11-0 run that got the crowd dancing on their feet. After a couple of free throws by Naji Marshall to stop the run, a Gobert offensive rebound off a missed Dosunmu corner three allowed the Wolves to close out the quarter with this Clark nuke.

The second quarter saw more of the same for the Wolves. After a sloppy turnover by Dosunmu led to a corner three by Zaccharie Risacher, the Wolves had given up 15 points off of six turnovers. Those numbers would balloon to 25 and 11 by the end of the first half, and it wouldn't matter.

Dosunmu continues to truck along as Mr. Consistency, a perfect cog in the absence of Anthony Edwards. He finished the half with 12 points by doing what he does best: being an absolute bully out on the break.

As for Ball, he was unconscious from deep, and finding cutters left and right. Much has been said about his fit with Gobert, and there were still a couple of miscues on the Ball-Gobert feed tonight. Near the end of the half, though, Ball slipped into the paint as the ball guided him around. He faked once, and then floated the ball up for a Gobert slam.

It was a thing of beauty, and exactly why sticking to the process matters.

Going into this game, Ball's assist-to-turnover ratio (1.62) wasn't pretty to look at, but for the most part, I don't mind it.

The way I see it is that they are mostly a statistical fallout of process-driven stuff that should temper with time. Some of the results might be an eyesore for box score perusers, but I love the process. I love that Ball is not afraid to continue to funnel the ball into Rudy, even if his individual numbers risk taking a hit. The box score won't tell the whole story. It seldom does. But Ball's commitment to the process should pay dividends as the season bears itself out.

The Wolves would go into halftime leading 67-52. And then…

Ball continued his unconscious streak from long-range, followed by a Dosunmu transition trey. Dusty May would call a timeout not even two minutes into the second half to try to stop the bleeding. That worked just as well as trying to stop a Beringer nosebleed.

The Wolves were playing loose and fast. McDaniels was gliding down the court for barely contested lay-ins. Kuminga was hitting threes, and the lead would soar to 32 points midway through the third after McDaniels was blocked, got the ball back, and then threw down a vicious slam.

Right before the McDaniels sequence, Beringer re-entered the game with a clear mask (!). Before the mask change, Beringer had zero points and zero blocks. After the mask change: 13 points and three blocks. Need I say more? That new mask is magic.

Although there were times through the third where it looked more like a horse race at Canterbury, with players running around with their manes on fire, any and all sloppy play was a moot point, and the Mavericks would end up waving the white flag before the third quarter had even concluded.

The fourth quarter was mostly a non-event because of the score (Wolves 103 – Mavericks 69 at the end of the third), outside of a Gobert and-one off a Kuminga miss (where he converted on the free throw!) and a smooth jump hook by the magic-masked-man Beringer, but I wanted to shout out Isaiah Evans on his first official points in the NBA.

I know it was on a goal-tend, but still, a milestone is a milestone.

And a shout-out to Jon "Boog" Sciambi on the call tonight, his first Wolves game of the season. I know he is beloved in Wrigleyville as the play-by-play announcer for the Chicago Cubs. As a Twins fan, I hold no ill will towards the Cubs. It's that other team on the South Side that I have problems with.

In the end, the Wolves were able to completely stifle Cooper Flagg for 12 points on just 5-12 shooting. Seeing the Wolves, he was probably having nightmares about his last game against them, when he went 5-19 for 12 points. I guess this game was an improvement? Baby steps, teenager. Baby steps.

The Wolves were also able to silence Kyrie Irving, who up until now had looked rejuvenated and was outperforming his career shooting splits across the board.

Caleb Martin just about doubled his scoring average (seven points tonight). He should be proud of that.

But this was perhaps the Wolves' best all-around effort in this season's infancy. Off a long break against a good team, Target Center was rocking, and from start to finish, it was just a rollicking good time.

Right now, the Mavericks have 13 guys logging double-digit minutes. It's clear that Dusty May and his coaching staff have spent the early part of this season seeing what works and what doesn't. I'd expect the rotations to get tighter as the season wears on, as players fill out their roles and the overall numbers flesh out into something a bit more comprehensive. So far, though, May has struck a good balance of thinking big picture while still keeping his team competitive on a nightly basis.

In a fairly perforated coaching pipeline, May's seamless transition from college to the NBA has been nothing short of impressive. I was late to the magic of May, only first hearing about him last year as the coach of the eventual national champion Michigan Wolverines. Chalk it up to object permanence on my part, but I know who he is now, and it's almost as if he was built in a lab to know ball and coach ball.

Yesterday also marked the one-year anniversary of the Mavericks dumping disgraced GM and possible secret Los Angeles Lakers operative Nico Harrison. Going from Harrison to Masai Ujiri seems to have stabilized this organization. Finally, adults have returned to the table.

Enmities from the 2024 WCF aside, I'm happy for Mavericks fans.

The Timberwolves continue their eight-game homestand on Saturday, as Chicago O'Hare International Airport's Bulls fly into Target Center. O'Hare ranks first as the busiest airfield in the world. Meanwhile, their team ranks first in a bunch of categories you'd rather not rank first in. Liftoff is at 7:00 PM CT on DAZN-MN and NBA League Pass.

Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need as the Giants sit atop the NFC East.

This knee injury was a new experience that drew Nabers into a scary, unexpected place. "Just my attitude," Nabers said of why he lost himself. "Everybody didn't know what my mindset was. Just at a loss for words. Didn't really have a lot of words to say. Didn't really have, I don't know, I kind of was empty. The name "Arvell" means "warrior" in French, "cried over" in Welsh and "Eagle Ruler" in Old Norse.

#2801. Trump says he wants to ‘get Cuba done’ before leaving office, would consider military force

U.S. President Donald Trump has said he wants to "get Cuba done" before leaving office in 2029, adding that he would "certainly consider" military intervention against the communist-run Caribbean island.

In an interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday, Trump said his administration was monitoring the situation in Havana "very closely" and described Cuba as a "failed" state.

"I want to get Cuba done before I leave," Trump said. His comments marked the first time he has put a timeline on possible military intervention to topple Cuban authorities, according to Politico.

Trump said Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose parents are from Cuba, "would love to do it" and said he would "certainly consider" a short military operation.

It comes as the U.S. continues to enforce a comprehensive economic embargo against Cuba, a campaign which has contributed to a deepening energy and economic crisis on the island. Cuba has suffered repeated nationwide blackouts in recent months, as well as fuel and food shortages.

The Cuban Embassy in Washington, D.C., estimated on Thursday that the cost of the U.S. blockade to Cuba between March 2025 and February 2026 amounted to $8 billion.

Earlier this month, the Treasury Department imposed further sanctions on Cuban oil tankers and shipping companies and threatened to target any international entity or person doing business within its marine or maritime industries as part of a push "to end the Cuban regime's malign activities, both in Cuba and across our hemisphere."

In response, Cuba's Embassy in Washington, D.C., said these steps "deepen an energy siege that already leaves hospitals without reliable power and families facing blackouts. The blockade is not targeted at a government. It is collective punishment that hits ordinary people every day."

Trump has previously talked up the prospect of a "friendly takeover" of Havana and said the White House could turn its sights on Cuba after the Iran war. The U.S. president has also said he could do anything he wanted with the country, adding that he thinks he will have the "honor" of "taking Cuba."

In May, Cuban Energy Minister Vicente de la O Levy said the country of roughly 10 million had run out of fuel oil and diesel, describing the country's predicament as "extremely tense."

Analysts have typically been skeptical about the prospect of a U.S. military campaign against Cuba, suggesting that further economic pressure against the island's authorities appears more likely.

#2800. Bears offense has been among most explosive in NFL this season

Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson had a lot of goals for his offense going into this season. One of those goals was to be explosive and so far, that is something the Bears have accomplished.

Through the first nine weeks of the season, Chicago is tied for the second-most explosive plays of any team in the NFL. Most of those explosives have not been on touchdown plays. In fact, the Bears only have seven offensive touchdowns of at least 20 yards and four of them came against the Carolina Panthers in the season opener.

All of Chicago's offensive touchdowns of over 20 yards have come from different players and their only rushing touchdown over 20 yards is from running back Kyle Monangai, who has been out since Week 5 against the Green Bay Packers.

While the Bears have had a lot of explosive plays, they have also given up a lot of explosives. In fact, seven of the touchdowns Chicago has given up this season have been at least 20 yards. Two of those were against the Packers, who are the only team with more explosive plays than the Bears.

With Jeffery Simmons now on Chicago's defensive line and rookie cornerback Malik Muhammad hopefully coming back for the Bears' Week 11 game against the New Orleans Saints, they should allow fewer explosive plays in the second half of the season. If they can continue to generate explosive plays, the Bears can continue to be a very dangerous team.

#2799. Outlook outage continues as Microsoft flags 'encouraging recovery signals'

Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday and Friday, causing disruption to millions of its customers as engineers scrambled to fix one of its biggest-ever server issues.

Connectivity problems began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday and continued into Friday, with Outlook and Teams, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, affected. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products such as Outlook Calendar were also hit.

In an update shortly before 8 a.m. ET, Microsoft continued to warn that users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 products, including Outlook on either web or desktop and many services that interact with email.

However, it said it was making "continued recovery progress" overall, with "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" in much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in Asia Pacific.

Intermittent issues are expected as recovery efforts continue.

Email and related tools were unavailable for Microsoft users on Thursday afternoon and evening, throughout the Asian business day on Friday and across the European and early U.S. morning.

Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online in stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages.

Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health.

The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said.

Microsoft shares were around 2% lower in premarket trade.

Governments and businesses in Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption.

The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X.

Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.

Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected.

Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported.

A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024, hitting airlines, banks and more.

Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users.

The incident highlights a business "resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making," James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone.

"We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities."

"Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals," he said.

Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday.

Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data."

At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.

"We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses."

But the Commerce Department is in charge, "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box."

#2796. Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, putting annual rate at 6.5%, the highest in nearly four years

Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon.

The producer price index, which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday.

Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations.

On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022.

The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike.

Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed.

Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected.

The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn't collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI.

However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal.

"Today's PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.

Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump's tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched.

"We've had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. "If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way."

Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October.

Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022.

Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight.

"We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," Goolsbee said. "Inflation is rising; it's it's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks."

Other items in the PPI report also showed multi-year gains. Prices for intermediate processed goods soared 14.6% from October 2025, the biggest annual gain since July 2022. Intermediate prices for services posted a 6.9% increase, the most since November 2022.

#2794. Abysmal NFC South keep proving it's time to fix NFL playoffs | Opinion

The NFL is too good to be embracing mediocrity.

The NFC South is on pace to have a division winner with a losing record for the second consecutive season, with the 3-5 Carolina Panthers leading the New Orleans Saints (3-5), Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) and Atlanta Falcons (3-6). If it happens, it will be the fourth time in the last seven seasons the NFL has had a division winner finish below .500, getting not only a playoff spot but a wild-card game at home.

It's a bad look, especially when the NFL has better options.

Home playoff games could go to the teams with the best records, as the Detroit Lions wisely proposed in 2025. Better yet, the NFL could follow the NBA's lead and adopt a playoff format that rewards the best teams. Period.

No more charity for division winners. No more rewarding bad teams simply because they happen to be the best of the worst. No more punishing good teams because their divisions are meat grinders. (We see you NFC North, where all four teams are three games above .500 or better.)

Seed the teams by win-loss records, divisions be damned. Award playoff berths, and home games, accordingly.

"We're trying to take care of ourselves. We're not worried about any other team in our division right now," Buccaneers coach Todd Bowles said Sunday, Nov. 8, after his team rallied to tie the game with just under 3 minutes left only to allow the Bears to march 49 yards and kick the game-winning field goal as time expired.

"We know if we take care of us, we're going to be fine."

But shouldn't the NFL want better than fine?

It's bad enough we have to watch terrible games during the regular season. Like the dog of a game Sunday, Nov. 15, that is the 1-7 Miami Dolphins against the 2-7 Indianapolis Colts. Or that ever-popular clash of the Panthers and Saints on the same day. Or, worse, all four NFC South teams going head-to-head in Week 18.

We shouldn't have to endure dreck in the playoffs, too. Especially when it means a better team is going to be on the sidelines because of some misguided attempt at fairness.

Take last year. The Panthers finished at 8-9. But because they won the NFC South, they made the playoffs while two teams with winning records, the Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings, had to watch the postseason from their couches.

And for what? The Panthers lost to the Los Angeles Rams in the wild-card game, giving up a fourth-quarter lead twice. At home.

Of the five teams that won their divisions with losing records, only two have won their wild-card games. Both then lost in the divisional round.

The last three teams to make the playoffs with losing records have all gone out in the wild-card game, and Carolina's 34-31 loss to Los Angeles was the closest margin.

The NFL prizes parity, with good reason. For 35-plus years, at least four teams have made the playoffs after missing them the previous season. The Kansas City Chiefs are the only team to repeat as Super Bowl champions in the last 20 years, and one of only three teams to make the Super Bowl in consecutive years.

That means every team begins the year with hope, with legitimate reason to think this year might be different.

Except for the New York Jets. They're just lucky U.S. leagues don't do relegation.

But parity should not equate to charity, and the NFL is devaluing the regular season with its current playoff format. The playoffs should be reserved for the teams that earned their way in, not backed in on a technicality. At the very least, home playoff games should be reserved for the teams with the best records.

The NFL's league office was in favor of Detroit's proposal, but the Lions wound up pulling it before it came to a vote. Probably because owners know their teams could easily be the best of a bad division one day, too.

But the NFL needs to revisit the issue. A playoff berth is too important, a home playoff game too valuable, to be downgraded into participation trophies.

Follow USA TODAY Sports columnist Nancy Armour on social media @nrarmour.

#2792. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.77%, nearly 6% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Thursday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 0.3% as markets digested the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Thursday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.75% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped 18% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2787. NFL hot seat rankings for every team: Coaches most likely to be fired

When will the first NFL head coach be fired?

As pessimistic as that sounds, the question looms large as the 2026 NFL regular season reaches Week 10. This marks the first time since 2022 that no NFL head coach has lost his job during the first nine weeks of the season. But the clock is ticking, and the list of coaches on the hot seat continues to grow.

Plenty of fan bases are already calling for action, even as owners appear more hesitant than usual to make a major move at this point. But change is inevitable in a results-driven business like the NFL. Ten teams hired new head coaches this past offseason, meaning 10 others were shown the door.

The debate now is what coach will get axed first this year. Dan Quinn of the Washington Commanders and Los Angeles Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh are among those feeling the most pressure, but they aren't the only coaches with reasons to worry about their job security.

None of the 10 coaches hired this past offseason should be in immediate danger of getting fired, although perhaps coaching retreads like Stefanski and Saleh might want to be cautious. Just last year, the Raiders fired Pete Carroll after one season. The year before that, the New England Patriots parted ways with Jerod Mayo after just one season on the job. But pulling the plug in the middle of the season seems unlikely, despite the recent one-and-done trend.

These eight coaches aren't going anywhere, unless they choose to leave on their own terms. It's no coincidence all eight coaches are also leading teams with legitimate Super Bowl aspirations this season. Reid, McVay and Shanahan are currently the three longest-tenured coaches in the NFL, while MacDonald is coming off a Super Bowl win Campbell re-established the Lions as a perennial contender, and Payton, Johnson and Coen have quickly done the same with their respective teams.

These five coaches have all been successful in their current gigs and don't appear to be in danger of losing their jobs. But they're also one bad stretch, or an ugly playoff exit, from feeling uncomfortable for various reasons. The Patriots haven't looked quite right since Vrabel's offseason drama with Dianna Russini. The Texans haven't been able to get over the hump as an AFC contender under Ryans. O'Connell bungled the Vikings' quarterback situation. LaFleur is 1-4 in playoff games over the past five years.

Each of these teams are struggling, underperforming relative to expectations or dealing with some combination of both. Sirianni's tenure with the Eagles has produced the incredible highs of two Super Bowl appearances, but the Eagles face questions about the direction of the franchise and a rebuild could be on the horizon. Schottenheimer wasn't a particularly popular choice when he was hired less than two years ago, and Cowboys owner Jerry Jones is already fielding questions about his job security. Bowles might be able to lead Tampa Bay to another NFC South title, but the Buccaneers haven't made much progress in the playoffs under his watch. Canales and Moore have shown intriguing flashes, but it's time for those moments to translate into more consistent results.

These are the coaches most likely to be fired, and perhaps before the 2026 regular season ends. Quinn has a 8-17-1 record since leading the Commanders to the 2024 NFC championship game and this season's issues have included a couple embarrassing game-management blunders. Harbaugh has the NFL's only winless team heading into Week 10 and his decision to hire Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator has completely backfired. Glenn's Jets have shown signs of improvement, but he's just 5-21 through 26 games as a head coach and he's dealing with a notoriously fickle owner and fan base. The Colts already fired general manager Chris Ballard and dealt several key players before the NFL trade deadline. Steichen's days appear to be numbered, too.

#2784. Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return

Paul George flips the script — and the bird — in Philadelphia return originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

PG-13 was rated R in his return to Philadelphia.

The middle finger Paul George directed toward one baseline fan only reinforced that rating.

Tuesday night was expected to revolve around Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum sharing an NBA court as opponents for the first time. Instead, the other headliner in the summer's blockbuster trade stole the show.

George scored a game-high 36 points in Boston's 123-101 win over the Sixers. He shot 14 for 22 from the floor, made six of his 11 three-point attempts and scored 14 consecutive Boston points in the fourth quarter.

The game was tied at 79 with 3:19 remaining in the third quarter. Boston outscored Philadelphia 44-22 from that point forward.

The Celtics went nine minutes and 20 seconds without making a two-point field goal during the second half. Instead, they made nine consecutive field goals from three, the second-longest such streak by a Sixers opponent over the last 30 seasons.

Payton Pritchard opened the fourth with consecutive threes. George followed with eight straight points, helping the Celtics begin the quarter on a 14-0 run that turned a competitive game into a rout.

George's return carried a complicated history. His two seasons with the Sixers were repeatedly interrupted by injuries, but he also played a significant role in their most memorable playoff run in years.

Last spring, George helped the Sixers overcome a 3-1 deficit to eliminate Boston in seven games. He averaged 17.4 points and shot 55 percent from three during the series.

Tyrese Maxey was happy to see his former teammate Tuesday, even if he disliked what followed.

"It was good to see Paul," Maxey said. "I love him, love his family. … He gave us everything he had while he was here. We know what he did in the playoffs last year. Great person, great family, and we'll see him again."

Maxey then added one important qualifier.

George instead scored from nearly everywhere.

"He had some open threes. He had some pull-up threes. He had some middies," Maxey said. "He played within the game, too. That's what Paul does. He plays within the game. He takes what the defense gives him, and we gave him too many open looks tonight.

"PG, we know what PG does. We shouldn't even be allowing him to get up 11 threes, and that's on us."

Nick Nurse watched George attack the Sixers in several ways.

"He really had it going," Nurse said. "He'd post up, and-one, fallaways. He went down the lane, high archer off the glass, and-one. He scored in about every way he could tonight."

George heard boos during his return and said the arena carried the atmosphere, though not quite the intensity, of a playoff game.

"This building can be very electric as well," George said. "It was fun. It was fun to play in this environment."

One interaction extended beyond the usual reception for a returning player.

During a stoppage, the ball rolled toward a fan seated along the baseline. George said the fan looked directly at him before dropping the ball instead of returning it.

"There was a fan being an a–," George said. "The ball rolled to him. He looked me dead in my eyes, dropped the ball on the ground as if I'm a dog to go fetch or go get it, instead of passing the ball to me like a normal fan would do.

"And so, yeah, then I rolled him a middle finger in return."

#2783. Patrick Mahomes on Josh Downs: You can tell the intellect, how he can pick things up

The Chiefs brought in a receiver at the trading deadline, acquiring Josh Downs from the Colts.

Quarterback Patrick Mahomes told reporters in his Wednesday press conference that he’s excited to get going with the wideout.

“I think you can tell just the intellect and how he’s able to pick stuff up and that he’s a professional, that he knows what he’s doing and he wants to come in and just compete and to have success, and he wants to win. And so, I’m excited for that,” Mahomes said, via transcript from the team. “And then you can just see him interacting with the other receivers in the room. You can tell that there’s going to be a great cohesion there, and that’s the type of guys you want on the team, that want to compete and that want to win.”

Mahomes noted he’s impressed with the way Downs can win his one-on-one matchups.

“He runs routes really well,” Mahomes said. “He sets them up really well where he will run a route early in the game that he sets up for another one later in the game. And then he has really good feel, you can tell, obviously, playing in the system that he has, he has a lot of read-type routes, and you can tell he knows how to get himself open, settle in the right zones, and win versus man [coverage] when he can.

“And so, I think it will be an easy transition for him to kind of do that stuff in our offense. Then, with how we do things, he can play a lot of different positions as we move receivers and tight ends around.”

The quarterback also sees it as realistic for Downs to play and contribute early on in his tenure with Kansas City. While that begins with plenty of reps at practice, Mahomes and the rest of the offense can direct Downs to where he needs to be during games if necessary.

“[W]e do a great job of kind of moving guys in and out of every single position, and so guys know the entire concepts of the plays,” Mahomes said. “We’re very detailed with how we call the plays in the huddle, which will help him out a ton.

“Then when he doesn’t know, being able to talk to me in the huddle or talk to the guys as they’re breaking the huddle, and that usually helps when the guys like each other. And so, it’s good to have a guy that you can tell everybody’s going to like, and that he has his head on the right way, and he’s going to make sure that he’s going to do whatever it takes to win.”

In nine games with the Colts this year, Downs caught 33 passes for 354 yards with one touchdown.

#2780. Bruce Arians says he wants to be a head coach in the NFL next season

Bruce Arians is thinking about coming out of retirement. Again.

Arians told Jordan Schultz that when he announced his retirement from the Buccaneers in March of 2022, it was because of health problems that have since been resolved, and he now wants to coach again.

"I had torn my Achilles early in that season, and I was wearing these prosthetic high heels, and it threw my back out, and I couldn't stand on the sideline for four hours anymore without a lot of pain," Arians said. "I was also monitoring an aneurysm on my heart, so I had some health issues. We did everything we thought we could do in Tampa after winning the Super Bowl, trying to get two, and then it was time to give it to Todd [Bowles]. Now that I'm all healthy again, I got the itch again. So, we'll see."

If Arians does come back next year, he'll be the oldest head coach in NFL history. That distinction currently belongs to Pete Carroll, who was 74 when he coached the Raiders last season. Arians will turn 75 next season.

Arians' first retirement announcement came from the Steelers after they did not renew his contract as their offensive coordinator following the 2011 season, but Arians later said he was forced out and didn't want to retire. He then took a job as offensive coordinator of the Colts in 2012, and was their interim head coach for most of that season while Chuck Pagano battled leukemia. Arians coached so well that he was named the NFL's Coach of the Year.

Once Pagano returned to the Colts, Arians became head coach of the Cardinals, and he won a second Coach of the Year award. He announced his retirement following the 2017 season, after five years as head coach of the Cardinals.

But in 2019 he came out of retirement to become head coach of the Buccaneers. He won a Super Bowl in Tampa Bay, then retired after three seasons. Arians thought that was it, but he said that his son is now coaching high school football, and in talking to his son about the job he realized how much he misses it himself.

"Another fire got lit," Arians said. "I had no desire to go back, and I was still fighting some health issues, but now after the open heart surgery I've got so much more energy, it's amazing."

Arians may find, like Bill Belichick before him, that all the accomplishments in the world don't guarantee an NFL head-coaching job. Or perhaps he'll convince some owner to give the oldest coach ever a chance to do what he's done three times before, and turn a franchise around.
