#2775. LeBron Log No. 4: A courtside sip, 16,000 makes and Cleveland's welcome

LeBron Log No. 4: A courtside sip, 16,000 makes and Cleveland's welcome originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James' latest week with the Sixers included a sip of a stranger's wine, yet another number no NBA player had reached and a return to the city where his career began.

It also included his worst performance with Philadelphia, followed less than 48 hours later by his highest-scoring game with the team.

Welcome to the fourth edition of the LeBron Log.

No chronicle of James' first season in Philadelphia could omit the time he helped himself to a fan's wine during a game.

James chased Tyrese Maxey's transition pass into the stands during the third quarter of the Sixers' Nov. 2 win over the Bulls. He collided with Philadelphia native Troy Clemons, spilled some of Clemons' wine and sampled what had landed on his arm.

The interaction received its own story on our site, and deservedly so. It also belongs in the Log.

Clemons did not keep the cup as a souvenir. He threw it away and got another drink.

James returned to the court and later broke into a dance after scoring over the 6-foot-1 Tre Jones. The wine clip generated millions of views across social media and became the defining image from an otherwise ordinary 19-point Sixers victory.

The following night in Detroit, James offered a broader explanation for why Philadelphia has already looked comfortable together.

"We've got a good team," James said. "Guys vibe with one another. Guys like each other. Guys enjoy being around each other. That has a lot to do with it, too. It makes the game a lot easier when you enjoy being around people."

Eleven games into his Sixers career, James appears to be doing exactly that.

James arrived in Detroit two baskets away from another unprecedented number.

His second field goal against the Pistons made him the first player in NBA history to reach 16,000 regular-season field goals.

James finished the Sixers' 112-106 victory with 13 points, 10 rebounds and eight assists. The near-triple-double helped Philadelphia improve to 8-1 and avenge its only loss of the season.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar ranks second in league history with 15,837 made field goals. Karl Malone is a distant third at 13,528. James is the only active player with more than 12,000.

His scoring record has long been secure. James passed Abdul-Jabbar in career points in February 2023 and later overtook him in made baskets. The round number in Detroit still illustrated the distance he has created between himself and every other scorer.

James began his career by making 5,361 field goals across seven seasons with Cleveland. He added 3,510 in Miami, returned to make 3,691 more for the Cavaliers and made another 3,421 during eight years with the Lakers.

Basket No. 16,000 belonged to Philadelphia.

The Sixers' 8-1 start also carried a notable James connection. Each of his previous four teams to begin a season at least 7-1 reached the NBA Finals.

James was not ready to entertain that conversation in early November.

"It's too early to be talking about the Finals and things of that nature," he said. "We've got to continue to buy into what we want to do."

Two nights later, James returned to the place where nearly half of those 16,000 baskets were made.

His first game in Cleveland as a Sixer brought out jerseys from every stop of his career. Cavaliers colors filled Rocket Arena alongside Heat black, Lakers purple and the Sixers' throwback look.

James received a warm ovation when he was introduced last among Philadelphia's starters. When he checked out late in the fourth quarter, with the result decided, the crowd stood for him again.

James has experienced both ends of Cleveland's emotional range.

He returned as a member of the Heat on Dec. 2, 2010, to one of the most hostile receptions in NBA history. Six years later, he delivered the Cavaliers their first championship and ended Cleveland's 52-year major professional sports title drought.

"I've seen the depths of hell when it comes to a reception here, all the way to the heavens above," James said. "Anything in between is easy money."

The reception fell somewhere in the middle. His performance landed much closer to the bottom.

James finished with eight points on 3-for-12 shooting, three assists and six turnovers in the Sixers' 119-95 loss. It was his first single-digit performance in Cleveland since he scored three points against the Rockets on Dec. 30, 2004.

He had scored at least 10 points in 396 consecutive regular-season games in the city. The run covered his first stint with the Cavaliers, every visit as an opponent and his entire second tenure with the organization.

It ended during his first trip back in a Sixers uniform.

"I definitely did not feel in a good rhythm offensively," James said. "A couple of them were careless. A couple of them were just trying to make the right play and not being successful with it."

It was only the 10th single-digit regular-season game of James' 1,630-game career. He still took time afterward to consider what an eventual jersey retirement in Cleveland could represent.

"The journey from being an 18-year-old rookie, to leading a franchise to a championship," James said. "And everything in between."

James did not carry the rough night into Chicago.

Less than 48 hours after struggling in Cleveland, he scored a season-high 22 points in the Sixers' 127-121 victory over the Bulls. Thirteen came during the second quarter, when James helped Philadelphia turn an early deficit into a halftime lead.

His first basket produced another milestone.

James entered Sunday trailing Abdul-Jabbar's 1,895 points for the most scored against the Bulls in NBA history. His first-quarter three-pointer moved him into the lead. He ended the afternoon with 1,916.

The most interesting play from his night was a pass.

With the Sixers ahead by four and 2:20 remaining, James drove into the paint. Three Chicago defenders collapsed toward him. Maxey stood between the left wing and corner, but even he did not believe James could see him.

James fired the ball through the defense. Maxey sidestepped Isaac Okoro and made the three-pointer, pushing Philadelphia's lead to seven.

After his postgame interview, James pulled out his phone and watched the play again.

"He didn't think I saw him," James called out from his locker as reporters asked Maxey about the possession.

Maxey acknowledged that he had positioned himself to rebound because he expected James to shoot.

"Honestly, I was like this," Maxey said, raising his hands. "I thought he was about to shoot a layup."

James has spent the opening weeks of the season teaching his new teammates to expect the unexpected pass.

"You've got to become a wide receiver or a catcher at that point," Maxey said. "You never know when you're going to get the ball.

#2774. 3 Landing Spots That Make Sense if the Hornets Trade Naz Reid

The Charlotte Hornets are just twelve games into their post-LaMelo Ball reset, yet NBA rumors linking Naz Reid to playoff contenders are already picking up steam. Even though Charlotte just brought Reid over from Minnesota in June's blockbuster deal, rival front offices are already keeping tabs on whether the Hornets will flip him before February.

And honestly, you can see why teams are calling. Reid, 27, is locked into a manageable five-year, $125 million deal ($23.2 million this season), and putting up 17.3 points and 8.5 rebounds a night while Charlotte navigates a 4-8 start and a wave of injuries. The Hornets aren't trying to win a title this spring—they are building around Brandon Miller, Kon Knueppel, and a mountain of future draft picks.

If a contender gets desperate enough to dangle real assets, the Hornets have to pick up the phone at least. Here are the top three contenders that could realistically make a move for Reid.

Portland Trail Blazers center Donovan Clingan (23) high fives guard Ja Morant (1) and guard Damian Lillard (0) during the first half against the Memphis Grizzlies at Moda Center. Photo Credit: Troy Wayrynen, Imagn Images via Reuters Connect

Portland added another dynamic layer to its backcourt this summer by trading for Ja Morant to pair alongside Damian Lillard and an established guard like Jrue Holiday. However, shipping out Jerami Grant left their forward rotation noticeably thin. Right now, Deni Avdija and Toumani Camara are anchoring the wing rotation next to traditional paint-bound centers like Donovan Clingan and Robert Williams III.

Reid would slot cleanly into Portland's frontcourt as a true stretch four who can also slide over to play small-ball five whenever Clingan rests, or Williams manages his usual workload. Better yet, the Trail Blazers have an obvious way to balance their roster. Packaging Scoot Henderson—whose role has shrunk in a crowded guard room—with a filler salary and future draft capital, like Orlando's 2028 first-round pick, gives Charlotte a high-upside lead guard while giving the Blazers the floor-spacing big they are missing.

Golden State Warriors forward Yaxel Lendeborg (1) and forward Gui Santos (15) look up during a review during the third quarter against the Houston Rockets at Toyota Center. Photo Credit: Troy Taormina, Imagn Images via Reuters Connect

Golden State's frontcourt rotation has been forced to lean heavily on veteran savvy and small-ball adjustments during an 8–4 start. With Kristaps Porziņģis stepping away from basketball due to health issues, 40-year-old Al Horford carefully managing his workload, and Stephen Curry sidelined for the next few weeks with an oblique abdominal tear, Steve Kerr needs dependable nightly scoring.

Reid would give the Warriors a durable frontcourt scorer who stretches the floor for Brandin Podziemski and rookie standout Yaxel Lendeborg. Best of all, Draymond Green is still mobile enough to guard opposing centers, taking the toughest interior matchups off Reid's plate. Packaging Porziņģis' near-expiring contract—the first year of a two-year, $40 million deal with only $3 million guaranteed on the back end—alongside a smaller salary like Gui Santos and a future first-round pick gives Charlotte massive cap flexibility and a valuable draft asset.

Toronto Raptors forward Scottie Barnes (center) participates in the player introductions, with forward Allen Graves (right) looking on, before a game against the Memphis Grizzlies at Scotiabank Arena. Photo Credit: John E. Sokolowski, Imagn Images via Reuters Connect

Toronto sits near the bottom of the league in both three-point attempts and shooting percentage. Adding a floor-spacing frontcourt piece who comfortably fires nearly seven triples a game opens up driving lanes across the entire half-court for Toronto's slashers.

On the other end, the Raptors have plenty of length on the perimeter—led by Scottie Barnes, Kawhi Leonard, and Collin Murray-Boyles—to cover for Reid defensively. Matching salaries is straightforward if Toronto puts RJ Barrett's expiring contract on the table, though Toronto would likely have to include its 2029 first-round pick to get Charlotte's attention.

Charlotte doesn't have to rush anything right now. With Grant Williams and Moussa Diabaté back on the floor while Miller and Knueppel work through their injuries, Charles Lee hasn't even gotten a clean look at what this roster looks like at full strength. Still, floor-spacing bigs on fair contracts are gold in February. If the Hornets decide to lean all the way into their youth timeline at the deadline, Reid won't be short on contenders lining up.

#2773. Browns have a penalty problem: All the stats and details- where does the blame fall?

If the 2026 Cleveland Browns were a 1970s TV sitcom, on Monday's game review they would have been saying, "Marsha! Marsha! Marsha!" But instead, the Browns are a professional football team, and as the game film continued, the coaching staff could be heard saying, "Penalties! Penalties! Penalties!" (or so we would assume).

The fact of the matter is, Cleveland is the most penalized team in the league. And that's no laughing matter.

RELATED: RECENT LOSSES – WHICH IS MORE DISAPPOINTING?

At the halfway point of the schedule, Cleveland is ranked #1 in team penalties. 82, to be exact, for 563 yards. That averages out to 9.1 penalties per game. 97 total flags, which also ranks #1. 13 declined, which is tied for #1. What is this called? The "best at something?"

Part of the problem is that the Browns' offensive line is a collection of five new starters. Has that ever happened before in the league's history? Probably, but wow, it stands out.

This is a critical aspect of this year's roster. Yes, the offensive line is five athletes, but more importantly, it is considered one group instead of a handful of individual players. An offensive line works more on cohesiveness rather than single-man stats.

OT Tytus Howard came from the Houston Texans during free agency. Another free-agent signing was OG Zion Johnson, inked from the Los Angeles Chargers. OT Spencer Fano and OG Austin Barber are rookies. C Elgton Jenkins was signed away from the Green Bay Packers.

This means none of these guys were on the Browns roster last year. And none of them have played together at any point until they showed up for Browns training camp. This means they had to get to know each other and find a way to communicate during a game. Even in camp, there was no certainty about who the starting five would be, so this group didn't get a chance to become cohesive right away.

Two holdovers from last year's group, OT Dawand Jones and OG Teven Jenkins, have barely seen the field. In Jenkins' case, he was penciled in at right guard before he started having back issues. He never started a game this year. On October 24, he was placed on IR.

Jones was expected to become one of the offensive tackles, but came out of camp as the backup and is more considered the "swing tackle," meaning he can come in at any point and play either side. He has played with the offense in just three games, but is on the kick teams, so he has played in every game as a blocker.

What has this group contributed as far as team penalties?

For starters, the Browns are ranked as the most penalized offense in the league. Yeah, there's that. This unit features 17 false starts and 12 holding calls across the roster. Great googly moogly. A whopping 41 pre-snap flags is leaps and bounds greater than any other team.

Is this because these five guys are still trying to figure each other out? Is it because there are two rookies starting? Is it because of the coaching style of OL coach George Warhop or his assistants? Is it because these players just aren't very good?

It has to be something, right? Nobody seems to be able to place a finger on the exact issue, though. It's a major problem and is keeping this Browns' offense from reaching its potential. One thing everyone knows: It just keeps happening.

RT Tytus Howard: 10 total (7 false starts, 1 ineligible downfield, 1 holding, 1 declined)

RG Austin Barber: 6 total (2 false starts, 4 holding)

C Elgton Jenkins: 1 total (1 ineligible downfield, 1 declined)

LG Zion Johnson: 9 total (2 false starts, 1 ineligible use of hands, 6 holding, 1 declined)

LT Spencer Fano: 6 total (1 ineligible downfield, 5 holding, 4 declined)

OT Dawand Jones: 2 total (2 ineligible formation, 1 declined)

CB Tyson Campbell: Fined $23,882 by the NFL for "use of the helmet" during Week 8 against the Pittsburgh Steelers

RG Austin Barber: Fined $6,944 for post-play involvement/celebrations.

QB Deshaun Watson: Fined $14,926 for celebration/vulgar acts following a touchdown

DE Sam Williams: Fined $6,361 for taunting during Week 8

RT Tytus Howard: Leads the team in 10 total flags with 9 accepted

RB Quinshon Judkins: Fined $11,941 for taunting in Week 8, and previously fined $14,926 for celebration/vulgar acts earlier in the season

In this year's rankings of most penalties in a single game, the Browns rank tied at #2 with 14 accepted against the Steelers in Week 4, a 27-24 win. In the Top-20, Cleveland is listed twice.

On defense, DE Sam Williams leads the team in penalties with six accepted flags: 2 neutral zone infractions, 1 taunting, 1 roughing the passer, 1 illegal use of hands, and 1 face mask. Right behind him is DE Jared Verse with 6: 3 neutral zone infractions, 1 encroachment, 1 unnecessary roughness, 1 defensive offside, plus one declined.

Illegal use of hands: 2 – ranked #2 (tie)

Unnecessary roughness: 1 – ranked #6 (tie)

Illegal downfield block: 1 – ranked #1 (tie)

Illegal block above the waist: 1 – ranked #4 (tie)

Illegal downfield pass: 1 – ranked #3 (tie)

Why do the Browns have so many penalties?

Take the game against the New Orleans Saints. Cleveland had six penalties called in the first quarter alone. But the team settled down and had 10 for the entire game. The week before, against Pittsburgh, seven flags were thrown against the Browns in the first half alone, with nine total. Seven were called on the offensive line, including two holding calls on the rookie tackle, Fano.

The pre-snap penalties are the ones most preventable. Every player knows when the actual snap will occur, so why jump?

LG Zion Johnson was asked about pre-snap penalties after the Saints loss in the post-game press conference. He said:

"It is a focus; it's a big focus for us right now. We're really attacking it in practice. When you're playing on the road, there's definitely an added level of difficulty with the communication and the pre-snap, getting the call in and cadence, all those types of things. But we're just working each week to improve on those things. We're going to have some games at home, which will definitely be better for us. We might be able to go verbal, those sorts of things that can help us. But each day we're just striving to get better, whether we're on the road or at home in those regards, and it just has to continue to be a focus and something we press on."

The offensive line must attack it harder. If the issue is problematic in practices, will running laps cure that? That and/or stiff game fines? HC Todd Monken addressed the penalties recently:

Cleveland jumped out to a 5-2-0 start, beating some of the most mediocre teams in the league (except for Pittsburgh). They lost to the only good teams on their schedule, which means the franchise can only defeat the downtrodden clubs. They also lost to two bad clubs, which is troubling. Now, they are on a two-game losing skid.

This means the Browns are an average team at this point, but perhaps on the rise. But they aren't talented enough to have a bevy of penalties that hurt key offensive drives or give the other team an advantage with some stupid defensive penalty.

Johnson's assertion of a lack of focus on details seems fishy. These guys are paid a king's ransom to pass-block and aid in the rushing attack. They are compensated extremely well to pay attention and already be focused. Nobody should have to remind them to be attentive to the details.

There is only one thing left to consider: It apparently is a lack of discipline. Is that coaching? The players? Both?

And if this problem persists, talk of a post-season berth will just get further and further out of the picture.

#2772. Jim Harbaugh: Broncos took advantage of a loophole the NFL should not allow

Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh is not happy with the way the Broncos backed out of a trade for Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley, or with the NFL rules that allowed them to do so.

After agreeing to trade a fourth-round pick and a fifth-round pick for Henley, the Broncos told Chargers GM Joe Hortiz they couldn’t go through with it because Henley’s physical revealed concerns about his knee. The Broncos were still willing to trade for Henley, but wanted to give up less. Harbaugh believes physical exams should only be to determine whether or not the player is healthy, not to renegotiate trade terms.

“What happened with the trade? Here’s what I know, from talking to Joe: The Broncos based a pass-fail on a medical grade based on whether we would take less compensation, and we wouldn’t and we didn’t,” Harbaugh said. “In my opinion it’s one of those loopholes that the league should really look into, because it sets a bad precedent.”

Asked if it’s permitted for teams to renegotiate trades after the trade deadline, Harbaugh answered, “It shouldn’t be, but apparently it is. That’s why it’s a loophole, and teams should not have the ability to do that.”

Harbaugh said the Broncos offered to say Henley passed his physical, but only if the Chargers would take something less than the fifth-round pick the Broncos had agreed to.

“It’s a medical grade. It’s a pass-fail for a medical grade, and they told us they weren’t going to pass him if it’s a fourth and a fifth, which was agreed upon — they would not pass him for that. They would pass him for a fourth and a fill in the blank. I don’t know what to call that, but that’s what it is,” Harbaugh said.

Harbaugh is right that the NFL has set a bad precedent. By allowing teams to renegotiate trade terms after the deadline, the NFL is incentivizing teams to engage in chicanery on physical exams to squeeze their trade partners into taking less favorable deals. The Chargers refused to budge, but the NFL rules shouldn’t have put the Chargers in a position where they had to make that decision.

#2768. Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors

Four things to watch as Sixers look to respond against Raptors originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers will not need to wait long for an opportunity to move past their most lopsided loss of the season.

Less than 48 hours after Boston's 123-101 win exposed several of Philadelphia's early weaknesses, the Sixers will host the Toronto Raptors on Thursday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

The Raptors are coming off a difficult meeting with the Celtics, too. Toronto led Boston by 22 points Wednesday before being outscored 61-34 over the final 29:24 of a 98-93 loss.

Philadelphia enters at 9-3 following Tuesday's defeat. Toronto is 5-6 and will complete a back-to-back and its third game in four nights.

LeBron James has been ruled out because of low-back and sciatica management. Joel Embiid is questionable with right plantar fascia injury management. Toronto will be without Kawhi Leonard, Scottie Barnes and Nate Bittle.

Here are four areas to watch as the Sixers try to respond.

Few teams have forced opponents into mistakes as frequently as Toronto.

The Raptors have generated 18.9 turnovers per game, the highest mark in the NBA. They are also averaging 10.9 steals and nearly 15 offensive rebounds.

The Sixers have countered that type of pressure well. Their 13.0 turnovers per game are tied for one of the lowest marks in the league.

Toronto's length remains disruptive even without Leonard and Barnes. The Raptors regularly crowd ball handlers, reach into passing lanes and send multiple players toward the offensive glass. Jakob Poeltl supplies size inside while RJ Barrett, Ja'Kobe Walter and Collin Murray-Boyles can create problems away from the ball.

The Raptors' pressure can punish a careless pass twice. It takes away a Sixers possession and gives Toronto an opportunity to score before the defense gets organized.

Philadelphia has largely avoided those mistakes while adjusting to a new lineup and playing at a quicker pace. Maintaining that control without James, who has handled a significant share of the playmaking, will be one of Thursday's clearest challenges.

Toronto has not built its offense around half-court shooting.

The Raptors are averaging 49.6 paint points and 16.4 fast-break points. Even while shorthanded Wednesday, they scored 18 points in transition against Boston.

That presents a direct test for a Sixers defense allowing 16.5 fast-break points per game, the fourth-highest figure in the NBA. Philadelphia has also surrendered 49.5 paint points per contest.

The first concern will be slowing the ball.

Immanuel Quickley returned Wednesday after missing two games with right hamstring soreness. He gives Toronto another guard capable of attacking early in the shot clock, while Barrett has consistently looked to get downhill with Leonard and Barnes unavailable.

Poeltl can create scoring chances without having a play called for him. He runs the floor, screens for Toronto's guards, rolls toward the rim and cleans up misses.

The Sixers have been effective in transition themselves, averaging 17.1 fast-break points. Maxey and VJ Edgecombe can change ends quickly after a stop, but Philadelphia must secure the ball first.

Thursday's game could swing on which team gets to run and which one is forced to create against a set defense.

Toronto provided an extreme example Wednesday of how quickly the three-point line can alter a game.

The Raptors entered their matchup against Boston shooting 31.8 percent from beyond the arc. They proceeded to hit 10 of their 18 attempts in the first quarter, tying a franchise record for threes in a period.

They went 6 for 25 over the final three quarters.

After Wednesday, Toronto is shooting 32.4 percent from three this season. The Sixers should not treat the Raptors like an elite perimeter team. They also cannot allow them to find early confidence through uncovered catch-and-shoot attempts.

Walter made five threes Wednesday and scored a team-high 17 points. Rookie Allen Graves added 13 points, while Quickley, Barrett and Jamison Battle are all willing shooters when the ball reaches them in rhythm.

Philadelphia's problems against Boston extended beyond the Celtics making difficult shots. The Sixers were late on several closeouts and occasionally allowed too much separation while navigating screens.

Toronto does not rely on the three as heavily as Boston. Wednesday showed it can still build a lead quickly when those shots start falling.

The Raptors expended significant energy Wednesday before traveling to Philadelphia.

They scored 38 first-quarter points, built a 22-point lead and then watched Boston erase the entire margin before the end of the third quarter. Quickley and Barrett each played more than 31 minutes. Poeltl and Walter both played at least 29.

The Sixers should have the fresher legs. Whether they take advantage could become apparent early.

Philadelphia has averaged 26.3 first-quarter points with a minus-2.2 scoring margin in opening periods. Slow starts have forced the Sixers to play from behind several times, including in their 29-point comeback against Cleveland.

An aggressive start would make Toronto respond quickly after a draining loss. Maxey and Edgecombe can apply pressure by pushing the ball after defensive rebounds instead of allowing the Raptors to set their pressure defense.

James' absence will require an adjustment. Maxey, Brown and Anfernee Simons should handle more of the ball and more of the decisions that come with initiating the offense.

If Embiid plays, the Sixers can make Toronto work through Poeltl by establishing him inside. If Embiid sits, Philadelphia's size concerns will become more pronounced with Adem Bona, Dominick Barlow and Ariel Hukporti also unavailable.

The Sixers have a rest advantage against a depleted opponent coming off an emotional loss. Their response should begin well before the fourth quarter.

#2760. Observations after Sixers lose 1st Brown vs. Tatum matchup, George scores 36

Observations after Sixers lose 1st Brown vs. Tatum matchup, George scores 36 originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Round 1 of the new-look Sixers vs. the new-look Celtics decisively went Boston's way on Tuesday night.

In the first meeting between the teams since the July trade that sent Jaylen Brown to Philadelphia and Paul George to Boston, the Celtics earned a 123-101 win at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

The Sixers dropped to 9-3 and the Celtics improved to 9-2.

George was the game's brightest star, scoring 36 points on 14-for-22 shooting. Jayson Tatum added 21 points.

Tyrese Maxey's 24 points led the Sixers. Brown was hampered by foul trouble in his heavily anticipated first outing against Tatum. He posted 13 points, five rebounds and two assists in 26 minutes.

The Sixers will host the Raptors on Thursday night. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Celtics:

To no one's surprise, Brown and Tatum guarded each other to open the night.

VJ Edgecombe defended a former teammate in George, who scored Boston's first four points with a pair of pure jumpers. On the other end, Maxey made the Sixers' first three field goals.

Judging by volume, the home fans cared most about the much-scrutinized Brown vs. Tatum matchup. The crowd was excited early when Brown snagged a steal and then dished to Maxey for a fast-break three-pointer. The fans also dialed up the noise when Brown sized up Tatum in isolation. He wound up dribbling the ball off his foot and out of bounds. Tatum pointed to signal it was Celtics ball.

Boston's star forward had a productive first quarter, posting 11 points. He scored an easy two when he used a back screen to break free from Brown and convert a layup that put the Celtics up 11-7. Boston began 9 for 12 from the floor as a team.

As for Brown, he sat shortly after being called for his second foul with 6:48 left in the first quarter.

Brown re-entered at the start of the second quarter. The Sixers still struggled to eat into Boston's lead.

A Sam Hauser triple extended the Celtics' advantage to 12 points. There was some audible frustration in the building after Brown missed two free throws on the next possesion.

The Sixers' deficit hit 16 points on a Hugo Gonzalez jumper. Meanwhile, the Sixers missed 12 of their first 14 three-point tries. While some of those shots were open looks that simply didn't go down, the Sixers also rushed up several contested jumpers before they made Boston's defense do serious work.

In the bigger picture, it wouldn't be remotely surprising if shooting stands out as a weak area for the Sixers come the trade deadline. They entered the game ranked 27th in the NBA in three-point frequency outside of garbage time and 22nd in three-point accuracy, according to Cleaning the Glass.

Joel Embiid (16 points, six rebounds) had an injury scare late in the second quarter when he fell hard after missing a layup in transition. He rose gingerly and limped through the final 30 seconds or so of the first half.

The Sixers' star big man was fine to start the third quarter and even drained a long-overdue three on the opening possession. He'd been in a terrible outside shooting slump (3 for 32 from deep on the season) before that shot.

Brown's foul trouble persisted. He picked up his fourth personal with 10:40 to go in the third quarter.

The Sixers stormed back without him and their defense played a large role. After LeBron James rumbled in for a layup, Dean Wade stonewalled Payton Pritchard on the perimeter to force a shot-clock violation. Wade later canned a three to even the contest at 76-all.

The Celtics responded and Tatum led the charge. His third-quarter exploits included a highlight slam on James and a top-of-the-key three to build Boston's lead back up to nine points.

Pritchard buried a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter and the Celtics' advantage kept growing. George celebrated a triple that stretched his team's lead to 100-82. The Sixers' spirits were considerably lower as they headed to their bench for a timeout. As a Sixer, George only had one higher-scoring game (39 points) than his performance Tuesday.

George and Tatum were each excellent in Philadelphia. Outside of Maxey, who finished 8 for 12 from the field, the Sixers didn't receive similar games from their stars.

Brown will be back in Boston on Jan. 21 when the Sixers visit the Celtics. He'll try to even the score.

#2758. Knoxville, Chattanooga Fox affiliates pass on Titans game, for now

The Tennessee Titans apparently need an asterisk on their name.

At least two TV markets in the state for which the team is named have passed on televising their Week 10 game against the Jaguars.

Drew Lerner of Awful Announcing explains that 506sports.com coverage map shows that the Knoxville and Chattanooga Fox affiliates will not televise the Jaguars-Titans game. Instead, Vikings-Packers will be shown in the 1:00 p.m. ET window.

It’s a preliminary map, as Lerner notes. The Fox affiliates in Knoxville and Chattanooga, the third- and fourth-largest cities in the league by way of population, could change their minds.

Making the situation even more unusual is the fact that Fox won’t get many Titans games, because they’re usually on CBS. The obvious takeaway is that the Fox affiliates in Knoxville and Chattanooga believe that more people will watch Packers-Vikings than will watch Jaguars-Titans.

It’s not personal, it’s business. And the affiliates think they’re business interests are best served by showing Packers-Vikings not Jaguars-Titans.

#2756. Game 10 Preview: Clemson Looks to Reverse Home Fortunes Against Georgia Tech

Welcome back STS readers! The air has finally gotten that autumn crisp, and the Tigers have managed to put some wins together to become bowl-eligible ahead of this last stretch of games. They aren't making it pretty or easy, but wins are wins and you will take them however you can get them. Here is my good, bad, and ugly from the win at Syracuse.

The Good: Nolan Hauser is still the man, and this team would be in a world of hurt if not for him. He did miss a 57 yarder a couple of yards short because he hit it fat. Wish I could hit something that far without a clean strike. Clemson's red zone problems persist, but at least Hauser has prevented those from being empty possessions. The defense was also very good for the majority of the contest and held the Orange under 20 points. It also provided the lone touchdown for the Tigers when Kortney Kelly and Jaheim Lawson combined for a sack-fumble-TD return that was the real difference in the game. Tait Reynolds shut the door for the second straight game with his running ability. He is becoming more and more dangerous as the season progresses. Clemson managed to hit a huge run by Jarvis Green right out of the gate as well as a deep ball completion to Wesco and a nifty WR pass play to TJ Moore. Chad Morris is certainly trying to get big plays back into the picture.

The Bad: Clemson's defense was good when it had to be but struggled with tackling more noticeably in this game. Sammy Brown hit Ahmad Miller two yards behind the LOS and Miller ended up getting a 4 yard run dragging Brown and at least two other Tigers along the way. Branden Strozier had a bad missed tackle in man coverage that led to an explosive play when the game was getting tight. Clemson's passing game continues to be plagued by either critical drops or Reynolds and the WR missing route adjustments post snap.

The Ugly: Injuries take my ugly designation for this week. Clemson went into this game with multiple starters out and then lost Donavan Starr for the season before it ended. Injuries are part of any season for every team, but Clemson has been hit pretty hard this year, including extended or season-ending injuries to Polo Anderson, Corian Gipson, Markus Strong, and Gordon Sellars. Elyjah Thurmon has missed two games+, Harris Sewell, Gideon Davidson, Kobe McCloud, and Tyler Brown all missed this past week. Hopefully the worst is behind the team now in this regard.

Speaking of injuries, Georgia Tech has had a lot of that happen to them and definitely comes limping into Death Valley after getting throttled at home by Louisville last week, which led to a large staff overhaul by Brent Key. GT's fortunes have turned significantly since last year. The Jackets were 9-1 going into November 14th, 2025 and have since lost 10 of their last 12 games. Clemson is in no position to take anyone lightly these days, and the Tigers have also been pretty poor in Death Valley against power conference teams since that ominous loss to Louisville in 2024. Clemson still has a small hope to get to Charlotte, but that would be a much stronger possibility had they not blown it at home to Virginia Tech. Clemson's fans could really use the shot in the arm a complete game would provide, not to mention a team that has improved but still has to take another big step on offense to think it can challenge a legitimate top 25 opponent.

Clemson Offense vs. GT Defense: Last year's loss to GT stung badly (pun intended). Clemson never really seemed to recover from that loss. Clemson's offense was not good that day in Atlanta against a defense that a lot of other teams punished. This year's offense has obviously been poor, especially when it comes to scoring touchdowns. CSU offered a great chance to get something rolling, but that didn't really happen. This is definitely the next best chance against a defense that just fired its coordinator and several other staff members. GT has been gashed by opposing running games the vast majority of the season and are currently giving up 222.8 yards per game on the ground. Clemson certainly needs to attack this weakness and will hopefully have Davidson back to bolster the running back corps. GT is likely going to do what is has to with loading the box to try to force Clemson to throw, so that should provide more single coverage chances for the wideouts. That unit has not punished people nearly enough this season and could build a sad lowlight tape of dropped balls on big play chances. More than anything, Clemson could really use something that hits for a TD and not just a big gain because the offense has routinely blown it when it has had to run more plays.

I certainly feel Tait Reynolds is getting closer to truly breaking out. He still had some issues last week, particularly with reading route adjustments based on coverages. He threw long to Moore and Burroughs when the coverage dictated either a back shoulder or a direct throw. However, he was better about avoiding sacks and was definitely a factor running the ball throughout the game. GT is not as good on defense as Syracuse and certainly is weaker at corner, so you have to hope Wesco and/or Moore can really dominate a matchup for the first time this season. Moore in particular could really use a strong game to snap out of his funk and get out of his own head.

I do theorize that the plan with Reynolds is to minimize balls in jeopardy, which would explain fewer throws to the middle of the field. The defense has emerged to the point that not putting them in a terrible spot with a turnover and forcing teams to have to drive on them is a key to success. This was a very Danny Ford era style of play and it led to many games that looked like last week's during that time. The key was the vast majority of those games were wins. Chad Morris is having to temper working to unlock the offense with not putting the defense in a bind or exposing Reynolds more than is necessary.

GT is only 2-7, but they did manage to beat Duke who is a good team. The Jackets were a bit lucky in that game, but at the same time they made star running back Nate Sheppard grind out his 97 yards on 27 carries and did just enough on defense to hold on. I don't put it past this Clemson offense to make any defense look good, but there really should be no excuse for not getting 30+ points against a team surrendering 32.2 points per game. It starts with taking care of the ball and cutting down on penalties. I actually felt the OL was better at this last week considering Grant Wise and Gavin Blanchard were starting. It felt like the most veteran of the group, RT Collin Sadler, was the weakest link of the night. I still hold out hope that Blanchard's play will allow for Thurmon to get a chance at RT to see if he can be a better option over there. But Thurmon is not yet clear of concussion protocol from that scary hit at FSU.

Do you want to support STS writers? You can do so by supporting our sponsor, Section 103. They deep dive school traditions to create thoughtful designs artfully applied to insanely comfortable tees, polos, hats, and more. Be sure to use our promo code STS10 so you get 10% off your first order and we get credit for sending you their way. Their founder, Steven, has been good to us and we think you'll love their Clemson, Virginia, Virginia Tech, and Georgia Tech merch. They just released a Louisville merchandise line as well! Click here to explore.

Clemson Defense vs. GT Offense: There are always those opposing players you are happy to see move on from a team you play every year. Haynes King is one of those guys and he was absolutely the difference in last year's loss to the Jackets in Atlanta. GT brought in Alberto Mendoza from Indiana, and while he is a capable player and probably a better pure passer than King, he is nowhere near the running menace that King was. Buster Faulkner took his talents (and a few former GT players) to Gainesville, perhaps seeing the writing on the wall for the current struggles GT is facing. GT has tried backup quarterback Grady Adamson some because he is more of a running threat than Mendoza but neither are nearly the physical force King was. This year's defense has been a lot better at bothering the quarterback, and we saw that last week when they got Angeli rattled. Tom Allen has had some excellent results in the initial parts of every game since Miami which is when you face the scripted portion of an opponent's gameplan. GT doesn't need anything that is going to offer them hope so hopefully that trend will continue this week.

GT does have two quality running backs despite some of their struggles running the football. Justice Haynes was a coveted recruit who started with Bama and then went to Michigan before landing at GT. New OC George Godsey played for Ralph Friedgen and has an NFL background, but the transition into his system from Faulkner's has not been very smooth (and Clemson fans can empathize). Former Tiger superstar Nuk Hopkins got elevated to WR coach after Key made his firings. Oklahoma had a better performance after making some offensive changes in their win over Florida, but it is difficult to really make a lot of wholesale changes to what you do at this point in a season. Sometimes a new voice can offer new motivation and guys just perform better as a result, so that is something you hope doesn't happen this week. Clemson's defense should once again be in good position to match up on GT's outside skill, so it comes down to making sure Haynes and Trelain Maddox cannot get anything going and force Mendoza and/or Adamson to do all the heavy lifting. GT has serious issues across its OL with injuries and also not being able to replace a talent like Keylan Rutledge, who was a serious dude on the Plains before being drafted in the first round. Unlike other position groups, Clemson's DL is actually getting healthier and should be counted on to own this matchup.

Clemson does have a wildcard situation at nickel after Starr's unfortunate injury. It will be interesting to see how Tom Allen and his staff adjust this time when there isn't as clear of an option to step in as there was when Corian Gipson went down. You can bet GT and other staffs are going to attempt to attack that area as opposed to testing Ashton Hampton or Elliot Washington.

Special Teams: Clemson's field goal kicking continued to be a strength but there was the first real gaff of the season when Bryant Wesco fumbled a punt return and really killed a great chance for the team to jump on Syracuse earlier in the game. They also gave up a longer return to offset a strong punt by Nolan Hauser. However, it is hard to be on your A game each week and the overall body of work suggests this unit can be expected to deliver for the Tigers. Clemson is back to being a solid favorite this week, and I always say that upset wins and losses usually feature at least one special teams situation going against the favorite. Perhaps the offense will finally take some of the pressure off this group and the defense and increase their margin of error.

Overall: I like Brent Key and think he is about as ideal a coach as GT could hope to have in the modern era of college football. He made some ambitious changes to try to get the Jackets out of their current spiral. He certainly knows that beating Clemson is always going to offer more credibility than just about any other game they play besides UGA. Clemson is built similarly to Tennessee this year and feature a strong defense but a spotty offense with some limitations at QB. GT had some success on that Vols defense back in September, but they were also healthier up front then than they are now. Still, you can't take anyone lightly and you hope this year's team is more cognizant of that than the last couple of teams. I will say this year's Tigers are decidedly more physical than last year's team and are not letting the opponents throw the first punches and having to react. That was GT's true edge last year in this matchup, and I feel a lot better about Clemson being ready this time. Above all, Clemson needs to deliver at home on senior day and start restoring the roar in Death Valley.

#2753. Lions vs. Patriots preview, prediction: On Paper

The Detroit Lions and New England Patriots are in Germany for a big international matchup. The Patriots are a bit desperate for a win, sitting at 5-4 and clinging to the final playoff spot in the AFC. The Lions are a little more comfortable in the fifth spot of the NFC playoff race, but if they want to contend in a competitive NFC North, they need this game, too.

So which team has that statistical advantage and will come out on top Sunday morning? Let's dive into the numbers with our Week 10 Lions vs. Patriots On Paper preview and prediction.

Note: Stats may be a little lighter this week because one of my bigger resources—NFL Pro—is not available in Germany.

The Detroit Lions had their worst passing offense performance last week against a bad—but improving—Dolphins defense. Offensive line struggles were the lowlight of the performance, headlined by the "suspension" of left guard Christian Mahogany and inconsistent play of rookie right tackle Blake Miller. Mahogany is back in the lineup, and that should help the Lions' passing offense which has remained near a top-five unit for most of the season. They rank:

And despite the poor offensive performance, the Lions offensive line is still grading out well as a unit. Though they rank 17th in sack percentage (6.5), they're fifth in pressure percentage allowed (19.4%), second in PFF pass blocking grade (75.1), and seventh in pass block win rate (54%).

The Patriots pass defense started off strong, but has struggled as of late, even against some of the most medicore-to-bad passing offenses. For the season, they rank:

For comparison's sake, all of these rankings except for dropback EPA are below the Lions' pass defense. So whatever you think of Detroit's ability to defend the pass, the Patriots have been worse.

But much like Detroit's pass defense, the one place they thrive is pressuring the opposing quarterback. Thought they're just 19th in pressure percentage (22.4), they're sixth in sack rate (8.0%), 11th in pass rush win rate (52%), and second in PFF pass rush grade (82.8).

While EDGE Elijah Ponder leads the team with 7.5 sacks, it's really New England's interior pressure that causes havoc. Look out for Christian Barmore (78.1 PFF pass rush grade) and Milton Williams (20 pressures) to give Detroit's interior offensive line some issues.

But New England's second is very beatable. Christian Gonzalez is having a down year (50.4 PFF grade) and the Patriots will be down Carlton Davis.

Player to watch: Amon-Ra St. Brown. This isn't just a Germany thing, St. Brown should thrive against the Patriots' zone-heavy defense. Brown is the Lions' best weapon when it comes to recognizing the soft spot in zones, just like last week's eight-catch, 86-yard performance.

Advantage: Lions +2.5. The Patriots' pass rush does have a chance to disrupt Jared Goff like the Dolphins did last week, but for most of the day, the Lions quarterback should be picking apart this poor secondary.

The inconsistency of this rushing attack is still very frustrating to watch, but putting things into perspective, it's still a very decent run game in Detroit. For the season, they rank:

Negative plays remain a huge problem, with Detroit's 20% stuffed rate ranking 25th in the NFL. They are improving in short-yardage situations, though, climbing to 18th in power success rate.

Still, the offensive line—though still plagued by some mental mistakes—appear to be moving people. Detroit ranks fourth in adjusted line yards, eighth in run block win rate, and, as a whole, the Lions entire team is fourth in PFF's run blocking grade.

Detroit will face a formidable test this week against a run defense that has allowed 100 rushing yards just three times this entire season, and each of their last five opponents have been held at or below 4.0 yards per carry. Though last week's performance against the Packers' worst rushing attack in the league should provide at least some hope.

Interestingly, the Patriots run defense appears more efficient than the sum of their parts. They rank just 16th in adjusted line yards allowed, 16th in run stop win rate, and 21st in PFF run defense grade.

One thing they do thrive in, however, is limiting explosives. They've only allowed six rushing plays of 15+ yards (third fewest) and just a single run of 20+ yards (t-fewest). But they're just okay in short-yardage situations. They're 10th in power success rate allowed (59%), but sport just a 16% stuffed rate (23rd).

Player to watch: LB Christian Ellis. While the Patriots are not particularly strong up the middle in run defense, Ellis sports the eighth-best PFF grade against the run (82.3), providing a strong second level of defense. The Patriots' secondary is also active and strong against the run.

Advantage: Lions +0.5. Detroit hasn't been as explosive as expected running the football this year, but they have found some consistency running for gains of 5-10 yards, and that could be exactly what we see on Sunday.

Despite a horrible start to the year, Drake Maye has seemingly righted the ship—outside of last week's performance against a very solid Packers pass defense. For the entire year, the Patriots pass offense ranks:

Essentially, if the Patriots could stop turning the ball over, they'd be a top-five passing attack. But turnovers have been a serious problem. Maye's 11 interceptions leads the league and his 4.0% interception percentage is third-highest in the NFL. To sport that dishonor and still produce the 10th-highest dropback EPA is pretty crazy.

So what's causing the high interception rate? It's a little bit of everything. An injured offensive line that ranks 21st in pressure rate (23.6%) and 18th in sack rate (6.6%), a quarterback who is still young and figuring things out, and a receiving corps that lost Romeo Doubs for the season and hasn't had a lot of A.J. Brown available.

But, again, the Patriots passing attack remains pretty dang efficient despite those problems.

I'm still hesitant to believe in Detroit's defensive improvement through the air. Much of that appears based on simply playing a bunch of poor passing attacks, but the one aspect they have seriously improved on is explosive plays allowed. In the first four games, the Lions allowed 20 passing plays of 20 yards (most in NFL). In the last four games, the Lions have allowed 14 (still t-10th most). For the season, Detroit still only ranks:

The pass rush (eighth in sack rate, seventh in pressure rate) remains solid, despite an ever-decreasing blitz rate (26.3%, 18th).

Detroit will be without top cornerback D.J. Reed for at least another week, but Brian Branch's return has allowed them to have a little more flexibility in their coverages, and it has calmed some things down (a little).

Player to watch: Hunter Henry. While Henry is far from 100% as he deals with a foot injury, he remains the biggest threat to Detroit's defense. Henry is first on the team in receptions (32) and second in yards (361). Meanwhile, the Lions is 31st in DVOA vs. tight ends.

Advantage: Patriots +3. This is the matchup that could change the game. New England, in my opinion, have one of the best passing attacks as long as they can avoid turnovers. The Lions aren't particularly great at forcing turnovers, creating just eight on the season—only three teams have fewer. So I would expect a pretty strong day from Maye.

New England hasn't run the ball very consistently, although injuries have played a large part in that, particularly as of late. They have a fullback, a running back, and three offensive linemen on IR. Running back TreVeyon Henderson has already been ruled out this week and top running back Rhamondre Stevenson could miss this one, too. Guard Ben Brown has been declared out already, and his backup Walter Rouse is working his way through concussion protocol. Put it all together, and the Patriots' running game ranks:

That said, running back Corey Kiner has stepped in and provided a bit of a spark in the last two weeks, rushing for 93 yards on just 15 carries, bolstered by a couple of 20-yard runs. Additionally, they are great in short-yardage situations, converting 75% of power situations, ranking fifth in the NFL.

The Lions' run defense is really starting to come on in recent weeks, with one of their best performances coming last week against a sneaky-good Dolphins run game. Overall, though, the numbers remain pretty pedestrian. The Lions rank:

They're still being victimized by some early-season explosives given up, but that has settled down considerably as of late.

What has been true pretty much all season is that Detroit has clogged the middle of the field. Led by the strong play of defensive tackles Tyleik Williams and Alim McNeill, anything between the b-gaps has been out of business. Yet, oddly, the Lions rank dead last in power success rate allowed, ceding an 84% conversion rate. So don't expect many third-and-1 stops from Detroit on Sunday.

Player to watch: Malcolm Rodriguez. Rodriguez is quietly having a very strong season, and with Jack Campbell out for the foreseeable future, his role will continue to increase. Currently, he sports an 83.9 PFF run defense grade (seventh in NFL among LBs) and the third-highest run stop percentage (11.7).

Advantage: Lions +1. With all of the injuries, I just can't trust the Patriots' rushing attack. And given that the Lions finally seem to have some answers on defense, this should favor the Lions. The one aspect that could tilt things in New England's favor, though, is Maye. While he still prefers to throw when he has escaped the pocket, he still does have 219 rushing yards this season, fourth most among quarterbacks.

While On Paper got wins both straight up and against the spread (6-2 overall, 4-4 ATS), it may have been my least accurate column of the year. I overestimated the Lions' advantage on offense and underestimated their advantages on defense. I expected a shootout and got a 19-9 win, instead. Sure, I had no idea Mahogany was going to be out, but that doesn't justify how bad I missed on that one.

To be fair, no one really expected a defensive battle. And the closest prediction in the comment section wasn't all that close: a 24-16 prediction from The Proudest:

I don't have photoshop on the road with me in Germany, so as your prize, enjoy this picture of me with a humongous beer in Munich:

The Lions come out with a slight +1 advantage, but the edge in three of the four matchups. As is the case with a lot of games this year, the outcome could come down to that one disadvantage: the Lions' pass defense. Maye is an electric player with a ton of explosive play potential. #2752. Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win

Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers brushed off their blowout loss to the Celtics and got back in the win column Thursday night.

They overcame a first-quarter deficit as high as 17 points and earned a 123-112 home win over the Raptors. The Sixers moved to 10-3 and Toronto fell to 5-7.

Tyrese Maxey had 27 points and eight assists. Joel Embiid added 20 points.

Jaylen Brown tallied 18 points and six rebounds. VJ Edgecombe posted 15 points, eight rebounds and a season-high eight assists. Anfernee Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range.

RJ Barrett recorded 31 points and 14 rebounds. Immanuel Quickley had 26 points and six assists.

The Sixers were without LeBron James (low back/sciatica management), Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain), Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear).

The team told reporters Thursday morning that Bona will be re-evaluated in approximately one week and that Barlow participated in shootaround. The 23-year-old forward also went through a pregame workout on the Xfinity Mobile Arena floor. There's no formal timetable for his return.

Toronto's sidelined players included Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes.

The Sixers will face the Pacers on Sunday afternoon in Philadelphia. Here are observations on their victory over the Raptors:

Dean Wade began the game in James' normal spot. The Sixers started slowly, missing their first foul field goals and opening 1 for 8 from three-point range.

He stayed down after setting a ball screen and having an apparent knee-to-knee collision with Ja'Kobe Walter. The Sixers called timeout with 8:30 left in the first quarter and Embiid grabbed at his right knee. He eventually rose with assistance from teammates and Sixers head athletic trainer Kevin Johnson, then limped back to the locker room. Jabari Walker entered.

At the 5:26 mark of the first quarter, Embiid checked back in to cheers from the home fans.

"I knew that he didn't twist it or anything," Maxey said. "I knew it was a knee-to-knee, so I wasn't too worried. He kept saying, 'I just got kneed.' That still hurts, though."

Embiid ended up logging 28 minutes, though he certainly wanted to play more.

"He was very, very motivated to play," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "It was hard to get him out for his scheduled rests tonight, which is a good problem sometimes."

While Embiid's return was a major positive development, the Sixers fell further behind. The Raptors' lead swelled to 32-16 with a Jamison Battle three-pointer and Nurse burned a timeout.

Simons sunk a buzzer-beating three to conclude the first quarter, cutting the Sixers' deficit to nine points.

"Those are big momentum plays that usually have some weight to them and carry you into the next moment," Nurse said.

The Sixers kept rolling against a shorthanded Toronto team playing on the second night of a back-to-back. Simons nailed a triple to kick off the scoring in the second quarter. Brown buried a mid-range jumper and Edgecombe jammed in a crowd-pleasing dunk to give the Sixers a 35-34 edge.

Brown and Edgecombe shined in the second quarter both as individuals and as a duo. The Sixers need Edgecombe to attack a bit more offensively when he shares the floor with Brown and bench players. It doesn't hurt for the second-year guard to have that clarity about his role in those units.

"He's one of our better playmakers," Maxey said of Edgecombe. "He's really good at getting downhill and creating for himself and others."

The Sixers' only three bench rotation players were Walker, Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope (11 points, five assists). In addition to Walker, Wade got center minutes behind Embiid.

Embiid picked up his third foul with 2:23 left in the second quarter and had to take a seat. The teams were tied at 60 apiece through two periods.

The game remained even for much of the third, but Maxey fueled an 11-0 Sixers run late in the quarter.

His speed and the Sixers' collective focus on pushing the pace whenever possible allowed the team to get regular points before Toronto could set its defense. Maxey zoomed in for a layup, then tossed the ball ahead to Brown for an easy bucket. Brown assisted a Simons three. Walker converted a fast-break lay-in and canned a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter. All of a sudden, the Sixers held a 101-87 lead.

Brown, Edgecombe and the bench gave the Sixers more good minutes early in the fourth quarter. They sealed the deal without any late drama. And the fans chanting for a Tacko Fall appearance got their wish with a final-minute entrance by the 7-foot-6 center.

#2749. Ausar Thompson Makes Bold Claim About Cade Cunningham After Pistons Win

Cade Cunningham delivered one of the greatest performances in Detroit Pistons history Thursday night, scoring a career-high 52 points in a thrilling 144-140 double-overtime victory over the Washington Wizards. But following the win, teammate Ausar Thompson made a bold claim about Cunningham that had nothing to do with his scoring.

While Cunningham's offensive brilliance grabbed the headlines, Thompson believes his teammate deserves significantly more recognition for what he brings to the defensive end of the floor. In fact, Thompson thinks Cunningham belongs among the very best defenders in the entire NBA.

May 13, 2026; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Pistons guard Ausar Thompson (9) during player introductions before the game against the Cleveland Cavaliers during game five of the second round of the 2026 NBA Playoffs at Little Caesars Arena. Mandatory Credit: Rick Osentoski-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Following Thursday's victory, Thompson was asked about Cunningham's defensive contributions, particularly his work against Washington star Trae Young during the closing stages of the game. According to postgame reporting published by Roundtable Sports, Thompson believes Cunningham deserves First-Team All-Defensive consideration.

"I tell Cade all the time he's First-Team [All-Defense]. He's First-Team. He's a great defender and he really wants it."

That's quite a statement coming from Thompson, who earned NBA All-Defensive First Team honors himself last season. The Pistons forward knows a thing or two about elite defense, making his endorsement of Cunningham particularly noteworthy.

While Cunningham is widely recognized for his scoring and playmaking, Thompson believes his defensive commitment deserves similar attention. Thursday's victory provided another example of Cunningham's ability to make important contributions on both ends when Detroit needs him most.

Cunningham certainly gave Thompson plenty to praise against the Wizards, finishing with 52 points, 11 assists, and five rebounds without committing a single turnover. According to the NBA's official game coverage, he became the first player since the league began tracking turnovers in 1977-78 to record at least 50 points and 10 assists without a turnover.

The Pistons needed every bit of his production, particularly after Washington forced overtime twice with dramatic last-second baskets. Cunningham scored 30 of his 52 points during the fourth quarter and two overtime periods, helping Detroit survive one of the wildest games of the young season.

Following the victory, Thompson also praised Cunningham's ability to carry the Pistons when the game was on the line.

"He led us through the fourth quarter and overtimes. He did what he does. One person can't just guard him."

Those comments, reported by the Associated Press, illustrate just how much confidence Thompson has in Detroit's franchise player. And when Cunningham is performing at this level, it's not difficult to understand why.

Interestingly, Cunningham wasn't the only Pistons player who made history Thursday night. Thompson recorded his first career triple-double, finishing with 17 points, 11 rebounds, and 11 assists while continuing to provide the defensive intensity that has made him one of Detroit's most valuable players.

The two young stars have developed a partnership that could help shape the franchise for years to come. Thompson's expanded responsibilities as a playmaker have also provided Detroit with another option for creating offense rather than relying exclusively on Cunningham.

Meanwhile, Pistons head coach J.B. Bickerstaff has repeatedly emphasized Cunningham's team-first mentality, praising his ability to recognize what each game requires. Thompson's comments suggest that same commitment extends to the defensive end, even when Cunningham is carrying an enormous offensive workload.

The Pistons improved to 8-3 with Thursday's victory and will look to continue their strong start Saturday against the Miami Heat. And while Cunningham's 52-point masterpiece will be remembered for years to come, Thompson believes his teammate deserves recognition for much more than putting the ball in the basket.

If Cunningham eventually earns First-Team All-Defensive honors, at least one of his teammates won't be surprised. Thompson has apparently been telling him he belongs there all along.

#2748. DeMarvion Overshown didn't know inactive players couldn't celebrate on the field

The Cowboys had 14 accepted penalties for 153 yards in the 27-23 win over the Colts. One of them was called unacceptable and undisciplined by Cowboys executive vice president Stephen Jones.

Linebacker DeMarvion Overshown, who was inactive and dressed in street clothes, came onto the field to celebrate after Quinnen Williams forced a Jonathan Taylor fumble that Shemar James returned to the Dallas 30. Overshown was penalized 15 yards, with referee Clay Martin saying, “After the play, unsportsmanlike conduct by Dallas. We have non-uniformed player in blue sweats and a stocking cap come onto the field to celebrate. That’s a 15-yard penalty.”

Overshown apologized to head coach Brian Schottenheimer and his teammates.

“At the end of the day, I talked to Schotty about it,” Overshown said Thursday, via Calvin Watkins of the Dallas Morning News. “I apologized about it. It was definitely in the moment, but earlier I had said that as a defense, we’re going to start celebrating more, getting takeaways. And I was just caught in the moment. So you can laugh at it now, because we won the game, but in the moment, fourth quarter, tied ball game or close ball game, you don’t want a 15-yard penalty from a guy, especially that’s not even playing. So that’s a lesson learned.”

Overshown said he didn’t know the rule until linebacker Dee Winters started yelling at him, which should prompt questions about why Overshown didn’t know the rule. But he defended Schottenheimer and said he accepted his “butt chewing.”

“It’s not an indictment on Schotty. It’s on me as a player. I own it,” he said.

#2744. ‘Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles

'Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker shared the floor for 128 games in Portland. The Trail Blazers won 43 of them.

They sat beside one another in the Sixers' interview room Thursday night after a victory and discussed what the other 85 taught them.

"Whether you've got a big role or a small role, it's hard to win in the NBA," Simons said. "We've seen it firsthand."

Their roles were considerably different then.

Simons was an established starter entrusted with creating and scoring. Walker, a 2022 second-round pick, was trying to establish himself in a rotation. During their three overlapping seasons, Portland went 33-49, 21-61 and 36-46. The Blazers missed the playoffs each year.

Both are now reserves on a Sixers team constructed to contend. In nine games they've both appeared in this season, Philadelphia is 7-2.

They provided 26 points, 11 rebounds and six three-pointers in the Sixers' 123-112 win over the Raptors at Xfinity Mobile Arena. Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range. Walker recorded nine points and eight rebounds, including four on the offensive glass.

The Sixers outscored Toronto by 24 points during Simons' 23 minutes. Neither former Blazer committed a turnover.

Their production helped Philadelphia overcome a 17-point first-quarter deficit and improve to 10-3 without LeBron James.

"You learn once you come off the bench to kind of read the game before you get in there," Simons said. "Obviously, we started off kind of slow. You just want to go in, bring some energy, get some stops, get out and run. I think everybody who got off the bench brought energy."

Simons supplied an immediate lift with a deep three-pointer at the first-quarter buzzer. His shot ended an 8-0 Sixers run and trimmed Toronto's lead to nine.

He remained involved during an 11-0 burst late in the third quarter, knocking down a three and setting up Walker for a basket. Walker then made a three early in the fourth before Simons scored on the Sixers' next possession.

When Toronto pulled within six with less than five minutes remaining, Simons answered with his fifth three-pointer.

Making those shots is the most obvious way Simons can help a roster already featuring James, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown. He said the Sixers have not made him feel as though every opportunity must go in.

"They encourage us to keep shooting the ball," Simons said. "Knowing that a team has that much confidence in us to keep shooting makes the game that much easier. Whether you miss or make, as long as we get the right shots in the right moments, I think everybody can live with the misses and makes."

Simons spent seven seasons in Portland before playing last year with Boston and Chicago. His move to Philadelphia reunited him with Walker and Rayan Rupert, another former Blazer who joined the Sixers on a two-way contract during the offseason.

Knowing familiar faces awaited him helped Simons enter another new locker room.

"It made the transition seamless," he said. "Just being able to have some comfortability with guys that I played with for multiple years. It's been fun, kind of feeling like a little bit of old times. Me, Bari and Rups have been through a lot."

Walker's path to Philadelphia began a year earlier and required an additional step.

After playing 188 games over three seasons with Portland, Walker signed a two-way contract with the Sixers in July 2025. He earned a standard contract in February and has since pushed his way into the backup-center conversation despite standing 6-foot-7.

Walker believes some of the work he did on losing teams was easily missed.

"When I first got to the league, I was part of a rebuilding process," he said. "I just felt like some of the little things I did didn't always get noticed when you're losing. I told myself, if I ever got to be part of a winning organization, then I'd go out and expand my abilities."

Rebounding has made Walker difficult for Nick Nurse to overlook.

Walker credited his timing and strong hands to lessons passed down by his father, former NBA center Samaki Walker. Those instincts have become especially useful while the Sixers piece together their frontcourt behind Embiid.

"Rebounding is a skill I kind of honed in on," Walker said. "My dad was a good rebounder. He was known for his rebounding and his timing. I think it's just a gift that he transferred to me."

Walker has made it clear that he expected to earn a role this season.

"I don't know if I was delusional, but I always felt like I was going to play and I was going to be a part," he said. "I read something where they said it's a surprise, but if you were around me this summer, it wouldn't be a surprise. This is expected, and I just want to continue to get better."

The freedom Simons once had in Portland is no longer necessary. Walker does not need a high volume of touches, either. Both understand that playing beside the Sixers' stars requires shooting when open, moving the ball and handling the less glamorous work.

"You've got to find ways to impact the game multiple ways, even if you're not scoring," Simons said. "Whether it's cutting, making the right read and pass to Joel, being the right swing pass to VJ, boxing out on defense or just being in the right position."

Their opportunities will fluctuate. Simons may take nine shots one night and only a few the next. Walker's minutes will depend on matchups and the health of Philadelphia's frontcourt.

Winning has changed what they are being asked to do. Their three years together in Portland taught them why the adjustment is worthwhile.

"You feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you're winning," Simons said. "That's something you can't take for granted."

#2742. McIlroy and Hatton tied as Chacarra stays in hunt

DP World Tour Championship second-round leaderboard

-5 T Hatton (Eng), R McIlroy (NI); -4 K Reitan (Nor), J Luiten (Ned); -3 M Lindberg (Swe), F Schott (Ger), V Perez (Fra); -2 J Schaper (SA), J Rahm (Spa), D Puig (Spa)

Selected others: -1 E Chacarra (Spa); E A Scott (Aus), C Hill (Sco); +3 T Fleetwood (Eng); +6 A Rai (Eng); +8 P Reed (US)

Rory McIlroy is tied for the lead at the halfway mark of the season-ending DP World Tour Championship as he chases a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title.

The six-time major winner followed a three-under opening 69 with an up-and-down 70 to join England's Tyrrell Hatton at the top at Jumeirah Golf Estates in Dubai.

Hatton mixed five birdies and two bogeys to shoot 69, while overnight leader Joost Luiten carded a 73 to lie one shot back alongside Norway's Kristoffer Reitan.

McIlroy, who is guaranteed to equal Colin Montgomerie's record haul of eight season-long crowns with victory this week, sits four shots ahead of Race to Dubai leader Eugenio Chacarra.

The Spaniard, who won three times earlier this season to lead the standings entering this week, birdied his final two holes to finish one under.

"I think it's been a bit eye-opening to see the scoring the first two days," said world number two McIlroy.

"I don't think the wind is supposed to be as up over the weekend, so the scoring might be a little bit better.

"As I said, the scoring this week, because of this course set-up, just isn't as good as in previous years. I've been coming back to the golf course for 15 plus years, and you just associate this course with pretty low scoring.

"And then when it's not, you just have to reframe what is a good score. Anything in the 60s, it seems, this week is a good score."

Race to Dubai leader Eugenio Chacarra trails the leaders by four shots after chipping in at the last for birdie [Getty Images]

Hunting a fourth DP World Tour Championship win and fifth successive Race to Dubai triumph, McIlroy seized the lead with four birdies in his opening 10 holes.

However, the back-to-back Masters champion's momentum stalled with a bogey five at the 12th and he squandered further shots at the 16th and 17th.

But the world number two made a closing birdie for the second day in a row to secure his place in Saturday's final pairing alongside Ryder Cup team-mate Hatton (08:40 GMT).

While Hatton cannot win the Race to Dubai, he boosted his chances of securing a ninth DP World Tour victory - and first since leaving LIV Golf - with another solid display in windy conditions.

The world number 23 made three birdies in a bogey-free front nine before slipping up at the 10th.

He knocked his approach to two feet to set up another birdie at 15, and while he stumbled at the par-three 17th after finding the greenside bunker, he bounced back with a closing birdie.

"It's been tricky. I thought the back nine played really difficult yesterday," said Hatton, who finished second behind Jon Rahm in Abu Dhabi last week.

"The wind was sort of moving round just enough that it goes from slightly off the right to then more down and club selection just becomes really difficult.

"Today it felt a little bit easier, but then just towards the end there, the wind sort of got stronger than where it was yesterday, so then that makes it more challenging.

"But overall, it's been a solid start to the tournament."

South Africa's Jayden Schaper (68) and Spain's two-time major winner Rahm (71) - both of whom can still clinch the Race to Dubai - are well placed at two under.

However, Patrick Reed's hopes of becoming the second American to lift the Harry Vardon Trophy suffered a significant blow after the 2018 Masters champion followed an opening 75 with a 77.

Follow live text updates of the DP World Tour Championship final round on the BBC Sport website and app on Sunday.
