#2737. Sixers, Brown have a ‘humbling' night in loss to Celtics

Sixers, Brown have a 'humbling' night in loss to Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Whatever Jaylen Brown and the Sixers dreamed up for their first matchup against the Celtics soon flew out the window on Tuesday night.

Brown was whistled for two early fouls, the Sixers fell behind and their early-season flaws were on full display in a 123-101 loss at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

"We've just got to get better," Brown said. "Tonight was humbling. We got outplayed, out-executed. So we go back to the drawing board and get ready for the next one."

Over 26 minutes, Brown had 13 points on 4-for-9 shooting and five rebounds against the team that traded him away this summer.

As for the endless dissection of his relationship with former co-star Jayson Tatum, Brown didn't have much to add Tuesday. There was no public reconciliation, no obvious on-court animosity and generally nothing to satisfy fans hoping for some kind of fireworks on that front.

"I'm just focused on doing what's best for my team," Brown said. "Everything else … to be honest, I wasn't paying attention. But credit to Jayson; he played well tonight. Credit to the Celtics. They executed, they shot the hell out of the ball and they were the better team tonight."

Tatum scored 21 points, two of which came on a third-quarter slam over LeBron James. Paul George continued his fantastic start as a Celtic by dropping 36 points and draining six three-pointers.

The Celtics dominated from beyond the arc, shooting 22 for 49 (44.9 percent). The Sixers went just 11 for 37 (29.7 percent) on another night of underwhelming offense. The team sits 22nd in the NBA in offensive rating, 24th in three-point makes per game and 21st in three-point percentage.

"I think that we've got some guys that are obviously shooting much lower percentages than their last season or their career average — almost a handful of guys," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "And I don't think it's because they're shooting fallaway, totally contested ones. I think they're shots we want them to take. So I think they'll continue to take 'em and I'm pretty sure those will even out into their career averages."

Joel Embiid is at 37 percent from the floor and 4 for 33 from three-point range (12.1 percent).

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center got through an injury scare when he rolled his ankle late in the second quarter and hit a three early in the third. It was his first long-range make since the Sixers' home opener back on Oct. 22.

"It's a work in progress," Embiid said. "I think the biggest thing is just not thinking. I'm probably overthinking it. The rhythm of the game is different. I'm so used to having to create for myself, so it's a little bit different.

"But I think I'm slowly getting better. You could see as soon as I made a three, the next shot in the short corner … I didn't even think about it. I just shot it and let it fly, and I made it. … I think it's just about taking what's in front of you. Make or miss, keep working on your game. It's going to get there at some point."

Even with the Sixers second in the Eastern Conference standings at 9-3, Embiid believes the team's defense has "slacked off a little bit" in recent games.

"I don't really look at the record," he said. "I just look at the process of, 'Are we getting better every day?' We can always do a better job at all phases of the game."

"They're one of the top teams in the league and they've been together for a while," Brown said. "We've got a lot to work on over here, so we've got to get to work."

The Sixers will face the Raptors on Thursday night in Philadelphia.

They'll have to wait until Jan. 21 in Boston to see the Celtics again.

"I was looking forward to this," Brown said. "I was looking forward to playing well, but s— happens. Just get ready for the next one."

#2733. #PostPulpit mailbag: What’s going on with Christian Gonzalez?

The New England Patriots have landed in Germany where they hold a pair of practices before taking on the Detroit Lions at 9:30 a.m. ET on Sunday.

So, let's get into this week's edition of the #PostPulpit Mailbag.

Like a lot of people, I was mightily disappointed (to say the least) in the recent performance of our resident highest-paid cornerback in the league. But I find myself wondering if he's the only one deserving blame. When he repeatedly lines up in such soft coverage, not pressing at the line of scrimmage — indeed, giving the receiver an obscenely huge cushion to release — that's not entirely HIS decision, right? Isn't that pre-snap alignment dictated by the coaches and their game plan, at least much of the time? How much of the problem do you think lies with coaching schemes that play away from Gonzalez's strengths? – BriGuy301

What happened to Gonzalez last game and why? Was it a one-off, or did the Packers figure something out that other teams might be able to emulate? – fdsafdsa

Gonzalez is certainly not blameless and needs to play better. However, he is also being asked to do a lot within a Patriots secondary that leans heavily on disguising coverages. While the All-Pro cornerback is at his best pressing receivers at the line of scrimmage and playing man coverage, he has been asked to handle a variety of responsibilities, including off-man coverage, inverted Cover 2 (where he is responsible for the half-field safety), playing the deep third in Cover 3 and more.

The question here is whether the Patriots have leaned too heavily into those disguises and reached a point where simplifying things would benefit the defense. New England has a talented secondary that is playing well below its capabilities as they rank dead last in the league in zone coverage EPA per dropback. Opposing offenses like the Bears and Packers have also appeared to be one step ahead with coverage beaters and using tools like quick snaps to catch the defense out of position and generate explosive plays.

At some point, the Patriots may need to prioritize letting their defensive backs play more straight up and to their strengths.

With all the pressure that Maye faces each game, and especially against teams like the Packers who blitz a lot (46.5% of his drop backs against Green Bay), why do we not see more hot reads or short patterns? It looks like the Patriots rely predominantly on mid- to long-range routes, which take more time and require the Offensive Line to hold up longer. I would think that Pop or Chism – who both have short-area quickness – would be great at those routes, especially given that they seem to run a lot of them during the preseason. So I'm curious if A) they're doing it but I just don't see it? And/or B) is there a good reason to not run quick slants and crossers and hot reads? – PatsFanFromNH

The Patriots' offense does feature sight adjustments and hot routes. Earlier this season, players credited opposing defenses for dropping defenders off the line of scrimmage to take away those routes. New England will need to find ways to counter those adjustments or develop other answers against the pressure packages that have repeatedly given the offense trouble.

In recent weeks, both the Bears and Packers have found success attacking the Patriots' offensive line with overload pressures, sending two defenders off the same side of the formation and dropping defenders off the line of scrimmage on the other side. In both games, New England struggled to pick up those pressures early before settling down and finding answers as the game progressed.

Moving forward, the Patriots need to determine how they want to handle those situations out of the gate, whether that means identifying the right protection calls before the snap or trusting Maye and his receivers to make plays after. Finding those answers earlier in games will be critical to avoid early deficits.

Brian, if the Patriots lose to the Lions to fall to 5-5 with 4 very difficult games left, is it time to switch gears and root for draft position? It's been a tough year full of injuries. That happens in football, and the draft is supposed to be a good one. On the other hand, if they pull off the upset in Germany, it's full speed ahead going for the playoffs, with a bye week plus the Chargers game to get healthy. – New England Guy

Sunday's game against the Lions feels like an inflection point on the season, so it will be interesting to see which Patriots team shows up in Germany.

As for the playoffs, 10 wins has historically been a good benchmark for securing a postseason spot. If the Patriots take care of business against the winless Chargers, Jets and Dolphins, they would need just two more wins from their remaining matchups against the Lions, Vikings, Chiefs, Bills and Broncos to reach that mark.

And looking at the current AFC landscape, the threshold could be closer to nine wins. There appears to be a relatively clear-cut top seven in the conference unless the Houston Texans catch fire during the second half of the season.

Why didn't the pats trade for a nose tackle, 3rd safety, or/and a 3rd outside cornerback? Any one, two or all 3 of these positions were a must have to right the ship! – sjamesbossports

After investing significant draft capital in A.J. Brown and looking to avoid taking on a major financial commitment, the Patriots were never likely to make a significant addition at the trade deadline. You could certainly make the argument for adding defensive depth in exchange for late-round draft capital, but the lack of movement at those positions around the league suggests there wasn't much of a market at those spots.

A question more long term :what are your thoughts about next year patriots cap big moves renegotiation with major players (or potential cut or trade) to absorb anticipated Maye super contract ? – 7i165

Who do you think will be the cap casualties next year? Onwenu, Barmore, Davis, Hunter, Byard, DeVitto, Moses, Landry? I know they are a veteran core, but almost all of them don't produce to what they are being paid at, so we might need to cut bait. How much would we gain from trading or letting them walk? – Maxxwell

The Patriots did not sell at the deadline as they still can be a competitve team especially as they get healthier on offense. It will be a different conversation this offseason as there is definitely an argument for the team getting younger and adding draft capital.

Among the names mentioned, I would imagine the team moves on from Christian Barmore, Harold Landry, and potentially Carlton Davis as the veterans have no guaranteed money remaining. Byard's play has not been worthy of a second contract while the guess would be Moses retires. Henry was extended this offseason while there's no rush to move off DeVito. All the moves would free up a substantial amount of salary cap space.

That's all for this week's #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you'd liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post on the Feed. Make sure to follow @iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.

#2732. Rams place WR Puka Nacua on IR

A day after Sean McVay said the Rams wouldn’t place Puka Nacua on injured reserve, the wide receiver went on IR.

McVay said “roster semantics” would keep Nacua on the 53-man roster, with every team getting only eight designated-to-return slots during the season. The Rams have used three of their designations and have Kobie Turner, Davante Adams, Terrance Ferguson and now Nacua on IR with hopes of returning.

But with Nacua set to miss “extended time,” as McVay said Wednesday, with MCL and PCL sprains in his knee and turf toe, the Rams opted to move him to the IR list.

Nacua will miss at least the next four games, with the Cowboys game on Dec. 20 the earliest he can return by rule.

The Rams signed wide receiver Brennan Presley to take Nacua’s roster spot and added wide receiver Tyler Scott to the practice squad.

#2731. Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup

Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers couldn't rekindle the magic of their comeback home-opening win over the Cavaliers.

They fell Friday night in NBA Cup action, suffering a 119-95 defeat in Cleveland. The Sixers dipped to 8-2 and the Cavs improved to 5-4.

The Sixers' top scorers were Jaylen Brown (20 points), VJ Edgecombe (19 points) and Tyrese Maxey (17).

The Cavs got 23 points from Donovan Mitchell and 22 from Evan Mobley.

The Sixers' injured players included center Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain). Cleveland was down big man Jarrett Allen (right knee contusion). Sam Merrill sat out the second half with a right elbow injury.

With Friday's loss, the Sixers are 1-1 in Eastern Conference Group B of the NBA Cup. Their next Cup game is scheduled for Nov. 25 against the Heat.

The Sixers will conclude their three-road trip Sunday afternoon against the Bulls. Here are observations on their blowout loss to Cleveland:

After a missed Merrill three-pointer, the Sixers steamed ahead on the fast break and Edgecombe opened the scoring with a slam.

The Cavs replied with a 15-0 run kickstarted by six straight Mitchell points. Much like in the Sixers' Oct. 22 win over Cleveland, they were many levels below their best in the first quarter.

The Sixers began 0 for 4 from three-point range, including two LeBron James misses. The Cavs were also the better team in transition and limited the Sixers' chances to attack in the open floor by taking excellent care of the ball in the early going. Edgecombe was called for his second foul with 7:34 left in the first quarter.

Meanwhile, Joel Embiid expressed his frustration about a couple of early no-calls. Embiid's larger problem was that he couldn't hit any sort of shot besides free throws.

He went 0 for 9 from the floor in the game. The seven-time All-Star finished with six points and seven rebounds.

Embiid has had a subpar shooting start to the year, especially from three-point territory — he's now 3 for 28 (10.7 percent) — but Friday was the kind of extreme night that's bound to happen here and there over the course of a long season.

Of course, it's notable that Embiid's been playing through right foot plantar fasciitis and the Sixers have been keeping a close eye on his minutes. We'll see how the team manages his availability moving forward and whether Embiid is able to bounce back next time out.

James didn't play anywhere near his finest game either. He had eight points on 3-for-12 shooting, eight rebounds, three assists and six turnovers.

As a team, the Sixers were 36.5 percent from the field and 25 percent beyond the arc.

Jabari Walker rejoined the Sixers' rotation as the backup center with Bona sidelined. Anfernee Simons, former Cav Dean Wade and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope all remained rotation fixtures.

With Walker and Caldwell-Pope on the court next to three starters, the Sixers cut their deficit to single digits in the second quarter. Walker threw down a fast-break dunk that cut Cleveland's lead to 48-41. He gave the Sixers some good defensive possessions when switched on to James Harden and provided his usual physical, high-effort work on the glass.

Edgecombe was fantastic in the second, sinking three triples, racking up 15 points and nabbing three steals.

Many second-year players would have a tough time finding a rhythm after encountering early foul trouble, but Edgecombe was great as soon as he checked back in and delivered a ton of valuable buckets in the Sixers' comeback push.

The Sixers pulled to within 66-63 when Maxey picked a steal and threw a pretty one-handed bounce pass to Edgecombe for a dunk.

With Embiid and James offering little as scorers, Brown hit several shots that helped the Sixers stay in the game. After his 30-point performance last time out against the Pistons, Brown reached the 20-point mark for a third consecutive game.

Still, the Sixers' offense never got rolling. The Cavs maintained their lead and extended it late in the third quarter. By early in the fourth, the Sixers trailed by over 20 points.

Embiid didn't play the fourth quarter and logged 25 minutes. He's had zero made field goals on just one other occasion in his career, back in Nov. 2019 against the Raptors.

Even with their tremendous first nine games, the Sixers knew they'd hit speed bumps throughout the year. They'll try to get back on track Sunday in Chicago.

#2728. Stampede Blue Reacts results (Week 10): Colts fan confidence falls again, down to 17%

The latest SB Nation Reacts survey delivered another troubling update on the state of fan sentiment in Indianapolis, with just 17 percent of Colts fans saying they are confident the team is headed in the right direction. It is another slight drop from last week's 19 percent mark, and it reinforces just how little confidence remains in the current state of the franchise.

At this point, the result should not come as much of a surprise. The Colts have lost five straight games, fallen to 2-7 on the season and spent the last several weeks making major roster changes ahead of the NFL trade deadline. Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, Keenan Allen and Josh Downs have all been moved, while other notable players such as Jonathan Taylor, Grover Stewart and Daniel Jones remained with the team despite speculation surrounding their futures. Taken together, it has been a clear sign that Indianapolis is no longer focused on salvaging this season, but instead trying to position itself for a longer-term reset.

That does not necessarily mean every fan opposes the direction the organization is taking. In fact, some of this low confidence may simply reflect how painful the current stage of the process looks rather than outright disagreement with the moves themselves. The Colts have finally started making the kind of difficult decisions that a struggling team often has to make, but that does not make the short-term product any easier to watch. Losing games, trading recognizable veterans and entering the second half of the season with significant uncertainty at quarterback, wide receiver and along both lines is not exactly a recipe for immediate optimism.

What this number really shows is that Colts fans are still waiting for a reason to believe. The franchise may have started its rebuilding process in earnest, but rebuilding alone does not inspire confidence unless there is a clear sense that the team knows where it is going. Right now, that part still feels uncertain. Chris Ballard is gone, the roster has been reshaped, and the next general manager will inherit a team with more draft capital, but also plenty of holes and no obvious path back to contention in the near future.

For now, the fan base remains deeply skeptical. Until the Colts start showing signs of a coherent long-term plan, or at the very least begin putting a more competitive product on the field, it is hard to imagine that confidence number rising in any meaningful way.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2721. Back in Philadelphia with Celtics, Paul George looks forward to ‘a regular game'

Back in Philadelphia with Celtics, Paul George looks forward to 'a regular game' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Paul George's presence back in town was one of the many swirling morning storylines at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

For good reason, former Celtics teammates Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum will draw immense attention Tuesday night. After all, Brown has said there "might be a little lamb chops with some gravy" between the two, if not a full-blown beef.

But George's return to Philadelphia is more than a tiny subplot. Following two seasons in Philadelphia, he was the centerpiece of the Sixers' summer trade package to acquire Brown.

George told reporters before the Celtics' shootaround that it feels like "a regular game."

"Had I been here eight, nine, 10 years, different story," he said. "I was here two years. Obviously, we didn't have the best of luck or had a great, I think, partnership in terms of my ability to stay healthy and on the floor. So that kind of played into a lot of it.

"But obviously, it's a tremendous fan base, a great sports town to play in. So that was appreciated. There's no ill will for me. It'll be fun to just compete. And outside of that, it's a normal game."

The 36-year-old George indeed had trouble staying available for sustained stretches as a Sixer. He dealt with a variety of injuries and served a 25-game suspension last season for violating the NBA's anti-drug policy.

George did play well on both ends of the floor for much of the 2026 playoffs. He helped the Sixers come back to win a seven-game first-round series against the Celtics in historic fashion. The nine-time All-Star also brought a veteran steadiness to the Sixers' locker room and was glad to mentor younger players like VJ Edgecombe.

"Just his routine … even when he got hot, he didn't try to force it," Jabari Walker said Tuesday morning. "His game was smooth and I think that's how he is as a person, just not forcing anything and having a calm energy."

George has certainly enjoyed his early days as a Celtic.

Through nine games, he's averaged 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 2.3 steals while shooting 42.5 percent from three-point range. Boston will enter Tuesday night's matchup second in the Eastern Conference standings at 8-2, the Sixers first at 9-2.

"I've been kind of blown away," George said. "I think it exceeded my expectations since being in Boston. You never know how much culture is involved and how much culture changes your outlook on things and the effect it has mentally, physically, just being in an environment … and the culture that Boston presents.

"So I've been thrilled. I've been playing some of my best basketball of late, and just been enjoying grinding it out with these guys out here. It's a fun style of play and I can't talk (enough) about just the thrill, the happiness and the excitement and joy that it has brought being here."

He was asked what sort of reception he expects from Sixers fans.

"Not sure," George said. "In some ways, I helped land them a future piece for them. So with that, not sure how the reception would be."

#2718. Justin Jefferson: It's a joy to see Kirk Cousins take over as a leader

Kirk Cousins is back in Minnesota, and perhaps no one is more excited about that than Justin Jefferson.

The wide receiver had career highs in catches (128) and yards (1,809) and earned the NFL’s Offensive Player of the Year award in Cousins’ last full season with the Vikings in 2022.

Jefferson, though, said he has “no expectations.”

“It’s really just going out there and just executing our plays,” Jefferson said, via Kevin Seifert of ESPN. “It’s not really getting too juiced up about him being here or anybody being back there. It’s just all about understanding the plays that are being called, understanding the jobs that we have and executing our responsibilities. And just the plays that are there, and the plays that could be made, we just need to continue to just make those type of plays. And I’m pretty sure that the results would be a lot better.

“He just understands the game. He’s a guy that studies the game a lot. He understands how the defenses play, especially covering me. And he understands, the plays that we have called that are kind of my plays and he understands the timing and the windows to throw those type of plays, but he also doesn’t force those type of plays to me and he just lets the game come to me.”

Jefferson said it was “a joy to hear [Cousins] just take over and be a leader in the meeting room, on the field.”

“He’s being vocal,” Jefferson said. “Just making sure that everybody hears the plays that he’s talking about and the notes that he has for certain routes, certain plays. And he’s just making sure that everybody’s on the same page. So it’s definitely cool to hear that type of leadership and command. If you know Kirk, that’s pretty normal from him. So it’s definitely kind of cool him being back in that room and him taking that control.”

#2716. Giants will regret blowing chance to bury Commanders in NFC East race

EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ — The laundry list of mistakes they made during their 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders on "Thursday Night Football" will haunt the Giants' for the duration of the mini-bye.

And potentially for the rest of the season. And in an even worse-case scenario, the offseason.

Because any drama in the NFC East for the remainder of the 2026 campaign could be traced to the final minutes of the affair here Nov. 12, when Jayden Daniels found Stefon Diggs for the go-ahead touchdown with 57 seconds left in the game.

Washington having a chance to take the lead at all felt shocking given the way the Giants (5-3-1) had come back with Isaiah Likely's 66-yard touchdown midway through the fourth and interceptions later from Jevon Holland and Ar'Darious Washington seemingly putting the game on ice.

Except the offense could not do just that, and the Commanders (3-5-1) ultimately escaped with a victory that kept them two back of the Giants in the loss column with eight games to play and ensured they held the tiebreaker over their divisional foe.

"It's a missed opportunity, but like I told the guys – it would've been great to win the game, but it doesn't change our goals or our opportunity going forward," head coach John Harbaugh said. "It's a tough loss. It's the National Football League, you're going to lose some games."

Giants fullback Patrick Ricard, no stranger to being on the wrong side of a tight outcome on a Harbaugh-coached team (having followed the coach from the Baltimore Ravens to New York this offseason), said the Giants' offense hasn't been able to put an opponent away without being bailed out by the defense since its Week 1 victory over the Dallas Cowboys.

"That's something that I've always prided myself, playing on an offense that's able to ice a game," Ricard said. "Like this year, we haven't been able to do that as an offense."

With less than four minutes remaining, the Giants turned to backup quarterback Jameis Winston to try and QB sneak his way to a critical first down. For a moment, it appeared he did. But head coach Dan Quinn successfully challenged the spot of the ball and the call was reversed. To have it overturned at that juncture in the game was frustrating, Ricard said. The Giants went three-and-out after both interceptions and their final drive stalled at midfield despite needing another first down and then some to attempt a game-tying field goal.

The missed opportunities irked several of the Giants, including Likely, who sounded like a philosopher while describing the failures of the offense.

"Very frustrating," Likely said. "When you want to be one of the best teams in the league, you got to be able to ice the game when the game is to be iced."

Defensively, the Giants could not put Daniels down despite blitzing him 17 times. He was 10-for-17 against the blitz with 119 yards, with all three of his touchdowns coming against defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson's heat. He was pressured on 17.9% of his dropbacks, according to ESPN, the second-lowest pressure rate he's faced in his career.

Linebacker Abdul Carter didn't walk into the locker room and encounter his teammates' heads hanging in defeat as if the season had just ended.

"I wouldn't say angry is the word. We just got to figure out ways how to stop making so many mistakes," Carter said of the defense. "We got to figure out ways to give our offense a better chance."

Arguably the Giants' most skilled player came up short in two of the biggest spots of the night with the ball in his hands – which is something Malik Nabers has been adamant about wanting all season. Except on a red zone drive in the first half, he had the ball knocked out of his hands by Washington linebacker Frankie Luvu for a fumble.

Then on the final Giants' offensive play of the game, McCarthy hoisted a jump ball for Nabers in double coverage. Nabers actually had a chance to high-point the ball and come up with a huge play that would have brought New York to the Washington 10-yard line. Instead the hand fight for the ball was won by Commanders cornerback Rasul Douglas.

"Obviously, absolutely sucks. No matter what, we've got to find a way to get the win. Credit them for making more plays than we did. We've just got to learn from this and find a way to get better."

The Giants' specialists also failed them in critical moments. Dominic Zvada, the rookie kicker, missed a 33-yard field goal on the team's first successful drive of the game. He later kicked the ball out of bounds to give the Commanders friendly field position. But the bigger culprit in that regard was punter Jordan Stout, who shanked a punt 12 yards to set up Washington's eventual game-winning drive to start at the 29-yard line instead of pinned deep near their own end zone.

#2715. ‘Let's check the ball up': Jaylen Brown ready for first game against Celtics

'Let's check the ball up': Jaylen Brown ready for first game against Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Jaylen Brown was asked Sunday whether he and Jayson Tatum had spoken since the former teammates addressed their relationship during the preseason.

Does he plan to approach Tatum before Tuesday night's game at Xfinity Mobile Arena?

"I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side," Brown said. "We're playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win. So it's nothing to talk about. Let's check the ball up."

After months of public comments, documentaries and questions about how their partnership ended, the basketball will finally take over.

Brown will face Boston for the first time since the Celtics traded him to Philadelphia for Paul George and four future draft assets in July. He spent his first 10 NBA seasons in Boston, played nine alongside Tatum and helped the Celtics win the 2024 championship, earning Finals MVP honors.

Tuesday's 8 p.m. game on NBC will also bring together the top two teams in the Eastern Conference. The Sixers are 9-2. Boston, riding a three-game winning streak, is 8-2 and sits a half-game behind Philadelphia.

"Another good opportunity for our team to be able to show what we're made of," Brown said. "I'm looking forward to it. Big-time matchup, two heavyweights in the East. Let's get it."

Brown has not hidden his appreciation for Boston, even as more has emerged about the deterioration of his relationship with Tatum and the organization.

"I love Boston," he said Sunday. "Boston's a great city. A lot of people I developed relationships with, you know what I mean? But I'm just focused on what's in front of me right now. And that's the most important thing."

He also acknowledged everything that accompanies an abrupt end to a decade with one organization.

"Decisions were made," Brown said. "It's life. It's business. Move on. It's OK. … It's emotions. You've got to pack up and move your stuff. Your family's got to pack up and move. But it's life. It's happened to numerous amounts of people, myself included.

"So I just look forward to being able to build with my team over here, trying to make the best of my situation."

Brown faced the Celtics during the preseason, but Tuesday will be the first meeting that counts. He said he did not know whether that would introduce emotions that were absent during the exhibition schedule.

"We'll see how I feel when we get out there," Brown said. "As of now, I've got no emotion toward nothing. So I'm just ready to go."

Tatum was similarly restrained after Boston's 117-97 victory over Milwaukee on Sunday.

"It's another game on the schedule," Tatum said. "It's the Celtics versus the Sixers. In the words of Brad Stevens, they all count as one."

Tatum called the Sixers "an incredible group" with a "great coaching staff," but declined to add to the discussion surrounding his relationship with Brown.

"Drama gets clicks and views," he said. "That's not my thing." CBS Sports reported Tatum's full comments Sunday night.

Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla was even more concise.

"It'll be fun," Mazzulla said. "It'll be a good atmosphere."

Brown is not the only centerpiece of the July deal who will face his former team.

George has settled quickly into Boston's lineup, averaging 20.4 points and supplying the high-volume outside shooting the Celtics have long prioritized. He scored 27 points and made five three-pointers Sunday as Boston beat Milwaukee for its third consecutive victory.

The Celtics have not needed George to duplicate everything Brown provided. He has fit alongside Tatum, Derrick White and Boston's returning core as another willing shooter and versatile defender.

Tatum is averaging 27.1 points, six rebounds and 7.8 assists. His playmaking has been especially important for a team that replaced Brown's downhill pressure with more shooting and ball movement.

Boston enters Tuesday ranked third in offensive rating and fourth in defensive rating. It is one of two NBA teams currently inside the top five on both ends of the floor.

The Celtics have also made 15.6 three-pointers per game, the second-highest average in the league. They set an NBA Cup record by hitting 24 against Charlotte on Friday, then made 18 more Sunday in Milwaukee.

That presents a clear challenge for a Sixers defense that has generally performed well but has occasionally surrendered clean perimeter looks after committing extra help toward the ball. Tatum, George, White, Payton Pritchard and Sam Hauser can all punish late rotations.

The Sixers have reached 9-2 without depending upon the same formula every night.

Tyrese Maxey leads them at 26.9 points per game. Brown is averaging 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and four assists while shooting 47.7 percent from the field and 39.2 percent from three. Joel Embiid and LeBron James have supplied scoring, passing and defensive flexibility around them.

Brown has repeatedly described the team as unfinished despite its record.

"From our perspective, it's been some growing pains for sure, even though we've been able to win," he said. "The result, we're not so much fixated on the result. It's more so about the process, and we've got to improve our process and our mentality to creating a winning environment."

Boston should provide the clearest early measure of that process.

The Celtics play considerably slower than the Sixers, but their half-court execution has been more efficient. Philadelphia will want to create turnovers and run before Boston can set its defense. The Celtics will attempt to control the pace, generate three-pointers and make the Sixers execute against a defense that has yet to allow an opposing player to score 30 points this season.

There is also the unavoidable Brown matchup. Boston could use Tatum, George and White against him at different points, giving the Celtics several defenders capable of absorbing his drives without immediately sending help.

Nick Nurse expects Brown to bring something extra, even if Brown has publicly downplayed the emotional component.

"It's going to be very different for him," Nurse said. "I think probably a little bit of emotion in there, too, but also I think he's going to be very motivated to play."

Boston's rotation is healthy entering the matchup. Two-way guard Devin Carter is out because of an illness.

Dominick Barlow and Ariel Hukporti remain out for the Sixers. Adem Bona could return after missing Sunday's contest.

The betting market views the matchup as essentially a toss-up. Monday afternoon listings had the spread moving between Boston minus-1.5 and Philadelphia minus-1.5, depending on the sportsbook, with the total at 215.5.

That fits the larger picture. Philadelphia owns the East's best record. Boston has the conference's strongest point differential and has outscored opponents by 10.7 points per game.

The surrounding conversation will center on Brown and Tatum until the opening tip. Brown does not intend to contribute any ceremonial small talk.

"He's on his side," Brown said. "I'm on my side."

#2714. Frustrated Malik Nabers pulls vanishing act after Giants’ loss to Commanders

Malik Nabers, who typically waits for the media as soon as the locker room opens, left without speaking after the New York Giants' 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders Thursday night at MetLife Stadium.

New York Post reporter Ryan Dunleavy noted it was the first time in three years he could remember Nabers leaving so abruptly, even though the receiver has faced the music before when frustrated.

It was a less-than-stellar performance for Nabers, who again got demonstrative on the field when things didn't go his way. He caught five passes on seven targets for 44 yards but was a near non-factor in the first half.

Late in the third quarter, after a 37-yard reception on a double move that briefly energized the offense, Nabers fumbled inside the red zone for the first time in his career. The ball was lost after Frankie Luvu forced it free at the 16-yard line, and Nabers tried unsuccessfully to sell the play as an incompletion.

On the game's final pass from J.J. McCarthy, Nabers failed to win a contested 50-50 ball, which Rasul Douglas intercepted to clinch the defeat. Though Nabers likely didn't fully realize Douglas was coming over the top as McCarthy was pressured, the outcome left him flat on his back in stunned disappointment.

The night concluded a challenging week that included broadcast criticism of Nabers' body language in the prior game against the Philadelphia Eagles. He has explained that his intense, raging style is simply how he approaches the game.

The Giants still lead the NFC East at 5-3-1 despite the setback.

#2712. Thursday Night Football: Stefon Diggs' late TD gives Commanders 24-21 win

With 3:27 remaining in Thursday’s game, the Giants lined up with Jameis Winston under center on fourth-and-1 from their own 11. The team’s backup quarterback, who runs the team’s quarterback sneaks, yelled, “Hut One. Hut Two. Hut Three. Who let the dogs out? Who, who, who, who?”

The Giants took a delay of game and then punted.

The Commanders got the last laugh, winning 24-21 on Stefon Diggs’ 32-yard touchdown with 57 seconds left. The Commanders are 3-5-1 and the Giants 5-3-1.

In an entertaining second half, the teams traded the lead four times.

The Giants took a 21-17 lead with 8:13 left on Isaiah Likely’s 66-yard catch-and-run.

The Giants then had back-to-back interceptions of Jayden Daniels. Safety Jevon Holland, who is having an All-Pro season, took the ball away from Chig Okonkwo at the 2-yard line with the Commanders on the Giants 24 with 5:27 left, and Ar’Darius Washington stepped in front of Okonkwo on fourth-and-2 at the Washington 45 with 2:15 left.

The Giants, though, couldn’t run out the clock, and the Commanders made the most of it. They needed only three plays to go 71 yards thanks to a questionable 33-yard pass interference penalty on Deonte Banks, who was covering Treylon Burks. Three plays later, Diggs scored.

The Giants reached the Washington 48 on their final drive, but J.J. McCarthy’s deep throw to Malik Nabers was intercepted by Rasul Douglas with 25 seconds left to end it.

The Giants outgained the Commanders 399 to 340, but missed a field goal and had two turnovers.

Daniels was 23-of-33 for 249 yards with three touchdowns and two interceptions. Rachaad White ran for 47 yards on 11 carries, and Diggs caught six passes for 83 yards. Antonio Williams and Ben Sinnott each caught a touchdown pass.

McCarthy was 23-of-36 for 293 yards with a touchdown and an interception. Cam Skattebo had 18 carries for 78 yards and two touchdowns and caught three passes for 44 yards, and Likely had nine receptions for 127 yards and a touchdown.

#2711. Game Preview: San Antonio Spurs vs Golden State Warriors

Left for dead by plenty of pundits over the summer, the Golden State Warriors came storming out of the gates this season, led by the somehow still otherworldly play of Steph Curry and the surprising play of rookie small forward Yaxel Lendeborg. They were riding an 8-game win streak before losing both their match-up with the Houston Rockets on Wednesday night and Curry, who suffered an oblique abdominal tear just 6 minutes into that contest, never returning. Curry, who was averaging 30 points on ridiculous efficiency in the lead up to the Houston game, is out for at least the next 2 weeks, leaving the Warriors without the engine that drives their entire offense. Golden State to their credit hung with Houston most of the night thanks to Lendeborg's shotmaking, a focused team defensive effort, and offensive contributions from both vets and young guys alike.

Coming into this one on a 10 game winning streak, the San Antonio Spurs have been taking care of business. Facing Golden State without Curry makes them that much easier to guard, but head coach Steve Kerr's defensive game planning, Draymond Green's orchestration both on offense and defense, and Lendeborg's breakout is the sort of combination that could still make life rough on their opponents. San Antonio was able to sleepwalk their way into a big deficit before their huge comeback back win against the Chicago Bulls Wednesday night in Chicago, but against the well-coached Warriors that could be a recipe for disaster.

San Antonio Spurs (10-2) vs Golden State Warriors (8-4)November 13 2026 | 8:30 PM CTWatch: Amazon Prime | Listen: WOAI (1200 AM)Line: San Antonio -10.5

Spurs Injuries: Tobias Harris, calf (OUT), Devin Vassell, groin (day to day)

Warriors Injuries: Steph Curry, oblique (OUT), Jimmy Butler, ACL (OUT), Moses Moody, knee (OUT), Brandon Williams, hamstring (OUT), Gary Payton II, knee (day to day)

Golden State has been notoriously small for years, but they have just a single player on the roster this season that's taller than 6'8. That should mean open season for Victor Wembanyama, who has been on a historical tear to kick off his 4th season in the league and is coming off another huge performance in the win over Chicago. Draymond Green is still a versatile defender with an elite IQ on the defensive side of the ball, but at age 36 and in his 15th season, he is no longer the perennial DPOY-candidate he once was in his prime that could make life difficult on opposing bigs for significant stretches. Regardless though, expect him to draw a decent amount of the assignment on Wemby with help sprinkled in from Golden State's wings. Green and Wembanyama had a notable moment between them last season at the Frost Bank Center almost exactly a year to the day.

With Chef Curry out for the foreseeable future, the bulk of the offense could fall on the shoulders of rookie Yaxel Lendeborg. Lendeborg has been a revelation for Golden State, averaging 21.7 points, 7.4 rebounds, and 3.7 assists on 51% shooting from the field and 43% from 3 on solid volume. An older rookie at 24 years old, he's proven to be adept at attacking closeouts and getting into the teeth of the defense, using his big body (6'9" with a nearly 7'4" wingspan) to go at smaller defenders in the post, and seeking out contact and either finishing through it or finding his way to the charity stripe (6 attempts a game at the line). Opposing defenses have been preoccupied with Curry's offensive blitz to start the season and leaving Lendeborg as the #2 option, but that obviously changes with Steph out now. San Antonio has a variety of defenders they can and will send at him to see how he holds up as the focus of the defense. Should all else fail, they have the always lurking Wembanyama as the ultimate insurance policy.

Golden State has been among the league's most proficient 3 point shooting teams to begin this season, ranking 1st in both makes and percentage. That's largely (and obviously) been because of Curry's volume and consistency from distance, but it's not just about the numbers he puts up. It's also because of the sort of looks that his gravity is able to open up for others. Without him to warp help defenses and open up the easy catch and shoot opportunities for guys like Lendeborg and Brandin Podziemski, their offensive efficiency is likely about to take a hit. That doesn't mean that they still aren't going to launch them though, as they showed with their 17/51 showing in the loss to the Rockets.

#2709. Curt Cignetti represents gold standard Lincoln Riley hasn't reached

USC versus Indiana is the kind of game which reminds us why we care about sports and, more specifically, college football. This is a late-season, mid-November battle in which reputations will be defined and months of offseason preparations will either be revealed as fruitful or futile. This is a game which either changes everything for Lincoln Riley or reminds us how little has changed over five years. Lincoln Riley versus Curt Cignetti with everything on the line is a defining moment in the Big Ten season and in Riley's USC tenure.

The great thing about USC versus Indiana is that there's simply no room for a middle-ground result, an outcome which is good or satisfying for both sides. A close loss for USC means absolutely nothing. Lincoln Riley has to get over the hump. "Almost" is something USC fans have been witnessing and reading about for five years. Falling just short of the playoff won't offer any added comfort to Trojan fans. It's time to knock the door down, not to arrive at the doorstep and ring the doorbell without getting entry into the mansion known as the College Football Playoff.

For Indiana and Curt Cignetti, a season defined by mediocre football will feel like a disaster and real slippage if the Hoosiers lose to USC by even the smallest possible margin. Curt Cignetti established himself as the gold standard in the sport the past two seasons. Losing his identity as the king of college football would hurt very deeply. Losing that identity against a coach who is known for failing in Big Ten road games would add to Indiana's pain if the Hoosiers lose.

There is only success. There is no reward for a good effort or a valiant performance. This is a bottom-line game in which Lincoln Riley has to finally conquer his Big Ten road woes and beat the man most regard as the best in the business. Riley either achieves a spectacular success which changes the conversation at USC, or he sinks into the same familiar pit of failure we have seen far too frequently since the 2022 Pac-12 Championship Game.

USC. Indiana. This is why we watch. This is why we care.

#2708. John Harbaugh expresses confidence in K Dominic Zvada

Giants rookie kicker Dominic Zvada has missed six field goals in nine games. He missed another on Thursday night, a 33-yarder.

While it happened in the first quarter and not on the final play, it stands out in a game that was decided by three points.

After New York’s 24-21 loss to the Commanders, Giants coach John Harbaugh was asked about his level of confidence in Zvada.

“Yeah, we’re confident,” Harbaugh said. “You know, you can’t — as soon as a guy doesn’t make a play, I mean, start firing people left and right. Especially your kicker who’s a rookie. So I’m confident that he’s gonna become a good kicker. I mean, if at some point in time, it doesn’t happen, it doesn’t happen.

“But I’m not gonna panic, you know, halfway through the season when the guy who’s made a bunch of kicks, if that’s what you’re inferring we should be doing.  So, you know, I mean, we’re just not gonna knee-jerk it like that. He’s gonna make kicks. He’s gonna make a lot of kicks, I believe in him.  I think he’s really good, really talented. And we’re gonna give him an opportunity to do it. It’s up to him to do it.”

That’s a fair assessment of a player who’s still new to the NFL. But a kicker has one job. If he can’t do it (especially from distances that should be automatic), at some point tough questions need to be asked.

Basically, how much time will Zvada get before Harbaugh decides it’s not going to happen? That remains to be seen, if Zvada keeps missing kicks he should be making.

#2702. Luke McCaffrey knew the rules and made a heads-up play, causing a kickoff out of bounds

Commanders kickoff returner Luke McCaffrey made the smartest play of the game by not returning a kick in Thursday night’s win over the Giants.

With McCaffrey back to field a Giants kickoff, the ball landed near the sideline at the 5-yard line. The kick stayed in bounds, and some returners would have grabbed the ball and started running. But McCaffrey let the ball bounce, then stepped out of bounds, and then grabbed the ball with his feet down on the sideline.

By rule, the ball is out of bounds if it touches a player who is out of bounds, even if the ball actually stays in bounds. By touching the ball while his feet were out of bounds, McCaffrey forced a kickoff out of bounds penalty on the Giants, putting the ball on the 40-yard line for the Commanders.

“I thought Luke McCaffrey made a really smart play that won’t show up on the stat sheet,” Commanders head coach Dan Quinn said. “That’s a difficult play. Is it out of bounds? Is it not? I was nervous about it, that’s one of the ones where you hold your breath.”

Every kickoff returner needs to know that rule, but knowing the rule is easier than having the quick-thinking ability to do what McCaffrey did, in the fourth quarter with the game on the line. It was among the smartest football plays you’ll see.

#2699. Bruce Arians says he wants to be a head coach in the NFL next season

Bruce Arians is thinking about coming out of retirement. Again.

Arians told Jordan Schultz that when he announced his retirement from the Buccaneers in March of 2022, it was because of health problems that have since been resolved, and he now wants to coach again.

“I had torn my Achilles early in that season, and I was wearing these prosthetic high heels, and it threw my back out, and I couldn’t stand on the sideline for four hours anymore without a lot of pain,” Arians said. “I was also monitoring an aneurysm on my heart, so I had some health issues. We did everything we thought we could do in Tampa after winning the Super Bowl, trying to get two, and then it was time to give it to Todd [Bowles]. Now that I’m all healthy again, I got the itch again. So, we’ll see.”

If Arians does come back next year, he’ll be the oldest head coach in NFL history. That distinction currently belongs to Pete Carroll, who was 74 when he coached the Raiders last season. Arians will turn 75 next season.

Arians’ first retirement announcement came from the Steelers after they did not renew his contract as their offensive coordinator following the 2011 season, but Arians later said he was forced out and didn’t want to retire. He then took a job as offensive coordinator of the Colts in 2012, and was their interim head coach for most of that season while Chuck Pagano battled leukemia. Arians coached so well that he was named the NFL’s Coach of the Year.

Once Pagano returned to the Colts, Arians became head coach of the Cardinals, and he won a second Coach of the Year award. He announced his retirement following the 2017 season, after five years as head coach of the Cardinals.

But in 2019 he came out of retirement to become head coach of the Buccaneers. He won a Super Bowl in Tampa Bay, then retired after three seasons. Arians thought that was it, but he said that his son is now coaching high school football, and in talking to his son about the job he realized how much he misses it himself.

“Another fire got lit,” Arians said. “I had no desire to go back, and I was still fighting some health issues, but now after the open heart surgery I’ve got so much more energy, it’s amazing.”

Arians may find, like Bill Belichick before him, that all the accomplishments in the world don’t guarantee an NFL head-coaching job. Or perhaps he’ll convince some owner to give the oldest coach ever a chance to do what he’s done three times before, and turn a franchise around.

#2695. Buccaneers have more rushing yards than passing yards, a rare feat in today's NFL

With the 2026 NFL season at the midway point, one of the bigger statistical oddities belongs to the Buccaneers, who are the only team in the league with more rushing yards than passing yards.

Through nine games, the Buccaneers have 1,475 rushing yards and 1,277 passing yards. Every other team has gained more yardage passing than running, and no other team is even close to having more rushing than passing yards.

The last time an NFL team finished a season with more rushing yards than passing yards was 2022, when the Bears finished with an NFL-high 3,014 rushing yards and an NFL-low 2,219 passing yards. That Bears team was led by Justin Fields, who rushed for 1,143 yards himself, but netted just 1,883 passing yards. With running back David Montgomery chipping in 801 rushing yards and Khalil Herbert gaining 731, the Bears were a team that could run effectively but couldn’t pass for anything.

The Buccaneers’ yardage totals come from some fairly unique circumstances. Baker Mayfield has played some of the worst football of his career when healthy, and he was also injured and missed three games, replaced by undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels. That has led the Bucs to rely more on their running game. And the weather contributed a huge portion of the Buccaneers’ run-pass yardage differential in Week 8, when the Bucs gained 322 yards rushing and minus-2 yards passing in a downpour against the Falcons.

Despite their one-dimensional offense, the Buccaneers are still playoff contenders, thanks to the NFC South’s status as the worst division in football. It won’t be surprising if there’s a playoff game in Tampa in January. If that happens, Bucs fans may be praying for another downpour.

#2693. Man United Poaches Pochettino From U.S. Soccer for $10M

Mauricio Pochettino is leaving the U.S. Men's National Team to become head coach at Manchester United, the federation and club confirmed on Friday.

The Premier League club will pay U.S. Soccer $10 million for Pochettino's release clause, and about $2 million for his assistants.

Pochettino will still coach the USMNT for its Saturday and Tuesday matches against Haiti in the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals. The Premier League returns from an international break on Nov. 21, with Manchester United heading to an away match against Liverpool at Anfield on Nov. 22.

U.S. Soccer hired the Argentine in 2024 after stops at Tottenham Hotspur, Paris Saint-Germain, and Chelsea. He won a French title with PSG and took Tottenham to a Champions League final.

Hedge fund billionaire Ken Griffin covered a large portion of his first $6 million annual salary. Griffin, ironically, helped the Glazer family take over United in 2005; the Glazers also own the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Pochettino led the U.S. Men's National Team during the 2026 World Cup on home soil, breathing new life into the young squad and its style of play. Yet the U.S. saw another Round of 16 exit following an embarrassing 4–1 loss to Belgium in Seattle.

The federation and Pochettino announced they had agreed to a contract extension for another World Cup cycle in August, with a contract again primarily funded by Griffin.

U.S. Soccer CEO JT Batson said in a statement that Pochettino "left a lasting mark" on the federation.

"He and his staff raised standards, strengthened our culture and created clearer connections from the Youth National Teams to the senior team," Batson said. "Those changes are now embedded in how we operate, and we will keep building on them as we pursue sustained success on the world stage."

United fired head coach Michael Carrick on Thursday, a club legend who came back to coach in January. He led United to a third-place finish in the Premier League last season to earn Champions League qualification.

This season, United has taken a nosedive. The club is the league's only team with one win through 10 matches, and entered the relegation zone last weekend at 18th place in the table.

Pochettino emerged as the potential favorite for the United job even before Carrick's firing, and United made contact with U.S. Soccer about the coach on Wednesday.

The Argentine said in a statement: "The opportunity to represent the USA crest was one of the greatest honors of my career." He is set to face the media on Friday morning.

#2692. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2690. NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Patriots in Week 10

The Detroit Lions (6-2) and New England Patriots (5-4) will face off in a Week 10 interconference battle in Munich, Germany.

"We understand the challenge here," Lions coach Dan Campbell said of the Patriots. "It's a very good team. It's a competitive team. They're going to clean up a lot of things, and we've got to be ready to go."

This week's prediction preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, who currently have the Lions listed at +1600 to win this year's Super Bowl and are currently 2.5-point favorites in Week 10. Let's take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will earn a victory over the Patriots in this week's Honolulu Blueprint.

For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 10 preview: Breaking down the Patriots' offensive and defensive schemes.

The Lions and Patriots both have old-school coaches who are both direct or indirect descendants of the Bill Parcells coaching tree. And as you might expect, like Parcells, both coaches prioritize controlling the trenches by establishing the run on offense and stopping the run on defense.

By the numbers, the Patriots' run defense looks strong. They're 10th in DVOA run defense, ninth in rush yards allowed per game (96.7) and per play (3.9), fifth in EPA per rush (-0.12), and third in yards before contact (0.57). Their success ties to a strong interior defensive line that can stuff the run in two- and three-down sets, featuring Milton Williams, Christian Barramore, and former Lion Corey Durden. It's tough to find room up the gut.

Complicating things even further is how the Patriots deploy the blitz. Entering this game, the Patriots blitz 40.1% of the time (6th most in the NFL), and most of those blitzes come from their linebackers and come straight down the pipe—stressing the A and B gaps.

However, teams run outside on Patriots 53.8% of the time (10th highest rate) because their EDGE players are more skilled as pass rushers and can be overwhelmed in the run game. Their vulnerability shows up most in explosive plays. Currently, the Patriots allow an explosive run on 10.9% of rushing attempts (20th), have allowed 22 rushes over 10 yards this season, and average 3.31 yards allowed after contact (24th).

When we flip to the Lions' rushing attack, we can see how they match up with the Patriots' weaknesses. The Lions run the ball on the edges 55.7% of the time (7th), lead the NFL in explosive run plays (16.5% of the time), have 33 rushes of 10+ yards (3rd), and average 3.15 yards after contact (10th).

If the Patriots blitz and the Lions attack the edge, Jahmyr Gibbs will have a chance to eat.

The Patriots' defensive line is built to stop the run up the middle, create pressure off the edge and with blitzing linebackers, then deploy their secondary in nickel sets 77.7% of the time (2nd most in the NFL) and run man coverage out of it 36% of the time (2nd).

While chunk yards on the ground will certainly soften the Patriots' defense, Lions quarterback Jared Goff will likely be the key to winning this game because he matches up so well with their coverage scheme. This season, Goff has an EPA of 40.57 vs. nickel defenses (2nd highest in the NFL), a per-play EPA of 0.23 vs. nickel (4th), and a per-play EPA of 0.36 vs. man coverage (3rd).

What makes it worse for the Patriots is that their coverage has been exposed in recent weeks, especially by NFC North teams. Last week against the Packers, the Patriots surrendered 372 passing yards to Jordan Love, and 308 to Bears QB Caleb Williams two weeks prior. Those struggles have shown up in their EPA numbers, too. On the season, the Patriots allow a per-pass play EPA of 0.07 (26th), but over the past four weeks, that number has plummeted to 0.35 (31st)

Goff's key will be efficiency with short routes and a willingness to test them deep. When the Patriots are in off coverage, use the space against them. When they blitz, having quick-hitter answers in the vacated space behind them will lead to yards after catch (YAC). Then, when success comes underneath with Amon-Ra St. Brown and Sam LaPorta, test them with deep shots to Jameson Williams.

As mentioned earlier, the Patriots want to control the game on the ground, but their results haven't matched their dedication. The Patriots run the ball on 46% of offensive plays (10th most) and gain 119.9 yards per game (10th), but their per-play efficiency is more middle-of-the-road.

As a team, they average 4.2 yards per rush (14th), but only Drake Maye and RB3 Corey Kiner average above 4.0 yards per carry; RB1 Rhamondre Stevenson and RB2 TreVeyon Henderson average 3.9 yards per carry. We see similar results in EPA and success rate. The team's EPA per run is -0.02 (11th), while Stevenson (-0.06) and Henderson (-0.28) fall below the average. The team's rushing success rate is 41.8% (14th), while Stevenson is close at 40.2, but Henderson is well below at 34.6%.

The high volume of run plays can make a middle-of-the-road rushing attack look better than it is, but the real catalyst skewing the numbers is quarterback Drake Maye's mobility. Maye has carried the ball 47 times through nine games, averages 4.7 yards per carry, has a per-play rushing EPA of +0.40, and a 51.1% success rate.

Aside from a poor first quarter against Bills QB Josh Allen in Week 2 (when he gained 40 of his 69 rushing yards that day), the Lions defense has done a good job handling mobile quarterbacks this season. Vikings Kyler Murray gained 35 yards in Week 8, but no other quarterback has rushed for 20 yards against the Lions defense: Jacoby Brissett had 19 yards, Geno Smith (12), Tyler Shough (8), Malik Willis (7, groin injury), and Bryce Young (3) were all held under 20 rushing yards.

Defenses have deployed a spy on Maye situationally, and I expect the Lions to do the same in this game.

The Patriots offensive line has dealt with several injuries this season, and they've struggled to keep pressure at bay. Entering this game, they've allowed 141 pressures (28th) and a 42.9% pressure rate (31st). Maye has done a nice job handling the extra pressure for the most part, only taking 20 sacks (17th) with a 6.6% sack rate (18th), but it has led to him making some poor choices with the football; he is currently tied for the most interceptions in the NFL with 11.

So where are the weaknesses in the line? Right up the middle.

New England lost both starting guards—Alijah Vera-Tucker and Mike Onwenu—to injured reserve. Backup Greg Van Roten was injured in the one game he started, landed on injured reserve, and has only recently opened his injury evaluation window. Backup center Ben Brown was then called up to shift to guard, but he's been dealing with an injury and has been ruled out for this game. Finally, Walter Rouse has been supplementing/rotating with Brown at left guard, but he is currently in concussion protocol.

Heading into this game, Matt Pryor has started at right guard the last three games and is expected to maintain that role, but left guard is still up in the air. The Patriots likely need Rouse to clear concussion protocol or Van Roten to be activated from injured reserve and step into a starting role.

Regardless of where they land at left guard, they'll have the unenviable task of trying to block Alim McNeill.

McNeill has been a monster this season, as teams have had to deal with the totality of the Lions defensive line. Most teams have focused heavily on Aidan Hutchinson, but the developmental progression of Tyleik Williams, a wonderful rookie season for Skyler Gill-Howard, the steady veteran presence of DJ Wonnum, and the recent emergence of rookie Derrick Moore have allowed McNeill to flourish even more.

Through eight games, according to the Lions PR, McNeill is:

McNeill taking advantage of the reserve guards could be a huge factor in this game. If the Lions rush four and drop seven, and the Patriots need to keep players in for Hutchinson and McNeill, Maye will have fewer targets and a muddied back-seven to sort through.

Both De'Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle took a moment out of their warm up to participate. The results…were not good. Fortunately the hoops in the United Center were larger and more fitting for the Spurs star guards.

As it turned out, the Bulls were feeling themselves in the first half, shooting over 80% from beyond the arc giving the Spurs a 21-point deficit. Chicago did regress to the mean for the remaining minutes losing their lead and allowing the Spurs to complete a their road trip with four wins. The Spurs winning streak is now at ten games as they head home to host the Golden State Warriors in Emirates Cup competition.

#2685. ‘Things I think’: Giants have themselves to blame for squandered opportunity

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — You wanted them to, of course. Did you really think, though, that the New York Giants were just going to waltz to the NFC East title without things getting interesting?

The Giants made things interesting, and much more convoluted, by losing to the Washington Commanders on Thursday and missing an opportunity to take firm control of the division.

The 5-3-1 Giants are still in first place, and will remain there through the weekend no matter how the second-place Dallas Cowboys fare on Sunday when they host the 7-1 San Francisco 49ers.

Their path to a first division title since the 2011 Super Bowl season is now much more difficult, and uncertain. If the Cowboys can upset the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday, they will be 5-5, just 1.5 games behind the Giants with eight weeks left in the season. The Commanders are now 3-5-1, and with a tiebreaker advantage over the Giants should also feel like their season is very much alive.

Giants head coach John Harbaugh called the loss "disappointing", a word he used multiple times in his post-game press conference. His tone, though, was meant to remind that the Giants had not suddenly turned into the Titanic.

"It's a missed opportunity, but like I told the guys, it would have been great to win the game, but it doesn't change our goals or our opportunity going forward," head coach John Harbaugh said after the game. "So, it's a tough loss. It's the National Football League. You're going to lose some games. And everybody in this league is good. The Commanders are good. Everybody's good. So, I mean, we have a really good team coming in herenext Sunday [the Jacksonville Jaguars]. A team that we can beat, so, we've just got to get back to work.

"It's disappointing, yeah. I mean, I think that's the best word. It's just disappointing, We worked hard for this, and we put a hard week in. And we were prepared. The guys came out with, I thought, tremendous energy. We played very hard. Plays were made. Plays were missed. But it wasn't good enough to win the game. And that's the disappointment of it. So it's disappointing, but you can't let it bring you down. That's why I said what I said about our spirit. Our spirit's going to be fine. We're going to be good. We're not going to curl up. We're going to come out fighting."

In his 19th season as a head coach, it was clear that Harbaugh wanted to project an image of calm amidst the storm.

"It would have been nice to open up a lead in the division. We didn't open it up as much as we could have if we had got the win. We've got a lot of tough games. What do we have, seven games left? [It's actually eight] So it's going to be seven dogfights. That's what it's going to be," Harbaugh said. "It's [the] National Football League. I'd like to say we're going to win all seven of them. But it's probably not very likely. You're probably not going to be putting any money down on that.

"So we've got to win enough. And this was one that got away. We've got to find a way to get the next one. And the next one after that. And the next one after that. And get as many as we need to win the division. That's what we've got to find a way to do. So just try to keep it in perspective is very important."

"This game would have obviously put us in a great lead in the division, but we're not dead," fullback Patrick Ricard said. "This division can still be won."

"This would have obviously helped us to get the division sooner, but that's still well in our grasp," said center Bryan Hudson.

That is kind of what this game felt like. From the beginning things did not go according to plan.

The Giants, somehow, managed to possess the ball in Washington territory six times without coming up with a point. Let's go through the litany of miscues and missed chances.

They surprisingly chose to take the ball after winning the pre-game coin toss. They drove to the Commanders' 37-yard line, but an Isaiah Likely drop ended the drive. Rather than go for it or try a 55-yard field goal, the Giants punted.

The Giants second drive stalled at the Washington 15-yard line, and Dominic Zvada [more on him later] missed a 33-yard field goal.

In the third quarter, the Giants reached the Washington 19-yard line only to have Malik Nabers fumble the ball away after catching a short pass.

On their first possession of the fourth quarter, the Giants punted on fourth-and-3 from the Washington 46-yard line. That came after a third-down drop by Theo Johnson, and analytics disagreed with Harbaugh's decision:

Honestly, so did I. I would rather have seen the Giants go for it there, especially trailing. My preference? Run the ball on third down and then go for it on fourth if you don't make the first down. It seemed clear from the play call, though, that Harbaugh did not see that spot as two-down, fo-for-it territory.

The Giants had two chances to ice the game in the final 5:27 after interceptions by safeties Jevon Holland at the Giants' 2-yard line and Ar'Darius Washington at the Commanders' 46-yard line. They could not generate a single first down on either occasion.

Washington coach Dan Quinn successfully challenged a Jameis Winston tush push that was initially ruled a first down on the first possession, forcing a Giants punt. The Giants caught a bad break to open that drive when Holland was ruled down at the 2-yard line after his interception, rather than in the end zone. A touchback would have given the Giants the ball at the 20-yard line.

On the second one, J.J. McCarthy was dropped for a loss on a designed quarterback run on third-and-3 from the Commanders' 39-yard line.

Instead of pretty much being able to run out the clock, the Giants punted. Jordan Stout exacerbated the failure with a terrible 12-yard punt, his first bad punt as a Giant.

On their final desperation drive, the Giants got to Washington's 48-yard line before a McCarthy deep pass intended for Nabers was intercepted.

After the Giants took a 10-7 lead with 2:35 left in the half, the Giants allowed Washington to run out the rest of the half with a nine-play, 67-yard drive that ended with a 1-yard touchdown pass to Ben Sinnott, giving the Commanders a 14-7 halftime lead.

The Giants' pass rush was virtually non-existent. They got one sacks and two hits on Jayden Daniels.

On their final drive, Washington went 71 yards for the game-winning score in just three plays and :49 seconds.

Zvada is now just 17 of 23 (73.9%) after Thursday night's miss, which was from extra-point distance. Misses by Zvada in both Washington games (three in Week 5) have proven costly.

After the game, Harbaugh tried to remain supportive of his rookie kicker.

"We're confident. You can't, as soon as a guy doesn't make a play, start firing people left and right. Especially your kicker who's a rookie," Harbaugh said. "So, I'm confident he's going to become a good kicker. I mean, at some point in time, if it doesn't happen, it doesn't happen. But I'm not going to panic halfway through the season when a guy's made a bunch of kicks, if that's what you're inferring we should be doing.

"So, I mean, we're just not going to knee jerk it like that. He's going to make kicks. He's going to make a lot of kicks. I believe in him. I think he's really good and really talented. We're going to give him an opportunity to do it, and it's up to him to do it.

At some point, though, it's not a knee-jerk reaction. Harbaugh lost his job in Baltimore last season in part because rookie placekicker Tyler Loop missed a field goal that would have put the Ravens into the playoffs.

As much as the Giants believe in Zvada's talent, you can argue that he has now cost them chances to win two games. How long can the Giants be patient?
