#2683. James Harden admits to being ‘James Harden’

Thirty-two points on 14 shots in a much-needed Cleveland Cavaliers win over the New York Knicks was a good reminder of who James Harden is. And in case there was still any confusion, the former MVP made sure to clear everything up afterward.

"My name is James Harden. I used to score a lot of points," Harden told reporters Wednesday evening.

That clarification was needed based on how Harden's first 11 outings had gone. He entered Wednesday's game in New York averaging an uncharacteristic 15.3 points per game, shooting a dreadful 36.4% from the field. Harden has been a step slow and unable to create space off the dribble.

There's a downstream effect to Harden not being able to score. The passing lanes dry up when defenders don't have to help cut off his drives. This has left him as an inefficient scorer and inept playmaker at the start of the season.

Wednesday, Harden showed that he still has the talent to be a dynamic scoring guard. He got the outside shot working in the second quarter, and then expanded his game from there. Defenders had to overplay him on the perimeter, which allowed him to attack inside. He used that to his advantage to score nine points in the fourth quarter, which included two finishes inside the paint.

In short, he was the Harden we've seen wreck defenses for over a decade and a half, not the one that we saw in the first 11 games this season.

Anything bought from the links helps support Fear the Sword. You can buy the comfortable Cavs hoodie HERE. You can also shop all of Homage's Cavs gear HERE.

The Cavs would be a championship contender if they could guarantee performances like this from Harden in the playoffs.

Being able to score and playmake at this level would mean teams couldn't load up to stop Donovan Mitchell, and it would create easy scoring opportunities for Jarrett Allen and Evan Mobley inside. But you can't ensure this version of Harden on a nightly basis, or even for big games he gets up for. Age catches up to every player, especially a 37-year-old like Harden who has played nearly 50,000 minutes in his 18-year career.

Instead of counting on Harden to play as he did in his prime, he's trying to find other ways to adapt his game to his current situation.

"I just focus on myself, things I need to do, and try to get in really good shape and learn my teammates and learn how to play a different brand of basketball, because I'm not the same fast person that I was like five or six years ago," Harden said.

Harden is still playing his way into shape, admitting that he wasn't as young as he used to be, so he "can't just be ready" at the start of the season. It takes a "bit of time to get adjusted to the speed, the pace, all of the above." But even when he does get back up to speed, the explosiveness isn't there for him to be the guy he was with the Houston Rockets.

Instead, Harden will need to find different ways to impact winning in this new reality he finds himself in. If someone can make that adjustment, it's a player as skilled and as smart as Harden. That adjustment won't happen overnight. There will undoubtedly be more lows like we saw in the embarrassing loss to the Charlotte Hornets earlier this week, but the Cavs are more than willing to endure those games if it means Harden can eventually find his way. Because in the end, the Cavaliers' hopes and dreams for this season and the next two depend on Harden putting the pieces together.

"Now I still score points, but I'm finding other ways to impact the game as well," Harden said. "And I think that's what people probably don't understand."

#2682. Arsenal wants to sign Barcelona midfielder in January

Arsenal already have a midfield packed with quality, yet the Gunners are reportedly looking to add another player to their squad in the next transfer window. Martin Zubimendi has struggled to secure regular playing time, highlighting the level of competition currently facing players in that department.

Their midfield is already among the strongest in Europe and continues to deliver impressive performances in matches. Arsenal have enough quality to remain competitive without further additions, but the club are determined not to become complacent and want to keep improving their squad.

That ambition has reportedly led them to consider Frenkie de Jong, who is regarded as one of the finest midfielders of his generation. The Dutchman has considerable experience at the highest level and could provide another quality option for Mikel Arteta.

De Jong has been at Barcelona since leaving his boyhood club, Ajax. The Catalan side has previously shown little interest in selling him, but their current ability to perform without him could make his future a subject of discussion.

#2680. Buccaneers have more rushing yards than passing yards, a rare feat in today's NFL

With the 2026 NFL season at the midway point, one of the bigger statistical oddities belongs to the Buccaneers, who are the only team in the league with more rushing yards than passing yards.

Through nine games, the Buccaneers have 1,475 rushing yards and 1,277 passing yards. Every other team has gained more yardage passing than running, and no other team is even close to having more rushing than passing yards.

The last time an NFL team finished a season with more rushing yards than passing yards was 2022, when the Bears finished with an NFL-high 3,014 rushing yards and an NFL-low 2,219 passing yards. That Bears team was led by Justin Fields, who rushed for 1,143 yards himself, but netted just 1,883 passing yards. With running back David Montgomery chipping in 801 rushing yards and Khalil Herbert gaining 731, the Bears were a team that could run effectively but couldn't pass for anything.

The Buccaneers' yardage totals come from some fairly unique circumstances. Baker Mayfield has played some of the worst football of his career when healthy, and he was also injured and missed three games, replaced by undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels. That has led the Bucs to rely more on their running game. And the weather contributed a huge portion of the Buccaneers' run-pass yardage differential in Week 8, when the Bucs gained 322 yards rushing and minus-2 yards passing in a downpour against the Falcons.

Despite their one-dimensional offense, the Buccaneers are still playoff contenders, thanks to the NFC South's status as the worst division in football. It won't be surprising if there's a playoff game in Tampa in January. If that happens, Bucs fans may be praying for another downpour.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2678. Real Madrid’s Arda Guler reveals private conversation with Kevin De Bruyne after wonder goal vs Belgium: ‘He told me he follows my matches’

Arda Guler delivered one of the standout moments of Turkiye's 2-1 defeat to Belgium on November 12, producing a sensational free kick that left goalkeeper Senne Lammens with little chance.

The Real Madrid midfielder opened the scoring in the 20th minute of their UEFA Nations League meeting, but Belgium responded through Kevin De Bruyne and Charles De Ketelaere to claim victory.

The result was disappointing for Turkiye, but Guler's performance attracted attention beyond the scoreline.

De Bruyne was among those impressed by the 21-year-old, with the Belgian captain not only acknowledging his ability during the match but also personally praising him afterwards.

Guler's opening goal showed the quality that has made him such an exciting attacking midfielder.

From a central position outside the penalty area, he used his left foot to send the ball over Belgium's defensive wall and into the top-left corner.

Despite the difficult angle of the free-kick, Guler generated the necessary height, curve and precision to beat Lammens.

It was an outstanding individual moment, although Turkiye could not build on the advantage.

After the match, De Bruyne explained how Belgium approached the midfielder, suggesting that Turkiye's reliance on him had influenced their preparations.

"We kept a close eye on him at all times. His teammates should take more responsibility, because all the responsibility fell on Arda and we planned the match accordingly," De Bruyne admitted.

Guler later revealed that De Bruyne approached him after the final whistle and offered personal encouragement.

"After the match, as I was heading into the tunnel, he grabbed me and said: 'Hey, Guler, what a game you've played tonight!'

"I just smiled because it came from one of the best and most experienced midfielders," he said, as per MARCA.

"He told me he'd been following my matches and that he likes the way I control the midfield. He also told me that the free-kick I scored was incredible.

"He couldn't believe I'd managed to score because I was too far from the goal. Finally, he said goodbye, wishing me all the best and hoping I'd keep it up," Guler added.

"I thanked him for all his kind and warm comments about my talent. They mean a lot to me, as De Bruyne is an inspiration to this generation of footballers," he concluded.

In the aftermath of the World Series championship, Brewers manager Pat Murphy was caught on a hot mic talking to first baseman and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, who heads into free agency this winter off a career year.

Murphy's message? "You're gonna be a rich f---er, but just remember when you were on that horseshit Yankees team and you guys were all playing for yourself, just remember, say, 'this is the way we used to do it.'"

The comment, predictably, drew backlash from those who assumed Murphy was taking a shot at the Yankees. Bauers was on the 2023 Yankees, when they went 82-80 and missed the playoffs.

"I called Brian Cashman right away when I heard it got out," Murphy said on the New York Post's "The Show with Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman released on Tuesday. "I picked up a phone and called Brian right away, and had a good conversation. And the best I could try to explain that I wasn't talking about the 2026 Yankees.

"After every celebration, I'd shake his hand. I'd say, 'You rich so-and-so, you're going to leave us,' " Murphy explained. "We're not going to be able to pay you. You're going to leave us and you're going to forget all about how we did things. … I would just give him this rhetoric every time.

"I was just referring to the teams that have a lot of high-paid, long-contract players," Murphy said. "That sometimes it's harder to get all those guys together to play together. And I used the Yankees because I knew Jake was with them before. … I regret saying it, but that was Jake and I's humor behind the scenes and I got caught."

First off, dudes talking to dudes when they don't realize anyone else is listening lends itself to a lot of comments they don't necessarily mean or, perhaps more importantly, don't include the context of a longstanding relationship between a manager and his player. There isn't anything really out of line here in terms of the Yankees shot. Any Yankees fan would tell you they agree with Murphy's assessment of that team.

Where I do believe there's a problem is the insinuation that a player getting a huge payday means that he'll just start playing only for himself instead of doing things as a team. The Dodgers' high individual salaries certainly didn't stop them from winning two straight World Series titles.

Further, Bauers made $2.7 million last season, double his previous high. MLB players have a finite shelf life and need the money they make to stretch, if they're lucky, for generations. He's set to make exponentially more in free agency in his one big payday to hopefully set up his family for decades. Some might think it insensitive of Murphy to mock that a player might need to look out for himself and his family.

Then again, take note of Murphy's quote when he says that's just their sense of humor. We don't know their personal relationship because it is just that: personal. Unless Bauers signs elsewhere and comes out guns blazing against Murphy, this whole thing is probably just much ado about nothing. It would be pretty shocking if Cashman took particular offense, either.

#2674. In 49-second drive, Daniels & Diggs rescue the Commanders’ season - Daily Slop

Editor's note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

This season, Daniels and the Commanders failed to convert a 2-point conversion in the opener against the Philadelphia Eagles, and Daniels failed to throw the ball away in overtime, preventing a chance for a game-winning field goal. In their previous two losses, the Commanders' final drive ended in enemy territory.

Last week the Commanders failed to throw a pass into the end zone despite reaching the 32-yard line with 8 seconds remaining in a 20-13 loss to the Los Angeles Rams.

The losses led to Daniels being scrutinized and criticized. He told ESPN last week that he was "for sure" one of the most scrutinized quarterbacks in the NFL.

Daniels, though, said Thursday night that he had only one thought as he jogged onto the field for the final drive: "One play at a time."

Then he did what he hadn't done since his rookie season: lead a game-winning drive. He did so five times in 2024 en route to being named NFL offensive rookie of the year.

Follow the action and share every cheer, question and instant reaction with fellow fans on the SB Nation app.

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Here we go again. The Commanders had a habit of making close and winnable games self-inflicted disasters this season, and this one — a must-win Thursday night matchup with the NFC East-leading Giants — was on the verge of becoming the latest. Owner Josh Harris, who typically comes down to the Commanders' sideline to watch the final few minutes of games, again took his place for what could've been a slow, painful ending to his team's season.

When the clock hit two minutes, Washington came alive, much like it did a couple years ago when it took the NFL world by storm with its late-game heroics. In three drives — a defensive stand, a quick go-ahead touchdown and a game-sealing interception — the Commanders saved their season, and possibly their coach's job, to collect its biggest victory of the year, a 24-21 win over the Giants.

Daniels hit Stefon Diggs on a slant and the veteran wideout sprinted upfield, stopping inches before the goal line before turning and falling backward into the end zone, a la DeSean Jackson.

"Well, he probably could have waited some more," Quinn joked afterward.

It appeared that Daniels changed a signal on the play before the snap.

"Maybe, maybe not. You never know," Diggs said facetiously.

"Baby Kobe," Diggs said of Daniels. "He ain't flinch. He's going to be the same kind of player he is at the beginning of the game as he is at the end of the game."

Cornerback Rasul Douglas intercepted McCarthy on a deep, last-gasp attempt on third-and-10 with 34 seconds remaining.

Maybe it was wishful thinking, the last, mournful hope of a condemned team that hasn't been able to stay out of its own way much of this season. But they put together eight great minutes when they needed it most. The defense made three consecutive stops.

Daniels is, obviously, Washington's North Star. But Styles, the seventh pick overall, is rapidly growing into everything the Commanders hoped he'd be. The speed and force is obvious; the reads are coming, rapidly. On that third and two, Styles' film work, with a verbal assist from defensive tackle Charles Omenihu, indicated to him that the Giants were running a crack back run, with the tight end coming down the line to clear Washington's edge defender, and give McCarthy enough room to get the first down. Styles brushed off Giants center Bryan Hudson, shot the gap, tackled McCarthy for the loss, and gave the offense the ball back.

"I think, if you're just the player you are, the moment can never be too big," Styles said. "I think everyone understood in that moment, 'We've got to get a stop right here.' So guys just bowed up."

Guard Sam Cosmi looked at his teammates as Washington huddled up.

"I have moments where I look, and everybody's just locked in," Cosmi said. "You have that, like, glare, where you know it's game time, this is game time. We're going to make big plays."

Washington is still two games behind New York, with eight to play. But the Commanders, now, have the tiebreaker with the Giants, if it comes down to that. If it comes down to that, though, this already wild ride of a season will have taken an even crazier turn than what happened here Thursday, when the Commanders merely saved their season. For a couple of weeks, at least.

"Back-to-back interceptions, that's hard. It would've been really easy to lose the faith in that moment," Quinn said. "So, to see us battle and stay in the fight, that's what I was looking for. … There's plenty to do, guys. There's a lot to clean up, a lot to get better, but I'm definitely proud of the group.

"Man, that ain't goin' do nothing for me — still dwelling on that," Daniels said. "Everybody was on the sideline saying, 'The defense is giving you an opportunity to go out and win this game.' When I had the opportunity to go out there and win the game, take a deep breath, go out there and just capitalize on the moment."

Daniels completed 23 of 33 passes for 249 yards, three touchdowns and the two picks. On the other side of the ball, the defense ended the game with three consecutive stops.

"We needed that," Coach Dan Quinn said. "We needed every bit of it."

When the Commanders' offense had success, it tended to be when it went to a more up-tempo offense. Offensive coordinator David Blough put an emphasis on huddling more often and slowing down the pace this season, but it hasn't resulted in better results. He showed a willingness to adjust in the first half against the Giants.

On offense, errors like false starts and a delay of game were present but significantly reduced, as the Commanders committed just four penalties for 17 yards. The offensive line, which allowed four sacks against the Los Angeles Rams last week, allowed just one sack against a defense that had the third-highest blitz rate heading into Thursday's game.

That extra time allowed Daniels to work comfortably from the pocket, and he was efficient in the first half, completing 11 of 15 passes for 112 yards and a score. He completed four passes on the Commanders' second drive, hitting Chig Okonkwo with an 11-yard pass to get them into field goal range. The Giants responded with a 16-play, 72-yard touchdown drive, but Daniels responded by driving the offense 62 yards downfield in the closing minutes of the first half and connecting with Ben Sinnott for a one-yard touchdown on third-and-goal.

The Commanders have 11 days to prepare for their next matchup — a home game against the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday Night Football. Many of the Commanders' players labeled the Giants matchup as a must-win moment, and to their credit, they rose to the occasion.

Now, as the NFC East remains up for grabs, they are still in the hunt.

Next Gen Stats Insight for Commanders-Giants (via NFL Pro): Giants QB J.J. McCarthy was blitzed on 50% of his dropbacks in the second half against the Commanders, up from 28.6% in the first half. McCarthy completed 8 of 14 attempts against the blitz for 155 yards, a touchdown and an interception, recording career highs in completions and passing yards against the blitz in a game. After completing the 66-yard touchdown to Isaiah Likely, McCarthy went 0-for-3 with an interception against the Commanders' blitzes. Washington safety Nick Cross blitzed eight times, generating five pressures — a career best.

NFL Research: Jayden Daniels improved to 4-0-1 in his career versus the Giants. The win came thanks to his 32-yard touchdown pass to Stefon Diggs with 57 seconds left. It's the second game-winning TD Diggs has caught in his career with less than a minute remaining. The first was for the Vikings in the 2017 Divisional Round, famously known as the "Minneapolis Miracle."

What to make of Daniels' performance: Jayden Daniels overcame his first two interceptions of the season and delivered when Washington needed him most. His strength has been shaking off bad plays, and after consecutive series ended with picks in the fourth quarter, he led the go-ahead touchdown drive — with a 32-yard touchdown pass to Stefon Diggs. Daniels had been highly efficient prior to that pass. He has gotten better at keeping his eyes downfield, which resulted in one play for 30 yards.

Trend to watch: Washington's defense has forced six turnovers in its past three games combined. The Commanders now have 14 takeaways this season, but none was bigger than corner Rasul Douglas' interception to end the Giants' final possession. Washington forced a fumble in the red zone, preventing a potential field goal if nothing else.

Most surprising performance: Tight end Ben Sinnott. He entered with one reception on the season, a disappointing total for the 2024 second-round pick. He was supposed to get more action in Washington's new scheme this season, but it took until Week 10 for him to play a bigger role. He caught four passes for 42 yards and a touchdown against the Giants. — Keim

The Commanders kicker started the season 3-for-5 but is since 13-for-14. He opened the game's scoring with a 46-yard field goal in the second quarter, Stevens' lone attempt of the game.

The hurdle over a defender's outstretched arms is reason enough for the Commanders' third-year tight end to appear in the winners' column. But the career night is the real motivation. Sinnott came into the game with one catch for 6 yards this season but finished with four for 42 yards. He caught Daniels' touchdown pass with five seconds remaining in the first half as the quarterback fell to the ground.

The more severe issue for the Commanders has been the optics. In three games, there have been questionable – at best – game- and clock-management issues. As a head coach that does not call plays on either side of the ball, Quinn has to be more on top of it. He's dealing with a pair of first-time coordinators, to be fair … but he also hired them.

"Who Let The Dogs Out?" Indeed, Jameis. The backup QB also barked in an effort to get the Commanders to jump offside during a faux fourth-down cadence.

Thirty-seven of Nabers' 44 yards came on one play. His fumble in the third quarter killed a potential scoring drive and he could not come down with a jump ball in the red zone that would have set up a game-tying field goal that was instead intercepted by Rasul Douglas.

Rather than giving the ball to Skattebo, who had 78 yards on 18 carries, offensive coordinator Matt Nagy made the odd decision to call a McCarthy keeper from an empty backfield. The Commanders weren't fooled, as linebacker Sonny Styles burst through the line to drop McCarthy for a 2-yard loss while Skattebo watched from the sideline.

"It sucks, and I think part of it is I put myself in a situation last time we played these guys that kind of killed the trust in coach maybe a little bit, me giving up the ball last time," Skattebo said of his overtime fumble in Week 5. "And maybe he didn't want to give me the ball again. I don't know. I'm not going to say that was something he was thinking. But I would think that as well."

Punter Jordan Stout has been one of the Giants' most reliable players, but he picked an inopportune time for a shank. His 12-yard punt after McCarthy got stuffed gave the Commanders the ball at their own 29-yard line with 1:46 remaining.

Daniels wasted no time attacking cornerback Deonte Banks, who has improved greatly but still doesn't locate the ball consistently on deep passes. Banks got tangled up with Commanders wide receiver Treylon Burks to produce a 33-yard pass interference penalty. Washington was facing third-and-4 from the Giants' 32-yard line three plays later. Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson sent a blitz and Daniels responded by firing the ball to wide receiver Stefon Diggs on a quick slant. Diggs beat cornerback Dru Phillips, who took out Banks on his tackle attempt to clear the path for a walk-in touchdown with 57 seconds left.

[A] jump ball to wide receiver Malik Nabers was wrestled away by Douglas for a game-ending interception with 25 seconds remaining.

It was discouraging that Nabers couldn't come down with the 50-50 ball, especially after all of his demands to get the ball. But it was puzzling that the Giants were throwing jump balls in that spot since they had two timeouts and only needed to gain about 10 yards to get into range.

It would have been hard to have confidence in Dominic Zvada to make the long field goal after he missed a 33-yarder in the first quarter. That came after the Giants elected to punt from Washington's 37-yard line on their opening drive rather than attempting a 55-yard field goal.

You can't totally ignore those interceptions, largely because both came at inopportune times. Yet Daniels was dynamic. He ran the ball effectively, his accuracy continues to impress, and he's finding a way to move the ball without Terry McLaurin, his top receiver, who's out for the season.

Outside of Daniels' heroics, what else stood out for the Commanders?

Didn't see this one coming but … Ben Sinnott? The 2024 second-round pick entered this game with only one catch for 6 yards this season and hadn't totaled more than 36 receiving yards in a game in his career (he got that off one catch against the Giants last December). For the past few seasons, the production from the Commanders' tight ends has come courtesy of two players: Zach Ertz in 2024 and '25, and Chig Okonkwo this season.

But Sinnott finally showed more of what he's capable of in the pass game, catching four passes for 42 yards, including a 1-yard touchdown at the end of the first half. He also hurdled a defender on a 12-yard catch and caught a 24-yarder that helped set up Antonio Williams' 31-yard score in the third quarter.

[T]he comeback victory Thursday lifted Washington back into the edge of the NFC East race. The Commanders are just two games back of the division-leading Giants, and they own the edge over New York, whom they beat and tied.

At this point in Quinn's career, optics matter. The sense at team headquarters in Ashburn, Va., is that Commanders leadership would rather not make a coaching change midseason. But Quinn and his team can't make any more game-management gaffes.

The Washington Commanders have begun warming up at MetLife Stadium for their Week 10 matchup against the New York Giants

Harbaugh wants to be the coach of a dominating running team. The Giants as currently constituted are not that, yet he (and Matt Nagy) play it conservatively until they can't, and then they still do anyway.

The Giants get the ball back at the Washington 46 with 2:15 left, and Harbaugh tries to run out the clock as much as he can and make the Commanders use their timeouts while doing so. The problem is that he doesn't have Derrick Henry, Ronnie Stanley, and Tyler Linderbaum on this team. He has one of the worst run blocking offensive lines in the NFL and a good but not great running back. Skattebo gains 7 of the 10 yards he needs to effectively close out the game on first and second down, and then with third-and-3, rather than have J.J. McCarthy pass to get the first down and seal the win, the Giants dial up another of those J.J. RPOs that I think have not yet worked even once. McCarthy loses yards, the Giants punt from the Washington 39 (that's two punts from inside the opponent's 40), and predictably, Jayden Daniels drives the Commanders downfield for the winning score.

The 49ers have owned the Cowboys in the 21st century. Is Sunday's matchup shaping up to be yet another San Francisco victory or can Dallas rewrite the narrative on a classic NFC rivalry?

Blogging the Boys' RJ Ochoa (in what appears to be a reverse jinx?) and Bleeding Green Nation's Brandon Lee Gowton discuss Cowboys vs. 49ers ahead of Week 10 in a new "Mixtape Mini" clip, an NFC East Mixtape production.

#2671. Former Yankees, Rangers All-Star Mark Teixeira wins U.S. House seat in Texas

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Major League Baseball star Mark Teixeira is headed to Capitol Hill after winning the election for the United States House of Representatives seat in Texas' 21st district on Tuesday. Teixeira, the Republican candidate, beat Democrat Kristin Hook, a former federal scientist.

Teixeira will now take over the seat vacated by Republican Chip Roy, who didn't seek re-election.

"Together, we can build a better future for our families, our neighbors, and every community across Texas 21," Teixeira said in a statement. "I'm excited to get to work. I will be praying for all of you and for the future of this great nation. God bless Texas, and God bless America."

He was a rare win for the GOP in Texas on Tuesday, as Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the gubernatorial race and Democrat James Talarico flipped the Senate seat.

Teixeira, 46, was born and raised in Maryland before attending Georgia Tech as a big-time prospect. He was selected fifth overall in the first round of the 2001 Draft by the Rangers. He then came up through the Rangers' system and spent the first four and a half seasons of his career with the ballclub. He was traded to the Braves in 2007, then to the Angels in 2008 before signing a long-term free agent deal with the Yankees prior to the 2009 season. He finished his career with the Yankees.

In parts of 14 seasons, Teixeira hit .268/.360/.509 (126 OPS+) with 409 home runs, 1,298 RBI, five Gold Gloves, three All-Star Games, three Silver Sluggers and a World Series ring.

Teixeira is one of several familiar sports faces up for election on Tuesday. Former college football coach Tommy Tuberville won the Alabama gubernatorial race and former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya lost the Minnesota Senate race.

#2668. MLB rumors: The only Oriole not on the trading block, Rays' Drew Rasmussen plan and Astros add to manager hunt

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Brewers have now been World Series champions for just one week (minus a few hours) and they should still be basking in the glory for quite a while. As the offseason marches on, the next big date will be Nov. 17, when decisions on qualifying offers are due from the eight players who received one.

In the meantime, the rumor mill should be ever-so-slowly churning. We'll round it up here.

The Houston Astros moved on from general manager Dana Brown in August and fired manager Joe Espada after the 2026 season. Newly hired general manager Randy Flores is now tasked with landing a new dugout boss, and a three-time MVP and future Hall of Famer is in the mix. The Astros will interview Albert Pujols for the manager job this week, per The Athletic.

Pujols has long made it known that he desires to be an MLB manager. He recently interviewed for vacancies with the Padres and Angels (both last offseason) and he also managed the Dominican Republic in the World Baseball Classic this past spring. It should be further noted that Pujols is in the fourth year of a 10-year, $100 personal services contract with the Angels that was part of the mega-deal he signed with them as a player prior to the 2012 season as a player.

Other known candidates for the Astros manager job are Rangers bench coach Luis Urueta and Yankees bench coach (not to mention former Tigers and Angels manager) Brad Ausmus. Former Astros third baseman Morgan Ensberg, the manager of the Triple-A Rays affiliate Durham Bulls, will also interview this week, according to MLB.com.

The Orioles are willing to listen to trade offers on any player other than Pete Alonso as they seek both rotation and outfield help, according to The Baltimore Banner. The  Orioles reportedly aren't "actively shopping" any players, but they are looking for upgrades at starting pitcher and outfielder and realize one of the ways that could happen is via a trade.

Surely they wouldn't sell low on Gunnar Henderson, given his immense upside, so we can probably take him off the table unless some team makes it worth their while. There is a glut of infielders, though. With Alonso at first base and Henderson at short, they have Jackson Holliday, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, Jordan Westburg and Coby Mayo for two spots. Even using one of the four at designated hitter, it's easy to see where a deal could happen.

Westburg and Encarnacion-Strand are under team control through 2029 while Holliday is controlled through 2030 and Mayo through 2031.

The American League champion Rays recently picked up the $20 million club option on All-Star starting pitcher Drew Rasmussen. That would be a franchise-record salary for one player in a single season. It might seem odd to exercise an option and then deal a player to an outsider, but locking Rasmussen in for a one-year deal makes him an attractive trade candidate instead of just letting him walk in free agency, and this is how the Rays generally operate. We've seen it so many times: they get ahead of losing guys to free agency, sometimes even dealing them a year or two earlier. They've done it with Randy Arozarena, Isaac Paredes, Tyler Glasnow and even going back to franchise legends like David Price, Evan Longoria and Ben Zobrist.

The Rays right now are saying they intend to keep Rasmussen for 2027.

"Not a declarative this, that, whatever, but I can sit here very confidently and say that every intention right now is thinking about Ras anchoring our rotation and how to make this team better going into next year," club president Erik Neander said on Tuesday, via the Tampa Bay Times.

If they want to contend again next year, it sure seems like they need Rasmussen, with Nick Martinez and Freddy Peralta off to free agency. That leaves Rasmussen atop the rotation, followed by Shane McClanahan, Griffin Jax, Ryan Pepiot and a bunch of question marks. There are questions attached to McClanahan, Jax and Pepiot too.

#2666. Pirates Should Strengthen Their Bullpen with Taiwanese Right-Hander

The Pittsburgh Pirates must add to their bullpen this offseason. The free-agent market will offer plenty of options for the Pirates to reinforce their bullpen. However, one especially interesting option recently became available. Taiwanese right-hander Jyun Yue Tseng was recently posted by his Chinese Professional Baseball League team, the Fubon Guardians. He is now looking for an opportunity in MLB, and the Pirates should consider kicking the tires on Tseng.

Mason Montgomery is entrenched as the Pirates' closer, with trade deadline acquisition Luke Weaver and breakout right-hander Yohan Ramirez, who went from a depth reliever to a high-leverage arm, as his setup men. The rest of the 'pen, however, is largely unproven. Relievers including Carmen Mlodzinski, Evan Sisk, Lake Bachar, Noah Murdock, Brandon Eisert, and former top prospects Wilber Dotel and Antowne Kelly will all be vying for major league roster spots on the Pirates' pitching staff to open 2027. Enter Tseng?

Apr 22, 2026; Pittsburgh, PA, USA; A general overall view of Honus Wagner statue at PNC Park. The stadium is the home of the Pittsburgh Pirates. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images

Tseng finished up his sixth season in the CPBL. Although Baseball-Reference does not list how many innings the right-hander pitched, he allowed only nine earned runs and three home runs in 48 total appearances. He struck out 65 of the 199 batters he faced, while allowing just 13 free passes and 36 total hits. Tseng has served as the Guardians' closer since his debut in 2021, recording 91 saves over the last six seasons. 2026 was his best campaign yet.

What we do know is that Tseng pitched extremely well in the five seasons prior to 2026. From 2021 through 2025, the Taiwanese righty posted a 2.02 ERA, struck out 26% of opponents, and handed out a walk to 8.2% of opponents he faced. Tseng allowed just seven home runs as well.

Don't let Tseng's 5'8″, 149-pound frame fool you; he has some power on the mound. The right-hander works in the mid-to-upper-90s, having topped out at 99 MPH in the past. He appeared in two games for Team Chinese Taipei during the World Baseball Classic and averaged around 95 MPH with his fastball. His four-seamer showed above-average induced vertical break at 17.4 inches.

Aside from his four-seam fastball, FanGraphs states he throws a slurve. He also used an upper-80s cutter during this year's WBC. Tseng has flashed solid command over his entire arsenal. He posted his lowest single-season walk rate in 2026, and his career BB% in the CPBL is only 7.9%. Tseng has stuff that would translate to Major League Baseball.

The question is what sort of contract could Tseng land in MLB? Tseng just turned 25 this month. Previously, Yuki Matsui, who was a dominant closer in his respective Asian league, in his case, Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball League, signed a three-year contract worth $28 million guaranteed with the San Diego Padres.

Of course, there are some differences. 2024, Matsui's rookie year in MLB, he was 28 years old, with ten years of experience in NPB prior to signing with the Padres. He is also left-handed, compared to Tseng, who is a righty reliever. NPB is also considered the highest level of professional baseball in Asia, while CPBL is considered below both Japan's NPB and South Korea's Korean Baseball Organization (KBO).

Regardless, given his age, the Pirates could sign Tseng for multiple seasons. That is important, as Weaver is a free agent after the 2027 season, and Yohan Ramirez is a free agent after the 2028 campaign. Tseng may not immediately start his MLB career in a high-leverage role; however, he could certainly work his way into one after accumulating some experience in US baseball and acclimating himself to his new environment.

Tseng would certainly be a step up from Evan Sisk, Brandon Eisert, and Noah Murdock, and would allow the Pirates to use Wilber Dotel and Antwone Kelly as starters or long relievers. Depending on how the offseason goes, Mlodzinski may not be an option for the Pirates if they trade him. Even as a middle reliever, the Pirates could find plenty of use for Jyun Yue Tseng, and could slowly work him into higher leverage situations as the season goes on.

#2665. Biggest MLB offseason questions: How long will lockout last? Will we see a free agency frenzy?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Not so long ago, the Milwaukee Brewers were crowned World Series champions, and at the moment of the last out, the 2026-27 Major League offseason began. So let's talk about that.

The winter ahead is one shot through with uncertainty, as labor strife figures to roil the sport and perhaps even compromise the 2027 season. Those matters, vital as they are, won't be the only story, and we'll still have the familiar presences of free agency and trade talk to sustain us.

To set the scene for all that's ahead in advance of the 2027 campaign – good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – we're here to take a look at the five questions that will inform an offseason that's going to be quite unusual and – for good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – probably unforgettable. Let's explore those five queries right now …

The current collective bargaining agreement – or CBA, the accord that governs the working relationship between clubs/owners and players – is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 of this year. At that time, MLB owners are all but certain to lock out the players. That's a labor stoppage, and that means the offseason will be brought to a sudden halt. The lockout, the purpose of which is to preempt a players' strike, will last until a new CBA is agreed to. Agreeing to a new CBA will be no simple matter, and owners and their hireling, commissioner Rob Manfred, are pushing for a cap on team payrolls. The players, as represented by their union, the MLBPA, have never shown any willingness to agree to a cap-and-floor system. There are a lot of other issues to iron out, as the CBA is an all-encompassing document, but the fight over a cap will be what drags out the lockout.

The heart of the matter is whether the lockout will last long enough to push back, abbreviate, or – perish the thought – cancel entirely the 2027 season. The latter is the worst-case scenario and is highly unlikely, but it's a possibility, however remote. More of a threat is a 2027 season that doesn't span the usual 162 games.

We have a recent precedent to guide us. The last time the CBA was up for negotiation during the offseason of 2021-22, owners locked out the players for 99 days. That meant a shortened spring training by about two and a half weeks and forced the regular season calendar to be compressed, albeit while still preserving the 162-game docket. As such, we can say that if the lockout lasts beyond the middle of March 2027, then we'll likely lose regular-season games.

For further context, here's a brief history of modern labor stoppages in the sport:

Just two, the 1981 and 1994-95 player strikes, significantly compromised seasons. The 1994-95 stoppage cost us the 1994 World Series, and it took years for the sport to recover from the resulting fan disaffection.

As for the 2027 season, the worst-case scenario may not be the loss of the entire season but rather the loss of 60 games off the regular-season slate. Here's the explanation from our recent Lockout 101 piece:

"… [I]f the lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That matters because Manfred and the league hope to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation in 2028. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. This amounts to a major incentive, at least on the league side, to agree to a new CBA before June arrives."

Obviously, the hope is that the lockout doesn't even affect the spring training calendar, let alone cost us a major chunk of the regular season.

As noted, the big fight is over whether or not MLB will have a cap-and-floor structure moving forward, as is the case in the NFL, NBA, and NHL. Owners have tied every single proposal wrinkle to date to the players' acceptance of a cap. However, it remains highly unlikely, at least until further notice, that the union would ever agree to such a thing.

The other major issue is a likely restructuring of the revenue-sharing system. Specifically, the next CBA is highly likely to revise the system so that local broadcast revenues are shared much more evenly. Fortunately, there's already some common ground on this issue, and a reordering of that system would directly address the revenue disparities within MLB that are such a reliable source of consternation – and misinformation – without the grievous labor war that a continued cap push would force upon us.

Otherwise, some other key wrinkles and changes may come out of the wash. That list potentially includes:

This doesn't get into evergreen matters like an increase in the minimum salary, draft bonus pools, the qualifying offer system, active roster sizes, and so forth. There's a lot to sort out, to say the least. The expectation is that the next CBA is going to lead to sweeping changes to the sport starting in 2027 and, perhaps by design, growing over time. Even if there's no cap and floor, the economic structure of MLB is almost certain to look very different after this winter.

Overall, this is one of the weakest free agent classes in living memory, but there is elite superstar value to be found at the tip-top with back-to-back (for the moment) American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

Skubal, who turns 30 on Nov. 20, remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and he's going to be paid like it. The expectation is that he'll wind up signing the largest pitcher contract in MLB history and perhaps also fetch the highest-ever annual salary for a pitcher. It's not out of the question that Skubal's next contract could approach or even surpass $400 million in total value. At those rates, the incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers and the free-spending New York Mets are the consensus favorites. The Chicago Cubs are also reportedly heavily interested in Skubal, and surprise bidders are always possible. Other notable free agent names include Freddy Peralta, Michael King, Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trevor Rogers, Adrian Morejon, and Teruaki Sato. Our ranking of the top 50 2026-27 free agents has you covered.

The "when" of all this is more complicated thanks to the upcoming lockout detailed above. Will premium free agents and their representatives rush to find some stability in advance of the stoppage, during which no major-league transactions will be permitted, or will they decide that the long game will be better for their markets? It's possible that the biggest spenders on the team side will look to make moves early, as the barrel of the next CBA figures to be leveled directly at them and their abundant revenues. Or maybe the unknown will have a chilling effect on spending before we arrive at the lockout.

The past is not always prelude, but let's note that we saw a flurry of spending leading up to the lockout of 2021-22. Indeed, in November 2021, MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents prior to the lockout. The Texas Rangers alone guaranteed $500 million to a new middle infield – Corey Seager and Marcus Semien – before the lockout put an end to such things. In all, teams put ink to paper on five nine-figure contracts prior to the 2021-22 lockout.

The comparisons may not entirely hold since this upcoming CBA should bring about a much more drastic re-ordering of the sport than the current expiring CBA did. As such, teams may proceed cautiously given all the uncertainties. Or, as just mentioned, they may seek to get business done before the ways of doing business change entirely. We'll see soon enough. If we do see the dollars start flying before the lockout, then the upcoming Nov. 10-12 general managers meetings in Las Vegas may occasion the groundwork for all those deals.

Will a lackluster free agent class mean more headline-grabbing trades? That may indeed be answered in the affirmative this winter. Yes, the CBA uncertainty will have a bearing on trades, especially those that involve the assumption of major salary obligations, but big trades still figure to be a prominent part of this offseason.

It's of course impossible to know who's going to be dealt ahead of time, but some big names perhaps on the move this winter include Francisco Lindor, Mason Miller, Spencer Strider, Hunter Greene, Otto Lopez, Jeremy Peña, Ketel Marte, Jacob deGrom, and of course others. Paul Skenes? Almost certainly not, but you'll just as certainly hear his name bandied about.

Turning back to last lockout, it was mostly minor trades before the sport shut down. Yes, we'll see big ones this time around, but they may not happen until we have a new CBA in place and the lockout is over.

Let's make time for the losers, shall we? The teams that didn't make the postseason in 2026 and otherwise qualify will take part in the draft lottery, which is presently scheduled for Dec. 8. That lottery will determine which teams get the top six picks in the 2027 MLB Draft.

This year, 16 of the 18 non-playoff teams will be in the lottery. Non-playoff teams can be barred from the lottery if they've had lottery picks in two consecutive seasons. If a team is a revenue-sharing payor, then it can't be in the lottery in consecutive years. Those wrinkles this year mean that the San Francisco Giants and Pittsburgh Pirates will not be in the lottery and can't pick higher than 10th in the 2027 Draft.

Here's how the preliminary lottery odds look for those 16 teams in the mix, based on how they finished the 2026 season:

It's too soon to know which players will be in the mix for that top pick since the amateur seasons haven't begun yet. However, two early favorites to go No. 1 are University of Florida shortstop Brendan Lawson and Mississippi State left-hander Tomas Valinicius.

The Phillies will seek a left-handed setup man this offseason, reports The Athletic. Manager Don Mattingly's late-inning unit is all righties at the moment: Jonathan Bowlan, Caleb Kilian, Jhoan Duran, and Alex McFarlane.

The Yankees need almost an entirely new bullpen this offseason, and they have interest in re-signing setup man Paul Blackburn, according to the New York Daily News. New York tendered closer David Bednar the $23.15 million qualifying offer and seems likely to get him back, either on the QO or on a multi-year deal, but they will need to improve the setup crew regardless.

We ranked Blackburn as the No. 33 free agent this offseason. He had a terrific season with the Yankees in 2026, his first year as a full-time reliever. The Yankees have shown the ability to drum up quality relievers almost out of nowhere. They tend to let those guys leave as free agents, then build up someone else to replace them. This happened when Blackburn replaced Luke Weaver.

Among their list of wants this offseason, the Marlins will look to add to their rotation and bullpen, as well as a corner bat, reports the Miami Herald. There are opportunities to improve aplenty for the Marlins.

#2663. Which receivers did Rams add after Puka Nacua goes to IR?

With Puka Nacua going on IR the Los Angeles Rams added Brennan Presley and Tyler Scott. This is a bit of a surprise (maybe) as Sean McVay reported Nacua would avoid IR, but then went back on his own statement when it was revealed that Nacua would be going on IR to miss "extended time".

The Rams will find out who steps-up in Week 10 against the Arizona Cardinals. Will anyone step-up? There is an expectation that rookie CJ Daniels could get some run, and that's exciting for the young man, but I'll believe it when I see it.

The Rams need to earn a win on Sunday to get to 6-4 before their bye, and they likely need to get healthy to hope to beat the Green Bay Packers after their bye week. One thing at a time, starting with Arizona.

"Sean McVay and the Los Angeles Rams have provided further clarity on Puka Nacua. Their latest roster moves only add further details on a noteworthy day.

"LA Rams Roster Moves," the team posted on X on November 12, listing their transactions.

Signed to Active Roster from Practice Squad WR Brennan Presley

"We're not going to put him on IR, just because of some semantics with the roster and things like that," McVay told reporters on November 11. "But he still is going to be out for an extende period of time. It wasn't any sort of new information."

"It's been good for me," Daniels said of these last nine weeks. "Really just staying the course, just learning the playbook, each and every (receiver) position, and battling against the defense each and every day has definitely prepared me each and every week for whenever my number is called."

With wide receiver Puka Nacua expected to miss at least a month with MCL and PCL sprains and turf toe, and veteran Davante Adams still on Injured Reserve, and Jordan Whittington now on IR, Daniels' number is expected to be called this Sunday against the Cardinals at State Farm Stadium.

"He's going to get that," McVay said Monday, when asked what Daniels needs to show to get time on the field. "He's done a great job. I don't know that I could really say any areas of improvement until he gets truly his opportunity. With the way that he's worked consistently, the way that he shows up day in and day out. I think if you asked a lot of our DBs (defensive backs) about him, they give you a bunch of positive feedback because of the looks, the challenges. He has a lot of maturity for a young guy, like I've talked to you guys about. He is a guy that, no question about it, will get an opportunity to play more snaps moving forward."

"This is the first week where that view is really switching to they could very much miss the playoffs. They have a difficult schedule ahead and some real significant injuries. The only thing keeping them from a big fall right now is there is still potential to get those key guys back. If they can somehow weather the storm and get in, they could be decently healthy by the playoffs."

"After Puka Nacua went down with a knee injury and turf toe on Sunday, Sean McVay said the Los Angeles Rams would probably place him on injured reserve. Two days later, McVay pivoted and said the Rams weren't going to put him on IR due to roster semantics.

One day after that, the Rams announced that Nacua was placed on IR, changing their minds for the second time. Regardless, Nacua was always expected to miss at least a month, but there's a slight difference between putting him on IR and leaving him on the active roster because of the bye week.

Players who are put on IR must miss a minimum of four games, not four weeks. That means Nacua will be on IR for Weeks 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14, because Week 11 is a bye. So when is he eligible to return?"

#2662. Broncos' (projected) depth chart going into Week 10

Story update: After this post was scheduled, the Daiyan Henley trade fell through. View our original post below, but note that the Henley information is outdated.

The Denver Broncos have not released an updated depth chart going into their Week 10 bye, but coach Sean Payton rarely makes notable changes to the published depth chart anyway.

The Broncos made several roster moves last weekend, including placing defensive lineman Eyioma Uwazurike (shoulder) on injured reserve and activating wide receiver Pat Bryant (ankle) from IR to the 53-man roster. This week, Denver acquired linebacker Daiyan Henley in a trade and cut cornerback Sean Fresch to make room for him.

Those moves are not yet reflected on the team's published "unofficial" depth chart, so we're putting Henley in brackets in your projected depth chart this week.

With those notes in mind, here's a look at the official "unofficial" depth chart for the Broncos going into Week 10.

Jarrett Stidham is the primary backup quarterback, a role he has held since Sean Payton arrived in 2023. Sam Ehlinger has remained loyal to the team as QB3 despite drawing interest from other clubs.

Kage Casey is listed as the backup guard for both spots, but Alex Palczewski filled in when left guard Ben Powers was injured last season. Jonathon Cooper (felony assault case) has a trial by jury scheduled for March, but he was reinstated by the NFL ahead of Week 7 and is back in the team's starting lineup.

LB: Alex Singleton, [Daiyan Henley], Jordan Turner

LB: Justin Strnad, [Daiyan Henley], Karene Reid

Daiyan Henley instantly becomes the team's best cover linebacker, but he's not expected to start right away. Denver also has seventh-round draft pick Red Murdock providing additional depth on the practice squad.

Jahdae Barron and Kris Abrams-Draine did an excellent job stepping up while Pat Surtain and Riley Moss were sidelined earlier this season. PS2 and Moss have since returned from their injuries, and Denver's extremely deep at cornerback.

S: Talanoa Hufunga, JL Skinner, Tycen Anderson

Seventh-round draft pick Miles Scott and veteran Taylor Rapp are also available on the practice squad.

Marvin Mims is on pace for 977 all-purpose yards this season, which would be the lowest total of his career. Mims has topped 1,000 yards in each of his first three seasons. He also scored multiple touchdowns in each of his first three years, but has yet to score this fall.

#2660. Kane to present Ballon d'Or and smash English appearance record against Croatia

Harry Kane will present the Ballon d'Or to the England fans at Wembley Stadium tomorrow ahead of the game against Croatia.

The Bayern Munich star will also break the record for all-time England appearances which he currently shares with Peter Shilton.

“It's definitely up there [with the biggest achievements of my career],” said Kane, speaking in an interview with GOAL.com.

“To have it on the same day when he gets his all-time record for 126 matches. It’s a beautiful, beautiful occasion,” he concluded.

#2659. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2658. How Much Women’s College Flag Football Coaches Make

As girls flag football explodes at the youth and high school levels, NCAA institutions are adding varsity women's flag programs on a near-weekly basis.

Activity is still largely limited to Division II and III. But the NCAA's January 2027 vote to establish women's flag as a championship sport is expected to spur a new wave of adoption by major D-I schools. (Nebraska is the only traditional powerhouse with a varsity flag team so far.)

To gauge the sport's emerging labor market, Front Office Sports reviewed women's flag football coaching salaries at 10 schools across all three NCAA divisions, drawing on public records requests, active job postings, and conversations with coaches and athletic administrators.

Head coaching salaries varied by more than $100,000 across our sample, from $18,540 at D-III SUNY Geneseo to $155,000 at D-I Cal Poly. The average salary is $72,545. Position terms generally span one to five years.

Of the employment contracts obtained by FOS, Nebraska is the only school with a full-time assistant head coach. It's also the only school offering performance-based bonuses to its coaches, and it allows them to make money on outside activities, such as endorsements, with the athletic director's approval.

California Polytechnic State University–San Luis Obispo

$5,000 bonus if program wins a conference championship

$5,000 bonus if program qualifies for an NCAA Championship or equivalent national championship tournament

$10,000 bonus if program wins an NCAA Championship or equivalent national championship tournament

5% of base salary bonus if program wins a conference championship

5% of base salary bonus if program qualifies for an NCAA Championship or equivalent national championship tournament

In October, Nebraska athletic director Troy Dannen told Sports Business Journal that its 21-player women's flag program cost less than $1 million to launch, providing an early benchmark for other major schools looking to stand up their own teams.

"I've had a handful of Power Four schools reach out to me and ask questions," Jami Hagedorn, Nebraska's associate athletic director of financial reporting, tells FOS. She oversees the women's flag budget and hired its two inaugural coaches—twin-sister duo Liz and Katie Sowers—earlier this year. "They want to know what our startup costs were, what the big expenses were … we kind of are the market right now."

The Sowers sisters came to Lincoln from the NAIA's Ottawa University in Kansas, where they founded the women's flag program and led it to five consecutive national championships. Liz served as head coach and Katie as associate head coach, the same roles they now hold at Nebraska.

Hagedorn says their compensation was primarily determined by "looking internally at [Nebraska's] existing coaching salaries for similar women's sports." She adds that finding coaches with prior flag experience was a priority—a sentiment echoed in most of the 10 active head flag coaching job positions currently listed on the NCAA's job board.

"I didn't target many tackle football coaches when hiring, just because there are lots of nuances between the two sports," Hagedorn says. "I don't know that [tackle experience] 100% translates"."

With a professional flag league backed by the NFL and TMRW Sports set to launch in summer 2027 and flag making its Olympics debut in 2028, coaching jobs will grow, prompting a more competitive ecosystem—and, likely, higher salaries.

#2657. Group of retired MLB umpires, including Joe West, file lawsuit alleging they are owed more than $2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former MLB umpire Joe West is part of a group of five retired umpires who are suing their pension plan and alleging they have been underpaid by the plan, the Associated Press reports. West, along with Tom Hallion, Gerry Davis, Larry Vanover, and Jerry Layne, filed the suit in late September in federal court in New York.

The suit alleges that the five umpires have been underpaid by the pension plan by more than $2 million. According to the AP, the suit "was filed against the American Leagues and National Leagues of Professional Baseball Clubs Retirement Income Plan for Umpires and that entity's retirement committee." The five umpires claim their benefits were not calculated correctly and therefore should receive additional money.

West, 74, retired from umpiring in MLB in 2021 after umpiring more than 5,000 games at the highest level starting in 1976. The man they called "Cowboy Joe" umpired a record 5,460 games in all, was known as a colorful figure in the sport and sometimes even a source of controversy.

In 2021, West won more than $500,000 in damages as the result of a defamation suit against former MLB player Paul Lo Duca after Lo Duca alleged during a podcast that West would "open up the strike zone" for reliever Billy Wagner in exchange for driving one of Wagner's vintage cars.

West referenced his "history with lawsuits" on Thursday. From the AP:

West said that when he brought up the issue to the retirement committee, he was offered a relatively small sum. West said MLB senior vice president and chief employment counsel Steven Gonzalez told him: "If you don't like the number, sue us."

"Does Steve Gonzalez not know my history with dealing with lawsuits?" West said.

Like West, Davis also retired after the 2021 season while Hallion umpired through the 2022 season and Layne and Vanover stepped away after the 2024 campaign. The five sued as individuals and did not involve the umpires' union, their lawyer, Paul B. Holmes, said, per the AP.

A pretrial conference in the case is scheduled for Dec. 11.
